EXCUSING HIMSELF.—Mrs. Brown: "Did you pick up that tack I dropped on the floor." Brown; " Yea : but I didn't mean to." Touoisr (to highland sentry on a cold frosty morning) : "Sentry, are you cold with the kilt?" Sentry : " N a, bat I'm near kilt wi' the could." . . "How. is your wife getting on ?" "She's im- proving slowly. She is not well enough to attend to hr household duties yet, but yesterday she was ontphoppibg." WHY HE CUT HEW " What made you cut Lom- bard, Harry?" "Heard something about him, y'litiow. He sells things, you know. Actually tlirnii his own living." " Aw, flaw, that won't do, y'know. I'll cut him myself tomorrow, I'll cut him bad !y,".

"FINE country, Elypt, but what a heat! One day, under the Pyramids, I cooked some eggs in the sun." "Bless you, that's nothing to Zanzibar. There we cook onr eggs in the moonlight." Wxem (impatiently) : "This new dress doesn't fit well, I know." Husband: "What makes you think so?" Wife: "It's too comfortable." " Witax a polite an Mr. Geestrinit*, the vieliniat, appears to be V' " Indeed ? I hadn't noticed it.' "Oh, yes; bowing and scraping all the time." "DoN'T you find the people round here very sociable ?'4 asked Cobwigger of a new neighbour. "Yes, indeed, I do," was the hearty response. "Only a moment ftgo I met a beggar and he held out his hand to me." IT always bothers a Frenchman who is learning English tz: read one day that a murder has been committed, and the next day that the murderer has been committed. Beows to Jones: "I say, lend me half-a-crown until to-morrow. You see I changed my vest this morning.' Jones: sorry, but I've just invested my charge." IN TICE ALPS—Guide: "If the ladies will only stop talking, your honour may hear the roaring of the waterfall across the valley.'' IT is said that tramps will never work. And yet six of them dug their way out of a new Hamp- shire jail with a tenpenny nail. " Hem! Your verdict seems to be decidedly mixed." "Foreman : "Yes, your hon- our. It's in accordance with the evidence." HARD lArrs.—Mr. Winks (looking over the paper) : Cheap, Drug, and Co. are selling all sorts of patent medicines at half-plice." Mrs. Winks : "Just our luck ! There isn't anything the matter with any of us." "MIKE, did you ever catch frogs?" "Ye., sir." " What did you bait with ?" "Bate 'em with a shtick, sir." "JAXIC wee madly in love with Cora, and she told him if he would look at her straight in the eye, and tell her that be never loved another, she would marry him." "Di I he do it ?" "No ; he couldn't." "lie loved another, had he ?" "Oh, no ;he was cross eyed." , talking so much about?" Irish Vi. (facetiously) : "Only a drip of the crater, Molly."

A DsFINITioN AND EXAMPLlC.—Sconolmistresa : "Edward, give me the definition ot excavate." Edward: "Excavate, to hollow out.' School. mistress: "Give me a sentence containing the word." Edward: "I hit Bill, and he excavated." A BRIGHT boy is not always a polished boy. Fond mother: "Tummy darling, this is your birthday ! What would you like best to do? Tommy darling (after a moment's reflection): "I think I should enjoy seeing the baby spanked !" "Tits dying millionaire (feebly, but firmly)— "I tell you I'll get even with my graceless posterity !' The D ictor: "By disinheriting them ?" The dying miliionaire " 'Worse! make no will, io.nd let them fight it out with the lawyer." "WHICH do you love most, your papa or your _mamma ?" Little Coarlie : "I love papa most." Charlie's mother : "Why, Charlie, I am surprised at you; I thought you loved me must." Charlie "Can't help it, mamma; we men have to hold together."

Tuz QUEEN ANNE STYLE.—A gentlemen recently returned from a drive through the country towns of New York asserts that he has not very much objection to a cottage that is consistently Queen Anne aU through ; but he evinces a strong anti. pathy to those lieu:tee—and their name is legion— " Chat are Queen Anne in front, and Mary Anne at the back." Tftr reporter had just come in from a murder Case. It was a rainy day, and he had to cross a ploughed. field on foot. "I see," observed the chief editor, looking with much displeasure at his large and muddy boots, "you have brought the scene of the murder with you." "Yes," answered the reporter, apoiegetically, "I've got to have some ground for my story, you know., ' WHY SHE BLusultu.—Rev. Mr. Goodman (on his way home after making a pastoral call): I wonder what made Mlss Phlypp blush so furiously when I stroked her little sister's curls and quoted St. Paul's saying that "if woman have long hair it is a glory to her." Mrs. Goodman: Is it pos- sible, Avery, you have not heard of her engagement to that tall young man named Beard? Husrisxn : "My dear, the air is very damp to- night. You'd better wear your furs." Wife : "I have them ready." Husband : "And tie your boa on cluaely. A little exposure often leads to sore throat, and sore throat leads to diphtheria, a most dangerous disease. Wear your thick rubbers, too, and gool thick shoes and warm gloves; and, my love, I think you'd better wear a warm veil. One can't be too careful when one's life insurance

premium is in arres.rs, and yours is." His own religion was found in the Sermon on the bl.amt. Ccee,la and formularies were not to his likiug. Th.e ap)eal fortlie completion of the memorial to to_the late Charles Bradlaugh bas been_signed_by men of all social grades and every shade of feeling. Among the latest signatories are Lord Spencer, Lord Hobhouse, Lord Dunsany, Sir Edward Hart- land, Sir Algernon Borth wick, Sir George Trevely- an, Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild, Admiral Mime, and Mr. Arnold Morley.

The exposure of big residental estates for sale at the Auction Mart is becoming a matter of form only. No one expects them to be sold. The bidding for Stisted Hall, for instance, one of the finest estates in Essex, three thousand acres in extent, With a rent-roll of £3,000 a year, was started at £25,000, and ran up to £34,900, where it stopped. For Stagenhoe Park, near iiitchin, no more than £20,000 was offered, although £48,000 was refused tor it three years ago.

In these" tight" times as regards money, art in • this country would fare badly if it were not for the American and Australian millionaires who visit our shores. Mr. W. D'Arcy, who hails from "down under," is at present proving a valuable patron to Wm. Morris's tapestry works at Merton. 4everal large pieces have been made from Mr. D'Arcy's country seat, Stantnore Hall, just outside the old world village of Edgware; but in spite of vicarious patronage the old art does not flourish now-adays, and the pet hobby of the late Duke of Albany, the Royal Tapestry Works at Old Windsor never obtained the patronage and support they un- doubtedly deserved.

Mr. William Tait, who is in charge of the royal stock, is, of course, like the keepers of the diary, the kennels, and other departments, a canny Scot, .whose father held the same position before him. There is, in fact, a very strong tendency in the royal household everywhere to carry out the hereditary prineiple. lie is a shrewd-looking, capable farmer, of exceptional intellectual attainments, and intro- duces into his whole relations with the outside world the economical habits of his race. Thus he will think nothing of conveying her Majesty's wishes GO one of the royal tradesmen on a halt- sheet of note paper, unheaded and uncrested. Of course his stock records are kept in absolute order, in books specially prepared for the'purpose.

• Zola furnishes the latest instance of everything coming to a man who waits. For years he has con- tested every seat that has become vacant in the Institute, and just as often the Immortals have hopelessly snubbed him. Nothing disconcerted, he has gone on trying; and had sworn that he would persevere at every vacancy. Now he is within measurable distanoe of realising his ambition. This welcome news to the' great realistic writer is on the authority of Francois CoMe—," Yes," he says to a correspondent," the Acat.emy is going to make Zolo a member this winter, the opposition to hia candidature has rapidly diminis.bed,and by February you will see the author of the ' nougon Alacquat.' series installed in the chair of either Taine or Itlazade. For my own part, I shall glory to see this great successor of Baizac in the Academy."

His Holiness Pope Leo XIII., in spite Of the tropical heat which is driving everyone away from Rome, in spite, too, of his advanced age is reported as being less of a sufferer than anyone of his house; hold. It is not perhaps, generally known that Pope Leo has never set foot outside the precincts of the Vatican during the whole 13 years since his acces- sion to the Papal throne. Only those who know Rome in summer can appreciate what this means. From classic times the further bank of the Tiber has always been regarded, during the summer sea- son, as far from healthy ; hence it was that the , palace of the Quirinal was built on higher ground; ' but this erstwhile home of the Pope is now in the hands of the usurping House of Savoy and forms the palace of King Humbert. The Pope, therefore, instead of a pleasant villeggiatura, as in the past, somewhere among the beautiful mountains round Rome, is confined to a daily walk in the retired gardens of the Vatican.

The Pope's royal neighbour across the TiberXing Humbert is, however, like "the prisoner of the Vatican," staying on through the Roman heats. This, 'however, is part of the conscientious fashion in which he performs his duty as a constitutional monarch. Till Parliament rises King Humbert remains at the Quirinal. His Majesty will, h-mever, very soon be released to pursue his favouritb stein- hock among the Alps in the beautiful Val d'Aosta. He is not so mighty a hunter as his father Victor Emmanuel, who was never happier than when, dressed in mountaineer's costume and away from the restraints of Court etiquette, pursuing wild game among the bills. " King Good Fellow," as he WAS rightly nicknamed, enjoyed above all things a humble dish of macaroni eaten in a peasant's hut, and he relished more than the wittiest sally of the last new comedy at Rome the broad jests and rough pleasantries of the Alpine villagers of his native Piedmont.

Horse-racing, cock-fighting, cards, have all borne their part in the dissipation of ancestral acres, but the most eccentric mode which ever came to my knowledge was that adopted by the bearer of an hi.,.torie name in the west of England some sixty years ago. Squire Weston and a kindred spirit having put their two bottles of port apiece safely under their belts one wet afternoon, took to racing snails along the dining-room table for £l,OOO a aide Snail-racing is a pastime which affords ample time for gambling. and by the time the journey had been cc.mpassed the stakes and bets amounted to no less than £13,000. ' Squire Western's snail was at this point leading by its horns, but the squire, dissatis- fied with its progress, thought to help it on by placing the red-hot end of his cigar against its shell. The result was analogous to Fred Archer's application of the spur to Peter in the Bo 'al Hunt Cup; the snail "curled up" (literally), and refused to try, leaving the opposing champion to romp in alone.

It is stated that Lord Harclwicke has matched himself to ride Watercress against Colonel North for a sum of .£l,OOO a side. Poor Watercress! He is worthy of a better fate than to carry a I6st noble- man over six furlongs at racing speed. Every lover of horse flesh should set his face against these cruel and senseless exhibitions. Some years ago a weighty baronet well known on the turf and in the prize ring, rode a similar match, with the result that his horse fell dead at the winning post.

Lord Hardwicke 20 years ago came into an in- come of £30,000 a year with his title, to which was attached a magnificent place in Cambridgeshire, Wimpole Hall, in which his father had accumulated a mass of treasure, artistic, literary, and other. Cigars, buttonholes, and abnormally shiny hats con- stitute his lordship's sole claim to distinction. Wim- oole has been long on the markets, but has not yet round a purchaser: The library, pictures, and plate, however, had a somewhat sensational sale some years ago. Amongst other things a service of Armada plate fetched £7 an ounce.

The Queen has come off as badly as most people this season in the capacity of a tenant farmer. A newspaper man who on Saturday took a turn round the royal farms at Windsor—for part of which rent is paid to the Woods and Forests Department—says the bean crop looked miserably inadequate, while the cereals, most of which are already cut, is not carried, are scarcely half what they should he in the matter of quantity, to say nothing of the poor quality. The iodder for the stock as well as for the stables is raised on the royal farms,and is rather scanty. The gardens have, of course, not ben per- mitted to languish during the drought, and there is therefore an excellent show of wall fruit and the like.

During her recent visit to Windsor the Queen was, as we said the ether day, as enthusiastic as ever over her dumb pets. She gave special instruc- tions for seversl new photographs to be taken. amongst them being cotlnterteit ?resentments of " two Shetland ponies with their respective foals," and "a dotikey and her foal." The interesting families were comfortably houses in the dairy buildings, where they are far removed from the general turmoil of the Castle Mews. Their most dangerous neighbour is a tame buffalo which was at one time in the Zoo. '

Few men can boast with 31r. 'Henri Jose, the ex- Liberal M.P. for Grimsby, of having successfully borne at once a business and a political role in two countries. At Westminster he was called the " French member," and a particular interest attached to him on account of his defeat of that very eminent gentleman, the reputed parent of the still-born " National party." Mr. Renew ; and be- cause there was a belief that while he stood for Grimsby Mr. Heneage, with ell his local status and with all the support of the M. S. and L. Rail- way Companys' magnates, would never more

be returned to misrepresent the borough. Unfortunately, however 31r. Josse's health gave way. Mr. Jo4se's part in French politics lasted somewhat longer and ended more tragically. He was 26 years of age at the time of the Revolu- tion of 1848,and he took an active part in the events of that tronblous time. After the coup d'etat he he was actually imprisoned for six weeks for his resistanae of the cause of Louis Napoleon, and at last he was expelled from France, to find .a home like many another exile in this country. Latterly his French connection was resumed. He left, many friends in Newcastle, Cardiff, and the Humber port, in which places successiVely he had carried on busi- ness.

div.head: .IF,f.'•lF:t. THE EXAMINER. SATURDA Y, AUGUST 5, 1893. •
div.p: .IF,f.'•lF:t. THE EXAMINER. SATURDA Y, AUGUST 5, 1893. •
LADIES' LETTER.

MT DEAREST NELLIE, The changes decreed by fashion -nearly every season follow one another so rapidly that to follow them you would require a new dress almost every month, and the fashions during the present season have changed even more rapidly than in former years. The fa Ihions in millinery have also changed with equal rapidity and it would almost seem that we had changed • the flowers in our millinery to correspond with tho pet posy of the month, Dar- ing the coming month our chief aim will be to provide dresses which look cool, even if they are not really suitable for that purpose, and to supply this want many of our fashion scaterers have ex- tensive stooks. Amongst these are some very dainty cotton dresses of the new crapes, with big square collars on the bodice, hemmed with a plain material, showing a small vest of spotted net at the neck; these are quite simple, with tied sashes round the waist made of the cotton, and plain skirts. A gendarme blue crApon, which is striped with white silk with raised blue silk spots upon its surface, has been most effectively made with a short coat of black satin, and a lace cravat falling from the neck to the waist. A very thin pink crpon has a design looking like crochet in white cotton ußon it and makes a delightful gown trimmed with white lace, whilst serpentine silk crepe, spotted with black, is an ideal costume for a young matron.

Amongst the many styles and fashions which mark this season's millinery perhaps the prettiest and most stylish is the hat known as the "Stephanie." This hat is made of deep Tuscan and sunburnt straw coml)ined, and has a band of black straw all round the edge, and a low black crown. The shape is fitted with a saucer brim on felt the side, whilst on the right it slopes down. The most tasteful trimming for this hat consists of black ribbon velvet, black lace wings and osprey, and pink or damask roses, or any other flower which you may think to be most suitable.

Sailor hats are the legitimate form of millinery for the river, and they are es popular as over. These share favour with Leghoms and Panellise, which are being worn either plain or trimmed with rosettes and quills. Very smart indeed you would look in a white linen dress striped with lace, with a Panama hat trimmed -alt.!' club colours.

Cotton frocks iutended for morning wear, are made in very eimp!e styks, and these always look fresh and cool. Tae skirts are either gored or cut in an umbrella shape, and are much fuller than they were last seasoa. A novel mode of trimming them is to arrange sots of the narrowest tucks in three hoops above the hem, and at wide intervals trot., each other; besides the tucks, other skirts have ribs fai mad by insertiug cotton piping in the material, and atuohimi it so that it forms a slightly railed band, when several rows of the cord are laid closely side by side. Either of these two trimmings, irons wall when the frock is washed, and is more novel thaa the gather flounces. The prettiest bodices t weir with these skirts are in a full blouse shape, with ample sleeves end an Empire band, which draws the folds of the bodice into the tier e at the waist.

A novel kind of soft silk front is made in white swab, and daintily trimmed with narrow lines of PornPadoor galon. These fronts can be obtained for 4s. 111, in all colours. The tailor•made hol- land coat to wear with this front is sold at ISs. 6d., and is so well finished and FO smartly cut that it Is by no means dear at the price.

Very little change is to be seen in bodices, which ate all more or less trimmed with lace as revers, epaulettes, wide berthas, or frills outlining yokes, and very pretty are the coarse laces over coloured silk. Large sleeves of the leg of mutton or balloon type continue to be worn, while coat sleeves with hugh puffs nearly to elbow are also fashionable; and since these are of a different material from the dress, a very good opportunity is offered to reno• vate a last season's frock, as a puff of velveteen or silk is quite in good taste, more especially if the bodice be trimmed to correspond.

A charming gown, designed expressly for deck and shore wear, is in cream serge, striped with fine lines of dark blue. The short mess jacket is faced with dark blue, and is ornamented with knots and loops of white and gold cord. The white linen vest is fastened down the front with small gilt buttons, and is left open at the neck, to show collar and cravat. A jaunty cap of blue and white serge adds a pretty effect to the costume. Yours lovingly, JENNIE.

div.head: Sprat_ Toast.
div.p: Sprat_ Toast.

This is an excellent dish for breakfast. Bone as many sprats as you require. This can easily be done if they are plainly tried tirst. Pcund them with butter,pepper, salt, and chopped parsley, and enough SWiSf milk to moisten the whole into a paste. Beat it up for a short time cv.r the Sr; ; then, when hoe, spread it on small
slices of fried bread, or hot buttered toast. Herrings can be done in Vex same way.
Milk Punch.

This fs More easily made and less expensive than ordi- nary punch ;it is also suitable for an invalid, and may be used hot or cold. If possible, have the milk warm from the cow, take one quart, add two glasses of sherry, the yolks of three eggs, and z'sugar to taste. First •beat the eggs and sugar together; then add the wine, and while you are Stirring it pour )12 the milk, which has been brought to the boiling point, but not al- lowed to boil. If preferred, put in nutmeg and cinnamon to taste.

div.head: Snowflake Cake.
div.p: Snowflake Cake.

;One cup of butter, three cups of powdered sugar, one gill (half:ctsp) of sweet milk, lour cups of flour, and the whites of nine eggs. Mash fine enough soda to make one level teaspoonful and add it to the flour; also, add three scant teaspoonfuls of cream of tartar. Sift three times. Cream the butter, add the sugar gradually, then the milk, next the flour, and last, the whites of the eggs beaten to a stiff froth. If the cake seems too stiff to beat easily, use part of the whites, putting in altern- ately a spoonful of flour and a little of the whites, but reserving the greater part to add after the flour is all in add tnoroughly beaten, as it destroys the lightness of eggs to stir the cake much after they are in. Bake in layers and use any filling desired.

•• Queen Pudding. Take one and a half cups of sugar, -me quart of niiik, two cups of very dry, fine crumbs, and one tablespoon- ful of butter, and one quart of red raspberries. Rub butter and one cup of sugar to cream ; beat in the yolks-. '1 he crumbs should all this time be soaking in the milk. Beat them into eggs and buttered sugar, and when light pour'the mixture into a buttersd cake dish. Bake until the middle is well set, draw to the oven door, cover with berries, strew sugar thickly over and among them, and spread deftly over all a meringue with two table- spoonfuls of powdered sugar. Shut the door, and brown the meringue lightly. Set away where it will cool quickly, then leave on ice till wanted. Eat with cream.

Two Palatable Puddings. For baked plum pudding, take half a pound sultana raisins, currants, 111,. raisins, Vb. suet, I.lb. of bread crumbs, ?jib. of mixed peel, one nutmeg grated, and one lemon grated, one full tablespoonful of flour, and fib. moist sugar. Mix these ingredients well together ; then crack six eggs, and be careful they are not musty ; beat well with a whisk, 'and mix these in also, adding about one gill of milk. Butter a pie dish and put the pudding in it, and bake in an oven not too hot, and serve it hot. A wineglass of brandy added to the pudding will improve it. A beautiful bread and butter pudding can be be made by following the instructions contained in the subjoined recipe :—Cut some bread and butter in slices, remove a portion of the crust, and place a row in a pie dish, and springle some washed and dried sultanas over. ThEn place another row with more sultanas, and so on till the dish is full. Then crack four eggs, beat them well, and add one pint of milk with sugar to sweeten, also a little nutmeg ; pour this ia the dish. B Ike in an oven not too hot. When done, sprinkle a little sugar (powdered lump) over, and serve.
Hints on Home Government.

The divine precept enjoining honour to parents recog- nises the fact Hint' without respectful, loving obedience to a reasonable government there cannot be comfort and real prosperity in the home. Of course, there will be occisional differences between parents and children, and it is in these crises of the family history that the wisdom of one and the obedience of the other are fairly tested. Young people, with their short experience and imper- fectly developed ideas, crave for unworthy objects, and sometimes go wrong out of pure perversity,. The parent is liable while under provocation to do or say that which is even more blameworthy that the original offence, and the child, while t uhmitting to the chastise- ment, may all the while be gaining an insight into our character such as will lower us considerably in his esteem. Home rule must be systematic and consistent if it is to be respected. Easy-going people are apt •to overlook breaches of discipline so long as they are not personally inconvenienced. It is otherwise when their own peace is at stake. Suddenly brought to a sense of duty, they exhibit a marvellous zeal in setting their house in order. The family brake is put on, and for a time almost martial law prevails in the household. The fit, however, does not last long, and the childien soon learn to despise a rule so vacillating and uncertain. I have no faith in that kind of home discipline which has to administer punishment in large and frequent doses in order to render it effective. To hang a birch-rod in a conspicuous part of the house,, and to shake it in the faces of the young sinners two or three times a day, is no sign of parental tact and ability. While it enforces present subjection, it also implants the germs of future rebellion and disorder. Our young people are not habitual criminals, to be checked and reprimanded for every offence. They are simply atoms of human nature without experience or judgment, and the truest thing that can be spoken abouLtheir misdoings was said the other day by a little fellow who had got into a serape. " Well, mother, I couldn't help it, or I would have done to please you."

div.head: D A RK WOOD. A TAE OF' LON6IOOR.
div.p: D A RK WOOD. A TAE OF' LON6IOOR.
HY MRS. HARRIET Luaus, Author of "her Double Life," " Old Life'. Shadowa,"" Lady Kildare," etc. .
CHAPTER A STP.ANGE RECEPTION OP NEWS.

The festivities at Dunholm Castle were not pro- longed until a late hour. The music was perfect, the dancing in the moonlit ruins romantic and Jelightful ; supper was served before n,liclnight, and by one -o'clock the ,carriages were announced and the guests took their departure, charmed with their entertainment.

Lord Darkwood accompanied .Miss Norreys to her carriage, in which Mrs. Kenright, Miss Ensor, and Cot Warburton were to return to Beechmont with her. There was no opportunity for loverlike speeches, although the marquis felt like indulging in them. .Col. Warburton was waiting to follow his hostess into the vehicle, the remaining carriages were close behind, and Lord Darkwood contented himself with pressing the hand of the East India heiress, and whisperings the word " To-morrow "a he assisted her into her place, ,Colonel Warburton, followed, the door was elgsed, and the carriage rolled away. . .
The marquis stood in evening dress upon the castle steps until the carriages had all departed; then he entered the house.

"To-morrow," he repeated to himself. "To- morrow. I shall see her then, and ur'ge her to allow me to proclaim our engagement." Ah, he little knew all that the morrow was fated to bring forth. Pietro waited upon him as usual with his toilet, but he was too occupied in his own hopes and schemes to note that the Maltese was strangely self -absorbed.

" Pietro," he exclaimed, arousing himself from his abstraction when his valet was about to depart, "I have something to tell you. You know that I have long been desirous of making a good marriage. Jam about to realise my desires. lam in love with Miss NorreYs, and I have asked her to be my wife. She has half consented. She agreed to consider my proposal, and let me know her.answer next week." "You could not make a better match, signor," said the valet. " She • has beauty, wealth, and family. Beechmont will make a handsome addition to the Darkwood manor. The lady has a fortune in the Three-per-Cents. besides, I have heard." "I see you comprehend the value of my intended connection," said We marquis, complacently. "I shall urge a speedy marriage. And, Pietro, you had better get that superfluous dirt out of the dun- geon below," he added, in a lower tone. "Get the dungeons into a presentable shape before my mar- riage, in case Miss Norreys, or anyone else, should desire to explore them. Keep the keys until the task is done." •

, "I shall have to watch my opportunities, signor. Upon a night like this I can do nothing. I like the dark for such work, and not moonlight." " Then the first dark night must be improved. Your reward shall be amide, Pietro. We will con- sider its amount when you bring back the keys with a statement that your work is completed." He dismissed his servant by a gesture. Pietro went.with an odd gleam in his eyes, and a very curious expression upon his lank, swarthy visaof,e. "A clever dog !" muttered the marquis. "And perfectly devoted to me—and my money. He knows that he's in clover. He'd do anything for money, the rascal 1 Now to dream of Sicily, and to-morrow."
The next morning at a late hour Miss Norreye eat in her boudoir.

t was nearly noon and she had just breakfasted. She was attired in a morning costume of mingled silk and.camel's-bair material in cameo shades, and wat about to take a walk in the park. It was evi- dent that she had not slept well during the previous night. Her lovely olive face was paler even than usual ; something of the carmine was missing from her lips, and there were bistre shadows under her velvety brown eyes. She was about to rise when her Hindoo attendant entered.
" Missy," she exclaimed, "Aga is come." A sudden flash of animation lighted up the lady's face.
"Semi him to me," she commanded.

A moment later, Aga was ushered into her pre- sence. He bowed low before her, after the eastern fashion, and awaited her questioning. " Well," said Miss Norreys, impatiently, "lean read success in your face, Aga. You went to York- shire—you found the house—you questioned the woman ?''

"Yes, missy," replied the Hindoo, rapidly telling her in what manner he had entered the house at Lonemoor and ingratiated himself in the favour of Mrs. Quillet. "And I got the address of Miss Granger, as you bade me. " She is in China?"

"No, missy; in London, at No. SO, Northumber- land-terrace, Queen-street, Notting Hill," replied the Hindoo, circumstantially, referring to the caird or address which Mrs. Quillet had given him. "In London !" repeated Miss Norreys. "Then I know the girl went to her. My instinct did not deceive me. The name, Aga ?" "Miss Granger married a curate, the Reverend Thomas Myner, missy." Miss Norreys started violently. "Myner !" she echoed. Aga repeated the name. Nis Norreys put her hand to her heart. " Myner !" she said to herself. " Why, that is the name of the Lady Georgina's governess ! That is s Myner's face made a vivid impression upon me. lam strangely interested in her. Can it be? liiipossible !" Yet the bare suspicion that the Miss Myner at Diiiiholm Castle might be in some way connected with the family of the Rev. Thomas Myner caused her a great secret agitation. "I must go to London by the very first train," she said. "No. I have guests—l cannot leave them. Whom can I send ? '

She thought of Lord Chilton. He was Gwen's lover. Why not send him? The mission would be safe in his hands. He would be cautious, secret, and not easily baffled. She heard Aga's story and dismissed him. She was about to send a messenger to Lord Chil- ton, when a servant entered, bringing a note upon a salver. The note was from the young viscount, begging a private audience. " Naya, said Miss Norreys, " Lord Chilton waits in the hall below. Tell him that I will see him here."

Naya disappeared, and almost immediately re- turned, ushering Lord Chilton into the boudoir. Then she again vanished. Miss Norreys welcomed her visitor with unusual warmth, but she did not tell him that she had been about to send for him.

There was a change in his looks that struck her at the first glance. The melancholy that had char- acterised him since her earliest acquaintance with him had disappeared. A joyous light shone in his blue eyes. He looked younger, brighter, and hap- pier than she had ever known him. "What has happened ?" she asked. " Have you received good news, Lord Chilton ?" "The best of news, Miss Norreys," he answered emphatically. "I have made you the confidant of my sorrows; now sympathise with me in my joys! The lady's face grew suddenly white. "You have heard of, or from, Miss Winter!" she exclaimed. Lord Chilton did not notice her agitation. "Better than that, my dear friend !" he cried. "I have seen her !" " You—have--seen—her!"

"Yes ; f—s.a; het:lasi-night at Ditnholm Castle. She was in the garden. I was with her during the hour or two you missed me. I have found my little Gwen, Miss Norreys. You have seen her—you know her I" "I ?" said the heiress, speaking with a painful effort. "Is she a servant there? I never saw Miss Winter."
"No," said the young viscount, all gladness, his face fairly radiant. " You did not know her as Miss Winter—you know her as the governess of the Lady Georgina. She is Miss Myner !" . .
Miss N.. orrei;' started back, gave a strange, gasp. in utterance, and fell to the fioor in a swoon.
CITAPTEM LTV. A BOLD STEP.

Lord Chilton sprang forward, gathering up the limp figure of his unconscious hostess in his arms, :tad laid it upon a sofa. Scarcely had this move- ment been accomplished, 'Slid he had turned his !yes in quest of the ball-pull, when the door of the Muer room flew open, and the Hindoo woman rushed into the boudoir. She had heard the fall of her mistress, and had nctively comprehended its meaning. She ran to the sofa, with half-articulate cry upon her lips. Miss Norreys's head was thrown thC iei;l..)2L., her olive face_ stFanz,-..!::

pallid, her eyes elased. .A.Lya pet her I,:thq upon the lady's heart. h seethed to hare ai0;...,,ed beat. Mg. •" do !" said. the TTiolno womtril al r, witihmt turning her head towards i,ht•ttc ct."• She has had some great shoek.. You have •iiited her du: Leave her to me . . .

. . The young viscount went with out a word, but he went no further than the ;tail wiihont. Here, anxious and perplexed, he woAlied to and fro, wait- ing for the recovery of his hostess. Her su d!fen i In ess seemed inexplicable. Ife had been telling her about Gwen. He had just declared to her that he had found his betrothed in the person of Miss Myner, the young governess of the Lady Georgina Charteris. What' was there in that statement to send his proud, self.contained hostess into a swoon like death.

"Nothing—nothing whatever," lie assureal him- self. "Miss Norreys is fatigued. The night before last was her own ball; yesterday we visited Dun. holm Castle and danced till one o'clock in the morning, and she is worn out. I have noticed for a day or two a singular nervousness and excitement about her. My statement about Gwen had nothing in it to affect her in any way." Yet he was singularly uneasy, and continued to walk back and forth, a troubled expression replac- ing the recent gladness of his countenance. The minutes passed; still Naya did not call him, and still no messenger was sent for a physician. He had waited nearly half-an-hour when the door of the boudoir opened, and Naya's black head, wound about with a gay Madras kerchief, was thrust out into the hall, and Naya's small black eyes search in one swift, restless glance for the young gentleman. She saw him, and beckoned te him with a nod of her turbaned head.

Ho approached her rapidly. "You can come in, my lord," said the Hinds° woman, not over graciously, evidently regarding him as the cause of her mistress's illness. "But you must be careful not to excite my lady." She opened the door and the young viscount re- entered the boudoir.

Miss Norreys was seated in a lounging-chair. She looked as though a great storm of agitation had passed over her; its traces were visible in the ashen face, the white lips, the sombre, stormy eyes. She tried to smile when Lord Chilton entered, but the. attempt was a pitiful failure. He approached her, distressed and anxious. "You look very ill, Miss Norreys," he exclaimed. "Do you riot Wish a medical man to be sent for?" "I am quite well," answered the lady. "I am not used o faint, my lord, but, in truth, I have been over-excited. Pray be seated." He resumed his seat, his fair face fill of concern for her.

"You were speaking of your discovery of Miss Winter," said Miss Norreys, quite oblivious of her- self and her recent sigular attack. "Tell me more about it. I am greatly interested in your love affair, Lord Chilton, much more interested than you can possibly think." , "You are very kind," returned the young via- count, "but I cannot obtrude any personal affairs upon you in a time like this, Miss Norreys. Let me go aivay now, and return when you are quite recovered."

"No; tell me all now," said the lady steadily, while the pained lines about her sweet mouth' deepened. "I can bear it—l mean that lam im- patient to hear your story, Lord Chilton." "I may divert your mind from your own weak- ness," said the viscount, at a loss to account for her persistency uppn apy other ground. "Since you insist upon it, I will tell you the sequel to the little story I told you in the garden the other clay. Then I mourned for my lost little Gwen; now I rejoice because I have found her."

"It is strange—very strange murmured Noi'reys, shrinking back in the shadow. " You :ound Miss Winter at Dunholm castle last night in the person of Miss Myner, the Lady Georgina's governess? That was what you said?' "Yes," assented the viscount, wondering that she should remember every word of the statement he had made to her almost in the moment she had fainted.

"Miss Myner is Gwendoline Winter." Norreya put one small, tremulous hand over her eyes. "Site was in my house for days," she said, as to herself, "she was under my care, and I never knew nor suspected her identity !" "No; how could you?" questioned the viscount, in snrprise. "You never knew her as Miss Winter ! And at the time she was here you had never even heard my story." "I never knew—l never suspected 1" said Miss Norreys, a low wail in her voice, "And yet there was something in the beautiful frank face that touched my inmost soul There was something in the fearless,glanee of her sweet eyes that made me love her as I have never loved any human being— save one! If I had only known !' Lord Chilton was bewildered. -Had Miss Nor- reys' sudden attack affected her brain?" "My dear friend," he said gently, "you seem to reproach yourself. How could you have known or suspected that Miss Myner was another person of whom you had never heard! You had never heard of Miss Winter until I told you of her?". "Never. I had never heard her name, nor sus- pected her existence." There was still that strange faint wail in her voice that had before perplexed him. " How does it happen that Miss Winter is living at Dunholm Castle—at Dunholm Castle of all places in the world !—and under a false name ?" asked 'Miss Norreys, after a brief silence. "She was driven away from Lonemoor, where she had no right, by the two old family servants who had protected her all her life," replied Gwen's lover. "In her great strait, she turned to her only friend, the governess, .who had been all the mother she had ever known. This governess, Miss Granger, bad married a poor curate who has established a boys' school at Notting Hill. These people, Mr. and Mrs. Myner, welcomed her with affection. I shall never forget their goodness to her," added Lord Chilton in parenthesis. " Their school is unprofitable, Gwen tells me. Fortunately I have a vacant living at my disposal, the incum- bent, a very old inan,diaving recently died. I skull present this living to Mr. Myner. Heaven bless him !" "And tbeee Myners adopted Gwen ?" . .

"Yes, after a fashion. They gave her their own name, the better to screen 'ber from insult, and from Orkney's pursuit. The friendless Miss Winter would never have obtained a situation as governess ; but Miss Myner, the supposed relative of the 'Reverend Thomas Myner, who is of good family, had no difficulty in establishing herself in a good position. Lord Dark wood advertised for a governess, and she, thanks to her good friends. obtained the situation 1" .
" What fate brought her to Dunholna Ca9tle ?" said Miss Norreys to herself. "I cannot under- stand it."

"There has been a providence in our re-union," said Lord Chilton. "1 had searched for her every- where in vain, yet when I came to Beechmont on a visit X found her. You know her, Miss Norreys: You know her beauty, her goodness,,her swee,tuess. I L,cannot leave her longer at Dunholm Castle, as companion to that vulgar Lady Georgina. I am impatient to take Gwen under my own protection. lam anxious to push forward our marriage. I would procure a special licence and urge Gwen to marry me this very day, but for the marriage set- tlementc"

"But she has no property." "True. If she had a father to look after her Interests I should probably be required to settle an annual income, a separate property upon her. And as she had no one to consider these things for her I must do so. The custom is an excellent one, Miss Norreys, and I fully approve it. And it is my wish to consider Gwen's own best interests, as a father might have done fbr her. I shall write to my lawyer to-day and bid him prepare the settlements." The lady's eyeslooded with tears. "You have a chivalrous soul, Lord Chilton I" she exclaimed.

He coloured. " I desire to remove Gwen from her present duties at once," he exclaimed. "She will return to the M.yners to remain until after our marriage." "Let her come to me," cried Miss Norreys.• "My house and my heart aro open to her. Let het come to me."

Lord Chilton thanked her warmly, saying— " That is what I most wished—that you would take charge of Gwen until after our marriage. You are very kind, and I am very grateful." "I will go with you to Dun-holm Castle, and we will bring her away with us," said Miss Norreys. "Her place is here. She must not be left at the castle another night. Does Lord Darkwood suspect her true history ?" "Impossible I How could he suspect a secret that had been so carefully guarded ?" Miss Norreys's head dropped back upon the cushions of her chair, and Lord Chilton was struck with her haggard looks and the brooding trouble in her sombre eyes. " Tord Chiltou,"_Cle &Nick aftetA w...41g, have

you weil eon siderea this mat t.:;r—thim entanglement of yours? You riah, with aristocratic connections. This 4!2;irl yell ir,ve is poor, friendless. She was educated by two to:yr servants out of charity or pity. She is ill born. Her mother sleeps in a (I:shonon red grave. She is Do match for you. Retlect well before you commit an act which you arc likely to regret throughout your whole after life."

" This from you!" Lord Chilton, said reproach- fully. " From you, you have kit4wn Gwen ! In herself she is noble, the peer of any lady in the land. No one looking in her dace would ask her pedigree. She is an angel, Miss Norreys." "I believe it. But her birth? Her social rank? Any scullion in your kitclmn might sneer at hor origin."

"She is of good blood—l know O. Any one looking at her must be convinced not only that gentle blood flows in her veins, but that she comes of an honourable race!" cried Lord Chilton. "Every instinct of her soul is noble. Such as she do not come from bad stock. And I mean to prove the truth of my belief. I mean to prove her of gentle blood, Miss Norreys, if it be possible to trace back the history of that poor wanderer who perished so miserably on the Lonemoor in York- shire seventeen years age." A look of wild alarm shone on the lady's face. " No, no ! Let the dead rest ; " she cried. "Believe me, Lord Chilton, it is better to let the mystery of this girl's parentage lie in its present obscurity. She is not well born. She is not a fit- ting wife for you. Find a more suitable bride, and leave this girl, Lord Clifton. lam older than you, and I know that nothing but misery can,spring from such an alliance."

"I refuse to believe it. I did not expect such worldly counsel from you, Mips Norreys. The lady did not answer, but the viscount saw her wring her hands silently in a dumb and terrible angtiish that frightened him. Then, suddenly, the forced outer calmness of the lady gave way, as a dam yields to the overpowering rush of the swollen, frenzied stream, and she cried out, in a,passionate• voice—

"Lord Chilton, hear Inc. Hearken to my warn- ing. This girl's mother was not fit to be mentioned in the same breath with your Own honoured mother. There is a taint in this girl's blood—l tell you so— I swear it."

"You know it of your own knowledge r cried the viscount, wondering. "I know it. It is my duty to warn you. This girl is good and pure in herself, poor child; but it is written that the sins of the parents shall be visited upon the children. She is a born outcast— a pariah from her birth. Be warned, Lord Chilton, and let her go !" , "I would not give her up, not though the whole world were against her," cried the viscount. "1 would not let her go for any crimes of her parents, for any sneers of society, for any social ban upon herself. She is mine. She loves me, and I love her. I know her for the purest angel on the earth. Give her up I Never !" He stood up, grand and noble, as he uttered these words, anti Miss Norreys knew that her appeal was wasted. He could not be moved from his allegiance to his betrothed, and the conviction brought her both sorrow and a rapture of delight. "You say that you know that Gvven's mother Was not what she should be ?" said the young vis- count presently: "How do you know this, Miss Norreys? I thought you know nothing of Gwen's history until I.told you.".. . _

" You are right. Until you told me, I did not know that there was such a being as Gwendoline Winter in the world," again said Miss Norreys. "Then how do you know of her parentage ? ' Some explanation was due to him. The lady comprehended its necessity. She was silent a minute, but a glance into his pale, stern, waiting face quickened her speech. She looked exhausted, however, with the strain of her emotions, and her tones were low and feeble, as she said—

"Lord Chilton, your story told me in the garden, interested me greatly. I liked you from the first, and the romance of your love affair greatly im- pressed me. I desired to help you, I will not deny that I had my share of woman's curiosity in the matter. I was anxious to discover your missing betrothed, and I sent my faithful Hindoo servant Aga to Yorkshire to make inquiries after Miss Winter. He returned only this morning, having heard her history, and gained a clue to her refuge after leaving Lonemoor. "And your knowledge of Gwen's ill parentage was, then, founded upon the report of your Hindoo servant ?" demanded the viscount.
A spasm of pain convulsed the lovely olive face of the .East India heiress. She bowed her head in assent.

"And you too, Miss Norreys, whom I believed superior to all fashionable weaknesses, are infected with the popular prejudice of caste to such an extent that you would condemn Gwen to a life of loneliness and sorrow because we do not know her parentage. You would Punish the child for the sins of the parents, and condemn the poor dead young mother upon hearsay ! I thank you for your interest in me. I appreciate it—but my friends must be Gwen's also."

"Tam her friend," cried the lady. "I love her, Lord Chilton, almost as much for her as for you. I could not bear that you should marry her and then repent the marriage, and so break her heart. Let us go to her. Let her return with me. She stall find in me her best friend, next to yourself. She shall be married from my house." Her eager pleadings eonquered Lord Chilton's resentment. He bent and raised her hand to his lips with chivalric courtesy. Gwen shall come to you, 'Miss Yorreys," he said. "I can promise for her. We will drive over to Dunholm Castle this afternoon, as soon as you shall be sufficiently rested. • Let me leave you now. You are very tired." He took a step towards the door. "One moment," said Miss Norreys. "Lord Darkwood must not be informed of Miss Winter's true history. He must believe herstill to be Miss Myner." " Yes ; every one must continue to believe that —to spare her scandal." "That is all," said the heiress, with a long-drawn

sigh. "I have a last word to say," said the young viscount. "Your very. words, Miss Norreys, have convinced me of mrdtity in regard to the occupant of that grave in Penistone churchyard. I will trace out her history. I will prove her true and honourable, the victim of treachery in others per- haps, but in herself virtuous and upright. I will clear Gwen's mother frem all shadow of shame. I will devote myself to this task. You shall know —and Gwen shall know—the whole world shall know if necessary—that the perfect flower I seek to gather and graft upon my own ancestral tree came from a good stock, and not from some worth- less wayside weed." There were words of entreaty on the lady's line. expostulations and beseectungs. he did not utter them,. and he went forth strong in his resolve. Ile hastened to his own room, wrote a letter to a famous detective officer, whose name he well knew as having been very often concerned in these delicate investigations before, and enclosed a cheque for a handsome amount as a retainer. The contents of the letter were an account in brief of the appear- ance at Lonemoor of the insane, wandering woman, who had there given birth to a child, and who had fled a month later in the storm of an awful December night. The dates were carefully ap- pended. "That woman lies buried in Penistone church- yard," the letter concluded. "A headstone .bear- mg the name of Magdalen marks her grave. Her name was never known. I desire you to discover her name, origin, and history, and report the same to me without delay. Let the investigation be strictly secret, and as speedy as possible. The task seems difficult, but I trust that your sagacity will suffice to unravel the mystery." He appended his name and address, and dis- patched the letter by special messenger to Shrove- bury, to catch the first post to London.
(To be continued. )

Sir Charles Russell, speaking at Hackney on Wednes- day night, said he believed tha Government was stronger to-day than twelve months ago. The mandate of the country regarding Home Rule was that there should be continued Irish Ter resentation at Westminster. Ellen if there were not a line in the kill providing for it the prin- ciple of Imperial supremacy would remain untouched and irremovable.

The following resolution was passed by the committee :—" That the common seal 6f the borough be affixed to the following documents : —Mortgages, No. G 252, on the borough rates (£5OO re- issue) ; No. 360, on the gas undertaking (£5OO re-issue). div.head: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
THE ANNUAL " SPEECH. DAY."

To the friends and parents of the scholars of the Warrington Grammar School the annual speech day is probably the most interesting occasion ol the year. Hence it is that on Tuesday, which was " speech .day," on the occasion of the annual distri- bution of prizes, the schoolroom was filled to the fullest extent of ire holding capacity, with friends and parents, and old scholars. ' As on former occasions the boys were accommodated on an unprovised platform, and trequently during the pro- , ccedings they testified their appreciation by applause of the wise remarks that were made to them, and also, as when the headmaster entered the room, their apprecia- tion and regard for those under whose guidance and tuition they are. They opened the proceedings by the singing ofc. Latin hymn, after which came the perhaps most important feature of the occasion, THE HEADMASTER'S SPEHER.

The Rev. E. J. Willcocks said Ladies and Gentle- men,—lt is usual for me in opening this afternoon's proceedings to plunge at once ' in medias res'—and to summarize briefly the progress of our work, and to record thesuccesses obtained during the last year by present and past members of this old educational foundation. The school is constituted a Special Local Centre under the Oxford Local Examination Board, and boys are examined annually both for-school purposes and the University Certificate. Certificates were gained last year by,eleven junior candidates—three of these winning distinctions in special subjects. (Applause.) Our other successes include :—H. K. Gornall—the head boy of the •school—(applause)—elected to an open Classical Exhibition at St. Catharine's .College; Cam- bridge. (Applause.) E. W. Coates—elected to an open Mathematical.Rehibition at the same college. We have now six boys at Cambridge—all scholars of their respective colleges. In the recent competitive examina- tion held by Fier Majesty's Civil Service Commissioners to select engines:. students for the Royal Navy. A. L. .Ficton obtained • the 27th place in order of merit among the successful candidates. F. Gornall passed the Lon- don Matriculation Examination in January last. The high standard of attainments required to pass this examination is shown by the number of f ailures. In this particular examination out of 1,341 candidates who presented themselves, no fewer than 81:4 were rejected by the examiners. Z. Fennelly has won the -" Bishop Trazer " scholarship- cif £4O per annum at Owenti' College. J. Healey, of Owene',College has passed the final exam- ination in the Faculty of Medicine for the degree of M.B. (Victoria University). J. W. Isherwood of Owens' College has graduated -B.A. in Classical Flonows (Victoria University). A. S. Kidd of St. John's College, Cam- bridge, who took a Second Class in Part I of theCiassical Tripoe last year—has after only a year's reading obtained Honours in the Moral Science Tripos. W. A. Stone— scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge—who was placed in the First Class of Part I of the Classical Tripos last year, has also attained a First Class in Fart 11. (Applause.) Stone is especially to be congratulated on the distinguished position he has achieved. (Applause.) I am glad of this opportunity to testify to the en- ergetic and loyal manner in which the assistant masters of this school have thrown themselves into their work.—Nor do I forget the boys who, as a whole, are eager and anxious to profit lay the instructions given them. The question of the amount of tuition fees required from parents has often been under consideration.—l wish to-day to call your particular attention to a resolu- tion of the Governing Body which was passed at a meet- ing in January last.—The resolution runs as follows : " Resolved that the Government approve of the pro- posal of the head master to have a Preparatory Form in in the school for boys from 8 to 12 years of age at a fee of £2 per term, which is the minimum fee allowed by the scheme." It is with the deepest regret that we have of late had to record the loss of so many good men and true who were members of our Governing Body. The last year has been again especially fatal, for both the late Canon Greenall and Mr. James Marson were among the fore- most in the interests they took in this Institution and by their ready help and regular attendance at the meetings of the Governors, they showed a practical sympathy with us in our work here. The following gentlemen have been elected to vacan- cies on the Board of Governors. Co-optative :—Major Pickmere, Mr. Charles White, and the Rev. R. Greenall. Representative :—Mr. W. Long, J.P., and the Mayor (Mr. E. Greenall.) Our thanks are due to Mr. Alfred Woods for offering yearly a beautifully designed silver medal to the winner of the School Champion Swimming Belt. Extracts from Examiner's Report :—"The general order and discipline of the school are very good. It is impossible to have looked through all the papers done in the Examination without seeing that the boys are being carefully taught, and that a general spirit of work pre- vails." "in all the Fornis the handwriting was good the papers were done carefully and neatly." "The general standard of the work in the Examination was distinctly good." The next item in the programme was the Latin essay " Roma Camillo duce restituta," by F. Gornall. ma.,and the English essay" Becket, Chancellor and Archbishop," by Gough, each being a production reflecting consider- able credit not only on the boys but upon the school.

subjects taught, and then at the success which was achieved. The subjects were extremely comprehensive. The boys were prepared for commercial and business life,shorthand was taught in the school as well as chemis- try and science ; there was in fact a very great variety of instruction, and nothing was omitted which could be supposed to be useful to impart to the youthful mind. Let them look at the success which had been aclsieved. He considered it most remarkable. He knew something about schools, boys, masters, successes and failures— perhaps more about the latter than anything else. (Laughter.) He was certain that the success of that day could not have been obtained without great perse- verance on the part of the masters and great application on the part of the boys. (Applause.) These successes were by no means confined to universities. They had successes at Owens College, and in the Naval Engineers' School, as well as in the Oxford local examinations and the London University matriculation examination, and so on ; and if the number of subjects taught was large, the number of successes gained was equally large. (Applause.) The question was whether it was in any sense desirable to lower the high standard which had been raised in that school? He thought most decidedly not. (Applause.) There might be difficulties—he was sure there must be—in supplying all that was required in these various directions; and it might be a question for the Town Council to consider how far they would be doing that which was right and just in subsidizing to a certain extent that secondary school in the same manner in which the London County Council had subsidized schools in its own district to the extent of nearly £50,000. There were things wanted in the school which money alone could obtain—a laboratory, for instance, and a science master, who could not be had without a salary. Whether such help was granted or not, of one thing he felt sure, and that was that it was most desir- able that the school should uphold a high-standard of learning, for it was a school midway between the elementary school and the university. By no means !et it sink or lower its high standard, but let it be main- tained, and he was sure that would be the case as long as the school contained within itself the same persever- ing masters, the same assiduous boys. He would close his speech, as speeches were usually concluded on that occasion with the wish " Floreat." He coneratulated Mr. Willcocks upon the high tone which prevailed among the boys, and upon the eminent success which had been obtained during the year. (Loud applause.)

div.head: SPEECH BY THE REV. CANON DODD.
div.p: SPEECH BY THE REV. CANON DODD.

The Rev. Canon Dodd then delivered an address, in which he said that when their friend the Headmaster told him that it was the wish of the governors that he should distribute the prizes, he experienced two sensa- tions—first of all the sensation of gratification, but far more forcibly a feeling of diffidence less by any in- feriority on his part he should bring a discredit upon the post which had been so admiralaly filled in past years by distinguished men. At the same time he would not yield to anyone in the irOerest he took in the subject of education generally, as he wished to see it based on sound principles—vigorous, intelligent and fruitful, and available without much difficulty to any boy, no matter what his position might be, er to whatclass of the com- munity he might belong. (Applause.) That had al- ready been partly realised in the fact that boys passed now from the elementary schools to the secondary school and so onward to the highest education the country afforded at their two great Universities of Oxford and Cambridge. However much they might differ, and of course they did differ as to the merits of many modern movements he thought that the movement in favour of education had been distinctly a forward and progressive movement, and one that i.ad great promise for the future. (Hear, hear.) It was early yet to attempt to realize, or rather he should say to estimate, what the results of all this education might be, but they could not but think that as knowledge spread through all classes of the community, many of those acts of violence and those lamentable excesses would gradually be lessened to which the uneducated or only semi-educated classes of the land seemed especially prone. (Applause.) The statement made in the House of Commons only last night by the Minister of Education was a 'highly satis- factory one. A larger number of children were pre- sented for examination than had ever been known before, and a larger sum of money was voted by the House for the purposes of education—money which, be ventured to say, would be exceedingly well spent. It was not always so. In times not so very far back, the education of the poor was partial and unsatisfactory, while with regard to the middle classes and the upper classes, those who went to school could learn if they chase to do so if they had natural application and ability to learn, but the rest were "sent empty away," and there was a large number.of boys who left the schools of this country with a much more intimate acquaintance with the birch rod than they did with the Latin gram- mar—(laughter)—in fact, to be a good caner was consi- dered almost as necessary a qualification as to be a good teacher. At the University something of the same kind prevailed. No doubt very often scholars were prodaced, men of great eminence in mathematics and other branches of science, but they might say of the majority who went to the universities that there was practically no education at all. If they could not say as the French did " We have changed all that," they could say "We have changed a great deal of it." And although a change had taken place in every department of learning, he thought that nowhere had the change been so marked as in those schools called the "grammar schools" of this country and the seconcluy sahools, such as that in which they were then assembled. (Applause.) The ideal education was a ladder where a boy could step from the lowest rung to the highest; and there was nothing to prevent him, if he had ability, from attaining the very highest position which the country had to offer. While it was a good thing for a boy to pass from an elementary and secondary school to the university, he must not think after he had taken his degree that everything was complete. (Applause.) He narrated two amusing stories, the morals of which were that they must not suppose that because they had passed through what was only the elementary stage there was nothing further to be done. True education did not consis4in stuffing a boy's brains with undi- gested and often indigestible matter which, like unas- similated food, would sooner or late disagree with him. , The boy who received a truly liberal education was one who learned how to learn. fie was provided with tools and taught how to use them, and thus he was fully equipped for any line of life to which he might after- wards be called. Ile must be sure of his facts, and of what those facts would prove, and not give way too freely to his fanciful conceits. (Applause.) When a youth he was fond of writing essays and prize poems. On one occasion be wrote an essay on St. Paul of Athens, but having soon used up his facts the rest of his essay consisted of fights of imagination on his part— very hard on Stoics and Epicureans, and very laudatory of the Apostle St. Paul. He thought he had written a very famous and magnificent essay, hut unfortunately for him the examiner was a very shrewd and immensely clever man, and he simply wrote across one page— Flow do you know all this'?" (Loud laughter.) He (Canon Dodd) felt at the tine rather indignant, as it was the most eloquent passage, but on further reflection he came to the conclusion that the examiner was right, and no question ever did him so much good. Indeed, in after years, he used to ask himself, after he had written a page, " How do you know all this ? He thus learned to verify his quotations, to be sure of his facts, and not to make his facts bear more than they could legitimately bear. True education must be liberal, morally, intellectually and physically. They wanted the thorpore sane together with the mens sans—games and sports of healthful recreation, formed a part, and no insignificant part, in the day school playground. Classics and cricket went extremely well together. (Hear, hear.) Did that school fulfil that ideal of education ? Did it offer the higher, wider, and fuller instruction, which was really impossible in an elementary school ? Be thought the answer must be " Yes." (Applause.) They must look first of all at the

div.p: THE PLAYS.

After Canon Dodd's- speech the boys sang the Latin song " Interger vitce," after which Kinross'" Hunter's Song" was rendered with very good effect. Two scenes from the " Midsummer Night's Dream " were next given. The interpretations were of an original cbarac- ter, and certainly amusing; the chief feature being, however, the freedom of declamation and the general elocutionary force which was introduced, The following was the caste : Bottom, 0. A. Newman; Quince, E. A. Davies ; Flute, J. Richardson ; Snout, R. Leigh ; Star- veling, F. G. R. Wood ; Snug, R. G. S. Tinney. Roland Rogers' song, " March like the Victor," was next rendered by the boys in a very creditable manner. Tbe next item was selections from " The Birds " of Aristop- hanes. The following were the performers :—H. K. Gornall, C. P. Gough, S. Walton, E. S. Kidd. This was given in Greek and must have been a task for the per- formers, which they may claim to have fulfilled with credit. A Latin song, " Strenua nos exerct inertia," was given by the boys, which was followed by a song entitled "At the thought of Britain's Glory." Au entertaining French farce, " Non-Coupable," was the next item on the programme, and the following boys are deserving of much praise for the excellent manner in which they acquitted themselves in their various parts : J. R. Evans, E. W. Coates, R. D. Willcocks, and J. S. Wallace. The scholars next gave" Dulce Domum in a very spirited manner. The various choruses were accompanied by Mr. W. S. Woods. The boys at the close gave three hearty cheers to the bead master, the governurs, and themselves.

div.head: ALLEGED SETTING FIRE TO A DWELLING-HOUSE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED SETTING FIRE TO A DWELLING-HOUSE AT RUNCORN.

At Runeern Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, Thomas Henry Spender, of 60, Greenway-road, lime merchant, was brought up in custody charged with unlawfully and maliciously setting fire to his dwelling-house, a certain other person named Frances Fleetwood then being therein. Mr. A. Linaker appeared for the prisoner. It appeared from the state- ment of Fleetwood. who is servant to the prisoner that on Sunday evening the prisoner was very drunk. He went upstairs and she followed him. He threatened that he would set the place on fire, and she saw him strike a match and set the bedclothes on fire. The woodwork of the window was also set on fire. Mr. William Anderton, of the Anchor Inn, was passing at the time and in response to a call he went in the house and extinguished the fire. The damage was computed at £s.—ln reply to Mr. Linaker the witness said the prisoner had not been sober the whole of the last week.—Superintendent Atherton suggested that the prisoner should be remanded• for a week ; he would have medical attendance and would doubtless then be in a better frame of mind. —Mr. Linaker said there was no doubt the man was very drunk, and as this was a serious charge he had no objection to the suggestion made.—The prisoner was then remanded until Saturday.

div.head: JABEI; BALFOUR'S PO RTRAIT.
div.p: JABEI; BALFOUR'S PO RTRAIT.
A DILEMMA.

The Debenture Corporation are, we believe, says the ‘. Westminster Gazette;" in a curious difficulty about the great picture of their Board of Directors, which Mr. Herkomer painted for them two years ago. This picture was exhibited at the Academy. The difficulty is that it contains an excellent portrait of Mr. Jabez Balfour, who was at one time a member of the board. A portrait of Mr. Balfour is naturally not a pleasing thing just now to hang in the board room, and if it were alone it would no douot be consigned to the cellar. But in this case it is One of a great group, and the question is can it be obliterated without spoiling the whole ? Several eminent artists have, we believe, been consulted, who have offered the opinion that it would be a shame to spoil so admirable an ensemble, and that to deface the portrait of Mr. Balfour would be to destroy a remarkable work of art—to say nothing of a record of a most remarkable man.
