div.head: I SEA SIDE AND HOLIDAY RESORTS ON THE CAMBRIAN RAILWAY.
div.p: I SEA SIDE AND HOLIDAY RESORTS ON THE CAMBRIAN RAILWAY.

The Cambrian Railway Company have just issued (price twopence) a pamphlet setting forth the at- tractions of the country traversed by their lines un- der the title " Where to stay and What to see." The company holds sway over so large a portion of wild and picturesque Wales that it would be diffi- cult to exaggerate the charms of its 70 miles of un- surpassed coast and mountain scenery along Cardi- gan Bay, and the same distance through mountain, river and woodland of the Upper Severn and Wye valleys. But the pamphlet sets out to describe. the beauties of the Welsh scenery in no inflated style or manner, the object being very wisely to make known the impartial observations of independent critics, with occasional references to standard guide books, in prefer- ence to relying eatirely upon the eulogistic comments of the company's own management. Some seventeen views, reproduced from photographs, by the now well- known Meisenbach process' adorn the book, and give, by their undoubted truthfulness, additional value to the testimony of the text. The Cambrian Railway consists mainly of two north and south sections, one inland reaching from Whitchurch to Brecon, and another on the coast stretching away from Pwllheli to Aberystwith, these two sections being united by an east and west cross country line about midway in their course. The question of " Where to stay' is conveniently and ex- haustively answered by a list given at the end of the pamphlet of the various hotels and inns, farm house and country lodgings to be found in the district served by the' Cambrian railways, and this list is usefully supple- mented by details of the accommodation offered and of the distances from the nearest railway stations, the in- formation being tabulated in a manner well calculated to economise time and patience. To the less prosaic and wider question of" What to see " a larger space is, of course, devoted, and it is in this part of the pamphlet that the pre-emmence of the country traversed by the Cambrian Railways as the "happy hunting ground" of the tourist, is at once apparent. Commencing at the northern extremity of the inland section, the attractions of Ellesmere, Oswestry and Lake Vyanwy are first noted. In the direction of places like the last named, lying some distance off the main line, offshoots of the railway have been constructed, and the tourists comforts have been further studied by the establishing of a well equioped coach service in connection with the trains. In regard to the fishing at Lake Vyrnwry it is—says I " The Sporting and Dramatic News,"—most satisfactory to have to announce a very successful opening of the above water, and that in the face of a very bright sun- shine (March 30th last) ; however, when evening came, 88 trout, weighing 51lbs. 10oz., were laid out, and a very eneouraging sight they proved, for en Friday the same number of rods brought in 164 fish, weighing 951bs. Boz., ten anglers having the limit (20 trout), and one angler who arrived late had eight from shore after 4 p.m. ' Saturday was a true fisherman's day, cloudy and showery, and produced 195 trout, weighing 106 lbs. 60z., there were seven limits, and two gentlemen who had 40 trout in their boat took 25 of these in three-quarters of an hour after six in the evening. All agreed they had never seen trout rise better." Continuing past the Briedden group of hills, with their magnificent outlook, with Welshpool for their nearest centre, Montgomery and Newton are reached. The route at Moat-lane now branches to Llanidloes, and for 60 miles runs through the Upper Severn and Wye Valleys to Brecon. Space does not permit giving a full account of the really ex- quisite and in some respects unrival*A scenery of this portion of the Cambrian Line. It may be said without hesitation that the public who travel over this section for the first time will be charmed with its many beauties, ever changing but never tiring. Further south about half a mile from Rhayader Sta- tion the Company have commenced to put in a junction with the proposed Birmingham Corporation Railway, which will run a distance of about five miles to Nantgwillt and Cwm Elan, where it is proposed to sub- merge these valleys for the purpose of constructing a large lake, similar to Lake Vyrnwy, as a reservoir for the Birmingham water scheme. The rivers Elan and Nantgwillt will be the source supply. This is a gigantic undertaking, and will cost several millions of money. After passing Doldowlod the picturesque residence and studio of Mr. H. B. W. Davies R.A.,on the banks of the Wye, we come to Builth Wells, widely famous for its medicinal waters. Brecon, on the river Usk, the southerly terminus of the Cambrian railway, is some 78 miles from Welshpool, and is noted for its far-famed beacons, rising cone-shaped on the horizon. Brecon was the birthplace of Mrs. Sidelong. The house is now called the " Siddons Arms Inn." The few remains of the ancient castle, interesting for its historical associations; the Priory Church ; and the Priory House, where Charles I. took refuge after the battle of Naseby, are amongst the attractions of the neighbourhood. No more beauti- ful drive in Wales can be found than from Brecon to Crickhowell by the banks of the river Usk, a distance of 15 miles. _ _

For those who are travelling to the coast of Cardigan Bay, we must bring the reader back to Moat Lane on the main line. The journey thence to Machynlleth and Ulandovey Junction—where the line branches in two directions, one to Aberystwyth and the other to Aber- dovey, Towyn, Barmouth, &c.—ts full of interest. Caeraws and Pontdolgoch Stations (the latter was awarded the first prize for a well-kept station in 1892) will claim the traveller's attention. Proceeding west- ward we come to Machynlleth from which place the magnificent Llyfnant Valley—one, if not the most beau- tiful valley in Wales—is within easy access. A walk of two miles over the hills brings the holiday maker to Glaspwll, the head of the valley. Another way to reach the Lllyfnant Valley is from Glandovey Station. About a mile walk, and the tourist arrives at the entrance of the valley. No visitor to North Wales should miss this exquisite spot, with the lovely Glaspwll Cascade, and two miles beyond the Cwmrhaiadr Fall, with its waters leaping from Llyn Pen Bhaiadr. The Llyfnant Valley is a veritable home of the fern ; it abounds here in many choice varieties. The line now reaches the shores of Cardigan Bay and running south through Borth pro- ceeds through a picturesque country to Aberystwyth. Quoting from the "Gossiping Guide to Wales" it may be noted that " David Cox painted its beautiful bay, Sir Astley Cooper and other fashionable physicians sounded abroad the virtues of its health-giving air, and in the days of stage coaches it already attracted num- bers of English visitors. The first attraction of Abery- stwyth, next to the beach, is the Castle. The ruins stand above the sea, westward of the town, upon a little rocky promontory reached by a gentle walk. The view, from Pembrokeshire, south, to Carnarvonshire. north, which bound Cardigan Bay, is seen to perfection on this spot, for we stand about midway between the extreme points, and have the curving shore in view a good part of the distance. Of course the look-out north is the most charming, for it includes the hills which rise round the estuary of the Dovey, and far beyond, with Snowdon itself on clear days." But the great attrac- tions of the neighbourhood are the Devil's Bridge and Plynlimon, both within easy access by coach. Harking back to Glandovey Junction and continuing north along the coast what a scene of enchantment now opens before the tourist! Far away are seen the mountains -extend-

lug from Machylleth and Glandovey to the Plynlimon range. To the south, Borth, with it steep cliffs, and the hills which hide Aberystwyth; and westward the blue waters of Cardigan Tay. We are now in dui county of Merioneth, and as the train emerges from f.ur tun- nels, delightful glimpses of sea and mountain meet the gaze until we arrive at Aberdovey. Further along the coast Towyn is reached in the neighbourhood of which the river Dysynni affords capital sport for anglers. A miniature guage railway runs from Towyn to Abergy- nolwyn Slate Quarries. Barmoah is so well known that it seems superfluous to add to what has already been said in regard to its many attractions and delightful surroundings. Every one who has time should see the glorious view of the estuary Cader Idris, and surrounding mountains, to be obtained from the Panorama Walk, about a mile from the town. A visit should also be paid to the rail- way viaduct, to which the public have access. There are also many magnificent mountain walks, and the walk or drive along the road to Penmaenpool and Dol- gelley by the side of the estuary is in many respects unequalled. For the greater part of the way by the side of the estuary, a run of ten miles from Barmouth brings the traveller to Dolgelley. On the journey Arthog and Pen- maenpool, with its bridge across the river, is passed. The visitor would be well repaid by paying a visit to the beautiful falls at Arthog, close to the hotel, and follow- ing the river for about half a mile with its numerous cascades. Arthog is, moreover, a favourable point from which to ascend Cader Idris. The famous precipice walk is about three miles distant from Dolgelley. A well-cut path has been made round Nsel Cynwch and the circuit known as the precipice walk is about two miles round the mountain. About two miles from Dolgelley is the beautiful Torrent walk, and for about a milu and a half there are a series of cascades, any of which might fairly claim a reputation of its own. Still along the beautiful coast northward the train travels to Harlech, famous for its castle. Yet further, past Minfford and Festinog, Portmadoc, the starting point of Snowdonian and Beddgelert Couches, is reached. The drive by the river Glaslyn through the Pass of Aberglasyln (the Switzerland of Wales) to Beddgelert, a distance of eight miles, thence to Llanberis or Bettws-y- -coed, runs through some of the grandest scenery in Wales,with Snowdon in view the greater part of the way. FrOM t'OrtMadOC to Cricceth the sea is left for a short distance, but the journey is still none the less interest- ing, as the neighbouring mountains and hills meet the eye in every directicn. Moreover, we are in " the land of the golden gorse." The whole of the country around is one blaze of light—the light of the golden gorse. On the wide plain the gorse reigns supreme, up the sides of the cliffs its yellow Bower predominates,whilst amid the dark green hedges its vivid colour seems brighter still by the contrast. Criccieth Castle, in ruins, is almost as fine as Harlech. It is beautifully situated on a hill, ris- ing perpendicularly from the sea. Both Criccieth and Pwllheli are amongst the most rising and beautiful watering-places on Cardigan Bay. A coach drive from the last named place brings those who delight in fine coast scenery to Abersoch, off which are the St. Tud- wall's Islands. No visitor to Pwllheli should miss seeing the magnificent coast scenery to be found at Porthdinl- leyn and Nevin. The panorama of sea and mountain is remarkable, extending from the Great Orme's Head to Pembrokeshire, with a magnificent view of Snowdonia, Carnarvon the Britannia Bridge, the Arans, and Cader Idris, included in the scene.

div.head: DRUNKEN MOTHE R NEGLECTS HER
div.p: A DRUNKEN MOTHE R NEGLECTS HER
CHILD.

Emma Carter, a middle-aged woman, was brought , before the borough magistrates at the Police Court, Warrington, on Tuesday charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street,and also with neglect- ing her child, one month old. The Chief Constable stated that the woman gave her name as Emma Carter and said she came to Warrington with her husband and children from Manchester on Saturday. The man with one of the children went to Bruchemite's lodging-house and the prisoner went to the Workhouse and stayed there on Saturday and Sunday nights. On Monday about four o'clock Elizabeth Griffin, a young woman and niece to Mrs. Walsh of the Crown and Sceptre Inn, saw the prisoner go into the yard of the Crown and Sceptre. She was smoking a pipe, and the child in her arms was covered with a shawl. Seeing the woman was drunk Elizabeth Griffin took the infant from her, and the prisoner then fell helplessly to the ground. When the woman got up again she asked for the child which was returned to her. She then went to Upper Bank-street and sat on some steps there and remained there some time. Elizabeth Griffin saw her there and was told by a young man named Bernard McFrance that it was time someone took charge of the child as the woman had fallen on it. The young woman took charge of the child and the police were sent for. P.C. Amson took the prisoner in custody. She was in a very drunken condition, and the child bad been neglected in every respect. Elizabeth Griffin washed the child and gave it some milk. The child ate greedily. Elizabeth Griffin corroborated. Inspector Uphill, of the N.S.P.C.C., said he saw the young woman with the child at the Police , Station. He found the child weighed 41b. ; the normal weight of a child at that age was 71b. 4oz. The child was in an emaciated condition, and had been much neglected. Bernard McFrance deposed to seeing the woman let the child slip out of her arms in Upper Bank- street. The woman had had some drink. P.C. Amson said from a complaint he received he went to the prisoner and found her smoking. She was very drunk and he brought her to the Police Station. He examined the child and found it raw on different pars of the body. The child's clothing was also unclean. The magistrates sent the prisoner to gaol for one month hard labour. The chairman (Mr. Guest) said the Bench desired to express their thanks to Elizabeth Griffin for the care she had taken of the child, remarking that her conduct had been most praiseworthy.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Co-n"--anoi-cs on Monday evening Dr. HUNTER asked whether the Prime Minister would move the appointment of a select committee to inquire hits the occurrences in the House last Thursday night, and after Mr. Labouchere had quoted a statement made in the press by Mr. Hayes Fisher, the Speaker invited Mr. Fisher and Mr. Logan to address the House. Both hon. gentlemen did so, Mr. FISHER offering the fullest apology for his attack on Mr. Logan, and the latter expressing his regret at having crossed the floor of the House, and disclaiming any intention to assault anyone. Mr. GLAD- STONE then said he thought there was a widespread sen- timent that in the circumstances investigation by a committee ought, if possible, to be avoided. Proceedings such as those of Thursday night were rightly regarded by the country as disgraceful, but he hoped that the House would, after the explanations which had been made, consent to regard this incident as definitely closed. Mr. Balfour concurred in the Prime Minister's remarks. Mr. JUSTIN WCARTHY expressed his satisfac- tion at the conchamnation which the proceedings of Thursday had received from the Premier and the leader of the Opposition, but felt it his duty to protest against the allegation of many newspapers that the disturbance of Thursday was " an Irish row," and to declare that no Nationalist member had anything to di) with the affair in the first instance or took any part hilt unless he was forced to act in self-defence, or sought to act as a peace- maker. He was disposed to ask for a formal resolution to this effect. Sir H. JAMES (in the absence of Mr. Ckamberlain) endorsed Mr. Gladstone's observations. The Speaker said he hoped the matter would now be allowed to rest both in the House and out of it, and the subject then dropped. MT.GLADSTONE informed Mr. Bartley that the Govern- ment hoped to take the Welsh Suspensory Bill and the Local Veto Bill when they had made sufficient progress with the Home Rule Bill. The House went into Com- mittee on the Education estimates for England and Wales. Mr. Acland made the annual statement on the progress of education, and moved a vote of £3,891,000. The total amount required was £6,200,000. Much of the right hon. gentleman's speech was devoted to the subjecti of overcrowding and insanitary echo, Is. free schooling, and secondary education. At midn ght the closure was moved, and was carried by 156 to 65, after which the vote was agreed. to.

In the House of Lords the Earl of Meath drew atten- tion to the evidence elven at the Victoria Court-martial as to the inability of many of the men to swim, and Earl SPENCER replied that the admiralty ;re fully alive to the importance of the question, and that increased facil- ities would be given to teach the men of the navy this necessary art.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday, Mr. ASQUI TR replied to Mr. Barlow regarding the exhumation of a child's body at Crewe. Mr. ASQUITII stated that the police were free from blame, and that the coroner was responsible for ordering the exhumation. Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY replied to questions regarding the inward American mails, stating that until he had seen the effect of the alteration which had been made in the sailings of the American packets he was not in a position to make any recommendation. Mr. H. GARDNER informed Mr. Chaplin that he could not yet state what would ba the terms of reference to the Royal Commission upon Agricultural Depression. The House, in Committee of Supply on the Civil Ser- vice Estimates, discussed the vote of £142,710 for ordin- ance survey. The vote was agreed to.

In the House of Lords Lord ROSEBERY, replying to Lord Salisbury, said that her Majesty's Government had signed an agreement at Paris, which provided for the establishment of a neutral zone or buffer territory be- tween territory in Indo-China and that recently taken by France. The effect of a geneul statement made by Lord Rosebery on the Franco-Siamese difficulty was that there was no truth in the rumour as to the French admiral having ordered her Majesty's cruiser Pallas and the gun- boat Swift to proceed outside the limits of the blockade newly defined. Lord Rosebery confirmed the accept- ance by Siam of the French demands, but asked for notice of a question by Lo-d Lamington on the gm, graphical effects of the French terms. WhDNESDAY. In the House of Cammons on Wednesday, in Commit- tee of Supply, Sir It. TEMPLE moved the reduction of the Foreign Office vote in order to ask for further infokrua- tion on the Siam question. He said there was an in- pression that British diplomacy had received a check, and that Siam had been hardly treated. He cengratulated the Government on getting quit of the blockade, but desired to know the extent of the territory ceded by Siam, and whether satisfactory negotiations were pro- ceeding for the establishment of a neutral zone. Mr. CURZON spoke of the supreme importance to this coun- try of the integrity of Siam, and urged the British Government to ask the French Government to give some assurance that Slain would now be left to work out her own fortunes. Sir EDWARD GREY, in reply, regretted that Mr. Curzon, at a time when delicate negotiations were proceeding, should have entered into a criticism of French policy. The attitude of the Government had been strong and emphatic. and the French Government had agreed to admit the principle of a buffer State and to negotiate on that basis. There was no reason to believe that the occupation of the islands in the Gulf was in- tended to be permanent. They had the assurance of the French Government that the blockade was to be raised that day, and he did not see that there had been any direct loss to British trade. The true policy and the one pursued by the British Government had been to define what their interests in that part of the world were, and with regard to the neutral zone, there was a real desire on the part of both Governments that it should be pre- served. There was every prospect of a settlement' with- out endangering the good relations of the two countries. Mr. BALFOUR and Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT spoke on the question. Discussion followed with regard to the atti- tude of the Gsvernment towards the Armenian prisoners in Angora, The amendment to reduce the vote was withdrawn, and progress reported. The House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock. THURSDAY. In the House of Commons on Thursday evening the PRESIDENT of the Board of Trade replying to Mr. Burns, said the Labour Department had a report in an advanced state of preparation dealing with the whole subject of unemployed labour and the various agencies in operation for finding work or other relief. The House went into Co.-nmittee of Supply on the vote on account for the Civil Service and Revenue departments. Mr. Tastmsost complained of the dila- tory procedure of the Committee now sitting on railway rates and charges, and of the publication of a report by Sir C. Boyle pronouncing as to the mode in which the Board of Trade ought to deal with complaints of traders under the conciliation clause, and he moved to reduce- the vote for the Board of Trade. Mr. MUNDELL& said he looked forward with a good deal of hove and satis- faction to the report of the Commission. The Board of Trade were doing everything they possibly could in the interests of the traders consistently with the prosperi y of the railway companies. Mr. Tomlinson withdrew his motion. Mr. WOODS repeated his complaint about the relations of Messrs. M'Corquodale (a firm of Government contrac- tors) with theirworkpeople, and moved the reduction of the vote. Sir J. T. Ilunicirr said there was nothing in the recent resolution of the House which enabled the

...„ . „..,- freasury to interfere In this flatter. After some dis- cussion. Mr. BUXTON said that when the contract cerminated one of the conditions of renewal would be that no preference should be given to nun-union work- men. Sir J. T. HIBBERT concurred, and on this undeva standing the motban was withdrawn._

Tho lietentien THE opponents cf the Government of make no secret of their intention to Irish Members. utilise to the fullest extent, for party purposes, the intention of the Governim,nt to retain eighty Irish members in the Imperial Parliament. The dealing with the Irish repre- sentation in the House of Commons, in the event of self-govermnent being extended to Ire- land, has been from the first one of the knottiest problems which the Government has had to encounter in developing their scheme of Home

Rule. Considering its importance and the com- plicated issues involved in it, it is pre-eminently a question which could best be solved by a patrio- tic combination of all parties. But, of coarse, an absolutely necessary condition for such a combina- tion is that the Opposition should be. prepared to place Patriotism before Party. At the present time such a condition is altogether wanting. In their dealings with this particular question the Opposition have been utterli unscrupulous in their inconsistencies, aid have disregarded all the best traditions of Parliamentary procedure. When it was thought that the Government con- templated the exclusion of the Irish memberk there was no limit to the denunciation of such a proposal. It was declared that this was nothing but "separation" in its nakedest form, stripped, in fact,of all disguise. Ws could not,we were told,con- tinne to tax Irishmen for imperial purposes when Irish representatives had no voice in the imperial expenditure. Then, when it was suggested that Ireland might be represented in the Bans° of Commons when imperial affairs were under con- sideration, it was objected that this was simply "dementing" Parliament, by involving the legisla- ture in hopeless confusion. The Governmentras Mr. GLADSTONE says in an important letter to one of his Midlothian constituents, which really takes the form of a iaanifesto, "have desired that nothing should be done in the dark 7 and finding that the House of Commons and the country were in favour of retention, they have chosen that method of retention which, on the whole, appeared least entangled in difficulties of principle. This is simply to retain eighty Irish members in Parliament for all pur- poses. But the sweet simplicity of this arrange- ment does not meet with the approval of the Opposition. They objected to exclusion ; they were equally vehement in their condemnation of partial retention, and now with that fine lack of consistency which has marked their conduct all through this Parliament they will not even have anything to do with full retentien. This, they now discover, is making Irishmen not only mas- ters in their own country, but also the arbiters of Great Britain. In other words, the nearly six hundred members returned from England, Scot- land, ana Wales, are to be so thoroughly weak, or unpatriotic, as to allow themselves to be domin- ated by the .eighty Irish 'members. The only evi- dence of this, is, as Mr. GrLansrorts points out, the "great manextuvre "of the Tory party in 1885, when, by inducements hold out to the Irish mem- bers, they procured the dislodgement of the Liberal Government of that period, and their own accession to office. "That proceeding of the Tory Party is," says Mr. GLADSTONE, "so far as I know,unexampled in our Parliamentary history ;" and, further than that, "it shows that the yeti. worst consequences now apprehended by some from Irish interposition in a political crisis has actually happened under or existing arrange- ments for the government tind representation of Ireland." It is quite certain, however, that the country would not tolerate very often such Parliamentary stratagems as that by which the Tories secured office in 1885; and it is puerile to urge that those parts of the Kingdom represented by more than five hundred members could be dominated by the eighty Irish votes. ,

The squab"; THE members who so greviously in misbehaved themselves in the Parliament. House of Commons are now, it seems, quits penitent. Mr. MYRA lemma, who ornaments the Tory benches; was the first to apply physical force against a Parliamentary opponent, land on Monday he made his apology to his fellow 'legislators. The apology amounted pretty much to this: Mr. Timm thought MT. LOGAN was going to assault'him, therefore he assaulted MT. LOGAN. The 10880 n which MT. FISHER'S political opponents may deduct from the apology is, that when they wish to approach that gentleman they must assume their meekest and mildest smile, otherwise Bir.Fxsitza may misconstrue their inten- tions.. Needless to say; Mr. Looari assured the House that he never intended to assault Mr. Fisher or anybody else; and, indeed, the fact that he was attacked from behind ratherdiscounts the Tory mentber's account of; the affair. There is no doubt that those who were most concerned in the discreditable incident wish it to be buried in oblivion,. but the public generally do not regard it in the Same light as hon. members, and therefore the account contributed to our columns ' by a Runcorn gentleman, who was a spectator,wiTh be read with interest. This account supports the ' conclusion that we put forward last week that the real origin of the fracas was to be found in Mr.. CHLMBEELAIN'S bitter harangue. By a series of studied flouts and jeers,the leader of the Liberal Unionists provided, so to speak, a pile of com- bustible material in the form of angry passions, and then in the last sentence of his speech,bycom- paring Mr. GLADSTONE to Herod, he applied the spark that was necessary to raise a conflagration. All the other events sprang from this, as it were,, bya natural sequence.

ACCORDING to a writer on agri- Oer Ahlk cultural topics the question of a supply. standard for milk is likely to come to the front before long. The adulterating of milk seems to have almost reached the elevation of a fine art. There are at least three ways of doing it. The first is the old and simple one of going; directly and unblushingly to the pump. All the • requisites necessary are a bucket and a hardy con- science. This method sufficed for our grand- fathers—or was it our grandmothers p—but then there were no analysts in those days. It seems j that the analyst can detect the presence of water j with certainty, and this of course, is rather dis- j concertimg for those people who wish to 1111 their j milk cans economically. This little impediment . jin the way of thrifty management has been sur- mounted by the using of separated or "skim " ' milk in place of water. The analyst, we are told, "is usually unable to • define the presence of separated milk." But there is jstill another and a j more refined•mode of adulteration, and that is by using the cow herself as an innocent accomplice. By keeping inferior cattle and feeding them upon j inferior and insufficient food, milk of a low quality 'is produced. Yet it is pure milk inarnueh as it :comes direct from the cow. In the present state of j the law there is little check eveu upon flagrant and undoubted adulteration so long as the quality of the milk does not fall below a certain low stan- dard. What the milk reformers are demanding is that the standard should be raised, or that there should be two standards. In this matter the pub- lic who suffer from the uncertain quality of the milk supply will take the side of the reformer. All they require is that they should be supplied with that for which they pay.

div.head: ENGINE.
div.p: ENGINE.

At about ten o'clock on Saturday night, a fire broke out in a house in Priestly-street, inhabited by Miss Kerinocie. The fire engine was quickly got out of the station, but owing to a large crowd having gathered around, the brigade was unable to go along heath-side, but had to go through Allen- street. In turning from Allen-street to Froghall- lane the reins broke and the driver lost 'control of the horses. This caused the pole of the fire engine to collide with the wall and it was smashed. -The horses were only slightly injured. When the brig- ade arrived at Miss Kermode's house, they found the bedroom in flames, but the fire was soon ex- tinguished. The damage is estimated to be about S5O. -

ALL HOUSEHOLD LINEN, .hemmed and marked, free of charge,—J. and W. DUTTON, Saakey-st.—Adrt. WARRINGTON FIELD CLUB. Several members of• the above named club journeyed to Hatcbmere via Frodsham. They de- parted from Bank Quay Station at 2.27 p.m., and after an hour's walk from Frodsham Station. they reached Dela Mere Forest, at Hatchmere, which is considered the nearest place near Warrington, where, it is possible to get into an open forest. Mr. Billups was the leader and .a successful day's botanizing was spent. The following plants were new to the club on its rambles :—Anagallis tenella, Montia fontana, Radiola linoides, Scutellaria minor, Calamagrestis lanceolate, Cladium mariscue, Veronica scutellata, Spharganium minimum, Narthecium ossifragum, Carexbiv'ervis, Geranium phteum, Ilypericum pulchrum. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.--J. and W.DUTTON, Sankey-st.., Warrington.—Adv'. WALKING DAY AT STRIOTTON.

The children have had their annual Sunday school treat at Stretton. They assembled at the school at half-past one, and headed by the Blue Coat School band, playing' Onward, Christian Sol- diers, proceeded to church, where a short sermon was preached by the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Dodd. On leaving the church they proceeded to the Vicar- age, where every child partook of wine and cake. They ufterwards joined in procession, and marched round the village headed by the band,which played lively airs. On reaching the schools, the children partook of a substantial tea,af ter which Mrs. Lyons distributed the prizes. The remainder of the day was spent in racing and other amusements. In the evening a dance took place in the schoolroom,which was well attended. A good band was in attendance, and dancing was kept up with spirit for several hours. ON "Thi Rocxs."

At the conclusion ni—i-14--b-u—siness at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, two lady artistes came forward along with Mr. 11. Taylor, tne police court missionary. The Chief Constable informed the Bench that these young women had been at his howe on Sunday wanting assistance. This was tha third time that such people had come to him. It was becoming a regulta thing to apply to the court to assist applicants of this class from town to town. Ile did not think the poor box was intended for that purpose. One of the actresses said they had been acting in the Theatre Royal. Their manager was on share system and had lost heavily, and had only paid them 2. They now wanted to get to Barrow,where they had an engagement. The magis- trates subscribed the necessary amount among themselves and handed it to the applicants, who appeared greatly relieved._

TUC WARRINGTON HAIRDRF.SSERS* ASSOCIATION. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Hair- dressers' Association was held on Tuesday night in the Horsemarket-st. Cocoa Rooms. There was a good muster of members present and the chair was occupied by the president, Mr. McClew.—The minutes of the last meeting were read and adopted, after which the question as to whether it was ad- visable to join the Trades Council arose.—Mr. J. Podmore, junr., explained that the subscription re- quired to join the Council would be 3d. per member per annum, which would secure tte sympathy and support of the rest of the trades unionists in the town. When the shop assistants joined the Coun- cil, they received practical support from i t.—M r. P. Green hoped that the AsQociation would pay the subscriptions of the members.—After further dis- cussion Mr. J. Podmore, senr., proposed, and Mr. liedgecock seconded, a motion that the Hair- dre: Association join the Trades Council and that the -Association pay the subscriptions. This motion was carried unanimously.—A long discus- sion then ensued- on the question of arranging to visit shops on Sundays. It appeared that there were two hairdressers who declared that they would not close on Sundays. It was decided to give them warning before further proceedings were taken, and on the motion of Mr. Wm. Podmore, seconded by Mr. Wainwright, the secre Airy, Mr. Smith was em- powered to cboose any member as visitor,—lt was also decided on the motion of Mr. C. Oldtield to have a large number of handbills and also large tainted bills to get the support of the public to their movement. It was further resolved that the Association meet the first Tuesday in each month to transact business. It was mentioned that 25 out of 32 of the local hairdressers had joined the Society.

div.p: TTIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 5. 1893.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT
RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
The Rev. J. Pafford, pastor of St. John's Presby- terian Church, has now completely recovered from the severe illness which afflicted him, and he will again occupy the pulpit on Sunday.

The Runcorn Commissioners will add greatly to the,efficienev of the Fire Brigade by the proposals adopted on Thursday. With the men scattered in all parts of the town, and a beil that caused the sound to travel a very short distance, it was not to he wondered at that sometimes there was delay in getting to the Fire Station. It is satisfactory to know on the authority of Mr. liankinson, that the hrizade has always been well equipped, and, with hall-a-iiozen firemen living in consecutive houses, we may expect the brigade to how even better work than they have aCcomplished in the past. Lightburn's idea of surprise alarms ought cer- tainly to be carried out.

A singular difficulty arose at the sale of the kiod- sham Auction Company, on Tuesday last. The auctioneer, Mr. Jones, either through the prevailing epidemic, or some other cause failed to put in ap- pearance and the officials and members present were in a quandary, because there was much live stock that required to be put "in the bidding." Of course, in the time of suspense mine kost • Yowl did not neglect business. At length Mr. Mitchinson the'secretary of the Company gallantly mounted the rostrum, and asked " 'tow much for this, gentle- men." lie conducted a first class sale, and next day to obviate any difficulty with the government officials he took out an auctioneer's license. As he made se capital a start, probably he will now enter the business.

div.head: LOCAL GOVERNMENT_ BOARD INQUIRY
div.p: LOCAL GOVERNMENT_ BOARD INQUIRY
AT WIDNES. THE BORROWING POWERS OP THE BOROUGH.

On Monday morning, at the Town Hall, Mr. E. P. Bard, an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry on behalf of the Local Government Board, who proposed that the Board should par- tially repeal, alter Or amend by provisional order, the Local Government Supplemental Health Act 1871 (No. 4), so as to provide for the repeal, except so far as it has been acted upon, of a provisional order far extending the borrowing powers of the Widnes. Local Board, and confirmed by the said Act, and to make such alterations in the Act as may be necessary in connection with the object of the proposal. There were present his worship the Mayor (Alderman F. 11. Gossage), Council- lor W. Christie, Messrs. J. Fitzpatrick (Appleton), H. S. Oppenheim (town clerk), T. Craik (assistant town clerk), and S. lloyD (accountant). The Town Clerk pointed out this order absolutely fixed the maximum period of repayment of loans at 30 years. The matter was of considerable importance in a borough like Widnes, where a large amount of new work had to be underttoken. An applicatiom . would shortly come before the Local °over:meat Board for power to borrew money for technical 6CIIOOIA, and it was considered by the ratepayers that a period of 30 years inflicted a hard- ship upon them and placed an unnecessary burden upon thedrates for the time being. . _ .

The Inspector said Parliament had fixed the 30 years. The Town Clerk thougbt it was left to the'cliscretion of the Local Government Board. The time at the dispo- sal of the Ccuncil had been very short, and the Finance Committee had not considned the matter, and he thought sufficient time had not been allowed. The order had not been acted upon, as it had never been brought before the authority when applying for loans. Ele wished to keep the position of the Corporation intact, and he could not consent to the s iteration of that Act of Parlia- ment which confirmed the limit of time allowed by the Local Government Board. The repealing cr altering, of the Confirmatory Act was a matter which the Local Government Board could only entertain on the applica- tion of the local authority. He was alive to the fact that the Local Government Board nevertheless took a different view of the matter. The Corporation pro- tested against any alteration of any Act of Parliament referring to their borourfli except by their own motion. He did not think there was anything likely to cause con- fusion, for, so far as he had been able to ascertain no loan had been taken up between 1871 and 187 b, when the law on the point, became general. It seemed that when the power might have been used it was not necessary. The Inspector : So far there has been no borrowing at all under the Act P The Town Clerk said that wail so. The Inspector said he found in many cases the power had not been acted upon at all. The Town Clerk, continuing, said the assessable value bad very largely increased since 1871, when the gross value was £55,180, in 1881 it had increased to £101,943, and at the present thee it was about £150,000: These were the only points the Town Clerk said he could bring before the Inspector, who promised to lay 1 the matter before the Local Government Board.

Mr. Fitzpatrick: I take it that this inquiry is to obtain powers for borrowing money? The Inspector: No, it is just the opposite. It is to repeal the borrowing powers of the local authority. Mr. Fitzpatrick said he thought the public ought to bawl a word in the matter. They had before them a question of spending £lO,BOO for a technical

The town Clerk said the public inquiry would beheld in connection with that in the ordinary way. Mr. Fitzpatrick, con!louing, said that was a public inquiry at any rate, and he considered it ought to be held at a time when the public could convesiently attend. He thought that in days when they heard so much of the privileges of the public and workingmen it was unreasonable that the meeting should be fixed for ten o'clock in the morning.

Bread and milk are almost as safe a diet for most animal's as for human beings, and 5,000 quarters of bread and 6,000 quarts of milk represent the quantity of this wholesome food coneurned at the Zoo. Most of thq insect-eating birds, many monkeys, and certain snakes and lizards are egg-eaters ; and nineteen thousand eggs probably ac- count for twice that number of breakfasts supplied to the smaller occupants of the houses. The total of car- cases eaten by ell the lions, tigers, bears, hyen.is,wolves, leopards,and other large carnivore in the gardens during I the year amounts to 230 horses and 152 goats. The fish- monger's bill is a heavy one, when not only seals, otters, and sea lions, which will eat nothing else, but also num- bers of piscivorous birds and even the polar bears, have to be provided with flounders, whiting, and conger eels daily-38,000bd whiting,lo,ooolb. of "rough fish," 630 quarts of shrimps,and 2,0001b.0f flounders were consumed by the seals and other aquatic creatures. The live gudgeons Whose pursuitand capture from the daily excitement of the penguins in their glass-fronted sank, do not appear in the list of food provided, any more than the army of mice and rats, and dozens of live frogs, which frolic be- hind the scenes in the snakehouse. Unhonoured in their lives, their deaths are unrecorded, or figure darkly I ainong " miscellaneous expenses." The fact is that the rearing of tame mice and rats, and the capture and pur- veyance of live frogs, is an interesting and unexplored side-industry of London life. Fruit is almost as neces- sary as fish at all seasons in the Gardens, and no visitor can have failed to notice the daintly arranged " desert" of sliced bananas, grapes, dates and apples, which is served up to the rarer monkeys and fruit-eating birds. Thirteen thousand oranges, 2.0001 b. of grapes, 1,2001 h. of dates, and 2001 b. of raisins and currants represent the fruiter's bill ; the greengrocer comes last, with 2,641 bunches of tares, 4,500 hunches of. greens, and 2,600 bundles of cress. Cherries, onions, melons, marrows, bananas, and figs vary the bill of tare, which we may close with the solid item of 139 cwt of carrots and nearly two tons of ground nuts.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART.
AWARDS TO PUPILS.

The Lancashire:- Cmnty Council on Thursday awarded scholarships and exhibitions which have been granted, as the result ef examinations held in June. For the four scholarships of £6O per annum tenable for three years at some college or institu- tion to be approved of by the Technical Committee of the County Council, there were 24 candidates. Of the four scholarships awarded, one was gained by Oswald Garside, of the Warrington School of Art. For the art exhibition of £lO, tenable at such college, institution or class as may be approved of by committee, 88 candidates presented themselves. Of the 28 successful candidates, the following were successful from the Warrington School of Art : Richard Daintith, Albert E. Uislop, Beatrice Lees, Eleanor Spinks and J. Millard. It will be remem- bered that in the competitions last year, two students, Messrs. Dooley, and Woodier secured the £6O scholarships. They have beep studying during the past six months at Julien Studio in Paris where it is probable that Mr. flarside will also study. The £lO exhibitions will be held at the Warrington School of Art.

The Medical offiee.Thi:McDougall) repOrted that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 59. • One of these was an inquest case, and of the remaining 58, 37 were due to diarrhoea, 3to mesenteric disease, 2 to bronchitis, 2 to senile decay, 2 to apoplexy, and one each to &avulsions, ascites, pneu- monia, excema, heart disease, gastritis, pernicious ancetnia, strumous disease,parturition, premature birth, puerperal fever; and whooping cough. The fifty-nine deaths show an average death rate 01354 per 1,000 for ' the twelve months, and exclusive of the inquest case of 34•8.—The Surveyor said there were 37 deaths in July last year.
HIGHWAY AND 2111LD1,0 AFFAIRS.

- The Highway and Building Committee recommended that the Postmaster, Mr. W. K. Orrell, having requested permission for a caretaker to reside on the Post Office premises, it is recommended that permission be granted on condition that the upper rooms only are used for such a purpose and sotely by the caretaker and his wife, and that such rooms are properly ventilated. That a sum of £BO be paid to the Runcorn Co-operative Society for a strip of land of 65 superficial .yards (marked yellow on plan) in front of proposed new premises in flaltou-road, such land being required for the purpose of the said pre- mises being put in a line with, the adjoining premises. That a shed for the steam rdler be erected at the Town Yard, Heath-road, in accordance with the plan sub- mitted, at an estimated nost of £55, and that the cost thereof be.defrayed out of the loan account e also that instructions be given to the Surveyor to proceed at once with the work. That the plan of Messrs. G. Marshall and Bate for the erection of two semi-detached villa residences in Weston-road be approved, subject to the box rooms being ventilated. Mr. Fisher moved the adoption of the minutes, and ex- plained that with regard to the payment of £BO to the Co-operative Society,that the foot walk and the carriage way in Halton-road were very narrow, and the Commit- tee thought it advi:able to get Ole society to put their property back so that the road and foot walk might be widened. The property would he set back six feet. The Committee had agreed to pay £.l a .yard for the land which would amount to £65, and there was a further £l5 for extra expense the society would be put to and for the loss of a cottage. Ttie society had met them very fairly, and the Committee would obtain a desirable public improvement at a very easy figure.—The Chair- man pointed out that Halton-road was the only approach to Runcorn and the traffic was very heavy. For the small sum of £BO the Board had an opportunity of carry- ing- out a most essential imnrovement.—Mr. Grice spoke in terms of praise of the favourable way in which the society met the Committee and the Chairman endorsed the statement.—The minutes were approved. .

This Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. T. Leach for the supply of uniform clothing for the Sanitary Inspector, consisting of one overcoat, one coat, one vest, two pairs of trousers and one cap, fur the sum of £7 es. be accepted •, and that the Sanitary Inspector be authorized to disinfect houses when requested by the owners thereof at a maximum ch irge of 7s. 6d. each.— Approved on the motion of Mr. Liglitburn, seconded by Mr. Lea. TME FIRE DRIGAIMI.—IMPORTANT IMPROVEMENTS.

The Canal Boats and General Purposes Committee recommended that six canal boats be registered. The committee submitted the following recommendations with a view of securing a quicker turn out of the Fire Brigade ; that six firemen two within close proximity to the Police Station, and that a sum of 303. each be paid per annum to such firemen in addition to their present remuneration. The superintendent to settle as to the situation of the firemen's houses ; that 23. 6d. be paid to the police constable who may warn the six firemen, call- , boys and die watchman at the Sprinch Works in case of a fire at night ; Is. 6d. to be paid to the constable for warning the call-boys and watchman if the fire occurs during the das -time ; that a distinctive steam whistle be fixed at the Spriuch Works, to be blown in ease of fire, the consent of the yanchester Ship Canal Company hav- ing been obtained subject to an agreement being entered into ' • that is. 6d. be paid to the watchman at the Sprinch Works for each occasion on which the whistle may be blown by him ; that not more than five firemen with the superintendent or deputy-superintendent be allowed to 'attend fires outside the district of the commissioners, thus ensuring the attendanoe of six firemen with the superintendent or deputy-superictenient at a fire which may simultaneously.oceur in the town ; and that the Water Committee, when formed, be recommended to instruct its staff to give notice to the superintendent of the Fire Brigade whenever it is proposed to turn off the supply of water in any past of the town. Mr. Hapkitison moved the adoption of the minutes. He thought they would all see the necessity for•adopting the recommendations with reference to the fire brigade. It would be a step in the right direction, and would en- able the men to act more expeditiously in case of fire, which would be a saving of property, and probably of life. The brigade was well equipped, and the appliances were considered quite adequate to cope with emergency. They had a manual which was reckoned by the Superin- tendent to be a very excellent one and capable of doing good service, and they had also all other necessary ap- pliances. They had thought it best to let the men live as near the station as possible, considering the expen- siveness of electric bells. The present alarm bell was like an old cracked pan, and it was therefore necessary to hare a whistle et a' distinctive sound, and Mr. Wis- wall had consented to tha one at Sprinch Works being put into order. Mr: Bisbrown seconded. By making the reCOMmenda- tions, the committee thought they would make the PH- gado more efficient. They were acting in perfect agree- , ment with Mr. Wright, the superintendent, and if the minutes were passed the public mind would be eased, and they would make matters far more satisfactory. I They had been assured by the Surveyor that the hydrants were all right. Mr. Lightburn, in supporting, recommended that " trial fires " should now and again take place, so that the brigade would become thoroughly efficient. 'I he exercises were arranged for stated periods, and the men were able to prepare beforehand. . . _ .
Mr. Wiswall concurred. He thought that the false alarms might be productive of good. The minutes were confirmed. PLEASURE GROUNDS AND COMMON LANDS COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that they had considered the offer of Mr. George Marshall to give land at " Bea- consfield " for a pleasure ground on condition that the Board pay the annual chief rent of £66 4s. 6d., and they recommended that the offer be declieed, the com- mittee being of opinion that any expenditure of money should be in the direction of obtaining the control of the common lands, and of the regulation of the same, and of arranging for the use of the cemetery field. Mr. Pritchard proposed the miuutes. Fie said it would be impossible to take all the schemes in hand,and the matter of the common lands had progressed to a cer- tain point, and the committee were of opinion that it should be pressed forward. They considered the project would be of the greatest advantage to the public. Mr. Bisbrown seconded. He was pleased that the committee had been resuscitated. They wanted to sup- ply a public want, and they were using their best endeavours to secure land for recreative purposes. A small committee had been appointed ta wait upon the freeholders for the common land, and they were in com- munication with the Burial Board, who, in their opinion would throw no obstacle in their way. Re did not thiak the provision of recreative grounds, in this uay pro- posed, would necessitate the incurring of much expense to the ratepayers..

- . . Mr. Pritchard, in answer to Mr. Meadowcroft, stated that there were probably 80 or 100 freeholders and they had obtained the'consent of more than 60, which enabled them to bring down a Commissioner to make an inquiry But it was necessary to obtain two-thirds of the rateable value, and the largest fre ehelders did not see their way to give their consent. If, licw*ver, they were person- ally waited upon, it was possible they weuld willingly agree, and thereby the existing difficulty would be removed. He understood that by the proposed legisla- tion the common lands would he placed under the con- trol of district councils, which would greatly facilitatc matters. _
Th ----------- were carried. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

_ ALLEGED ROBBERY.—Thomas Conroy, John Conroy Caroline-st. ; Margaret Gilmore, James McCann; Mar- garet-st. ; and Robert Stapleton, Charlotte-st., were charged with entering a bakehouse, and stealing bread valued at 4d.—Pat McCracken, baker to William Hale- wood, Ann-street, said he left the bakehouse safe about six o'clock en Tuesday night, and when he returned about nine he found the window smashed, but lie was not sure that there was any bread missing.
