div.head: • WARRINGTON AND THE CANAL
div.p: • WARRINGTON AND THE CANAL

Since the London and Nortle-Western Railway " have commenced to run the passenger trains on the new embankments at Latchford and Moore, the Ship Canal Company have made rapid progress in their work near Warrington. At Latchford, one is struck with the busy appearance under the new rail- way bridge near the locks. The wooden structure for pas- sengers over the cutting in Thelwall-lane has been pulled down, and for the future anyone wishing to go to Thel- wall or Lytnin will have to cross the new swing bridge nearer Latchford station. There are four steam navvies here hard at work cutting through the old line. The house which was formerly the habitation of the man to look after the crossings at this spot is almost pulled down, being of no further use. At this part of the cut- ting there arn about 100 hundred men engaged in blasting and other work, and very soon the old line of railway will no longer block the way. The swing bridge over which Knutsford-road will soon cross is practically finished, but the temporary bridges in Knuts- ford-road and Grappenhall-lane are not yet demolished. From Grappenhall-lane to the cantilever bridge near the ' new station, nothing of any consequence is to be seen. The cantilever bridge is now open to footpassengers but is not sufficiently completed to allow vehicular traffic to Use it. From the top of this bridge owing to its elevation, a fine view can he obtained of the country round. Beyond the station can be seen Mar- tinscruft and Rixton, and further still Rivington, from vbence -Liverpool' obtained their water before they acquired the Vyrnwry Works. The view extends far past Warrington, and smoky Widnes can also be seen in the distance. 'rho outlook into Cheshire is rather limited owing to the woody nature of the country. From the top of the cantilever bridge, two roads branch off, one towards Stockton Beath and the other towards Thelwall. A little past this bridge, pre- parations are being made for pile drivtng., owing to the sandy nature of the cutting not being sufficient to stand the wear and tear when the canal is finished. The War- rington side is completed, and the space between the piles and the side filled with rock. Coming to Twenty Step Bridge, we again arrive at an animated scene. AI, steam navvy is at work at the soil near this old bridge. By next week probably, the read over this bridge will , be stopped, and the •;.:blic will have to go across the new swing bridge to Stockton Reath. The barge leek into the Old Quay Canal is not yet, finished, nor ere the I pipes belonging to the Warrington Water Works, laid under the cutting. The most striking feature about this part of the country is the large number of new houses which are being built, and Stockton Heath has grown to be a very populous village in consequence. In fact,any- one who has not been in the village for three or four years will scarcely recognise it. Proceeding from Twenty I Step Bridge, another uninteresting length is passed un- til we come to Tom Paine's Bridge. The hydraulic house near this structure is so far completed that the roof is being put on. Of the fine row of houses which oace were here there only remains the crumbled ruined walls of a single room. The syphon pipe, down which a boy fell a few weeks ago with fatal consequences, is now barricaded to prevent like accidents occurring again. On the opposite side of the river a large number of men are to be seen, commencing the Warrington docks. The swing bridge at Acton Grange, over which will cross the road from %Vilderspool crossings to Moore, is practically finished? very little now remaining to be done. *Mere is still a lot of work to be done to the bridge, however, before it will be ready for use. Near this bridge at the entrance to the new cutting of the river, a dredger is hard at work deepening that part a the cutting. From here till we get to the old railway at Moore, thecanal is finished, but at Moore, the busiest part of the section is arrived at. No fewer than six steam navvies are tearing up the earth within abut 50 yards, and there are about 200 men at work in addition. The old line is now eutthrough although not yet to the full depth of the canal,hut in a week or two thie portion of the canal will also be complete. At the opposite side of the railway is the engine house and store house in which are a large number of engines and cranes,and large quantities of coal, ceinent.fen. Beyond the railway the canal is almost complete as far as Runcorn, ~nd within a few months, should no iinooward circumstances occur, the canal will be open,alinost, if not as far as Warrington,

At a meeting of the Town Council, on Tuesday II igh•, Councillor R. T. Fairclough, the chairman of the Ilivt-rs Committee, reported that in company with Councillor Bolton and the Borough Surveyor, lie had waited upon the Engineer to the Manchester Ship Canal Company with reference t.) the construction of the lock and sluices at Walton, and also the dredging of the river. Mr. Hunter, the deputy-engineer, stated that the con- tract for the lock alul sluice was 1,413 te the contractor, who was proceeding with the work, that the dredging of the river was commenced on Monday, the 25th ult., and that no time would be lost in completing the works. According to the amended plan, a tracing of which has since been sent to the Borough Surveyor, it is proposed to construct the lock at Walton 150 feet long and 30 feet wide,'its position being on the north side of the river, nearly opposite the cutting forming the entrance from the canal to the Warrington Dock. It is ale proposed to construct the lock on land forming part of Arpley Meadows, and to widen the river at the point 150 feet, to enable the work to be carried out without interfering With traffic on the river. This is considered an improve- ment upon the plan previously prorwsed. Council/or Fairclough added that proviously the proposal was to make the lock at Walton 125 feet by 25 feet, but the Ship Canal Company had fallen in with the Committee's ideas and had congented to make it 150 feet by 30 feet. —Alderman Harrison remarked that they had reason to congratulate themselves, and especially Councillor Fair- dough, upon having been so successful with the Ship Canal Company. He co:ild not help but think that the concessions obtained from thcl company would ultimately result very advantageously to Warrington.

div.head: SOLDIERS ROUTED BY A SWARM OF
div.p: SOLDIERS ROUTED BY A SWARM OF
BEES..

BERLIN, WEDNESESY Numr.--The following detailed account of an expedition through East Africa, under the command of Freiherr van Manteuffel has reached Ber- lin. In Kwaruguru, where the Sultan Lonjo had been appointe I Vali by the Germans, three insurgent chime who refused to recognise German rules and organized forays, were to be tried. Two submitted, Out the third, Matura, from Pongwe, had to he forced Co submissinn. The head of the troops reached Nime, a thousand metres from Pongwe, upon which the guns were planted. A number o people were seen in front of the village heat- ing the war drum :tmidst howls and yells, and several shots were fired by them. fierenpon the Commander gave orders for the village. to be bombarded with grenades. After the fourth shot a remarkable incident took place. The troops as well as the bearers were at- tacked by a gigantic swarm of bees and completely routed. It took about an hour for them all to collect to- gether again, Sergeant-Major Mittelstaedt and an Ascari being missing. The guns and arnmonition had been left behicd on the mountain. A patrol was sent out to search for the sergeant, and he was found at his gun nearly stung to death. An hour afterwards,, when the sergeant had recovered, the fight was resumed ambthe village stormed. The eflect of the grenades had so frightened the enemy that the village was asuipletely deserted.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENTS YtESTERDAY.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENTS YtESTERDAY.

Another addition to the already long list of fatal accidents caused in the conbtruction of the Dial- cheater :Ship Canal, occurred at Latchford yester- day. John Ball, aged 16, residing in Dial-st., War- rington, who was employed on the Latchford sec- tion of the Canal, was following his employment there yesterday. at 12 o'clock, when he got crushed between the buffers of two loaded waggons. He was immediately conveyed to the Latchford hospi- tal, but died an hour after adtaittance. Deceased who had Worked on the Canal previously, was only re-started two or three weeks ago.

About live o'clock yesterday afternoon, a fatality occurred in a large sand hole at Stockton Heath. A nurnbtr of children were playing mit burrowingholes under the sides of the pit, when over a ton of sand and stones fell in. A .child named James Percival, seven years of age, son of James Percival, horse- driver on the Bridgewater Canal, Nva. embedded .in the tailing mass. Prompt assistance was ren- dered in extricating the lad, but a few minutes elapsed before he was reached. On being recovered Dr. Parker was immediately on the spot, and pro- nounced life extinct. The body was still warm,and had received a few slight bruises. Death was duei to suffocation.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held yesterday at the Worksouse. There were present Mr. R. Heaton (chairman), Messrs. A. Jolley, J. Houghton, W.Houghton, Smith, Dalharry, Ratcliffe, and Swinton; Mr. S. Sutton (clerk), Mr. Wm.Ovven (surveyor), and Dr. Seph ton (medical officer).

div.head: ORFORD WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: ORFORD WATER SUPPLY.

The SunvEroa reported that the Clerk and he at- tended the meeting of the ‘Vater.Committee of the War- rington Corporation at the Town Ball, to negociate for the laying of water mains into the village of Orford,and to discuss the minimum sum which the Corporation wou!d require as a guarantee. About 1,300 yards of main are required,and the Corporation offer to lay it for a guaran- teed revenue of £35. The Water Committee pointed out that they considered it unwise to lay a main of smaller diameter than six inches, and that the cost would be £570, which at 8i per cent, would mean £4B 93. per annum ; but as a smaller one would do for the time be- ing, they consented to accept a guarantee of £35 in- stead of the 8L- per cent.—The matter was discussed,and the Clerk advised that any deficiency in the guarantee would have to be made up out of the rates af the Autho- rity's district. It was ultimately decided to hold the matter over until there has been an interview between members of the Authority and the Water Committee.

div.head: LIEDICAL OFFICRR'S REPORT.
div.p: LIEDICAL OFFICRR'S REPORT.

Dr. Sepßon submitted his report which showed that the deaths for July were 28 and the Nails 25. There had been 12 deaths from diarrhcea. Eleven deaths out of the 28 were thoseof children under 12 months old. There had been two cases of smallpox reported from Thelwall.
THE LONGFORD DEPOT QUESTION.

_ Mr.Morcristaa, junior, of Orford, appeared before the Authority to complain about the nuisance caused by the Longford Depot, and he wished to know what steps the Authority intended to take to prevent the continuance of the nuisance.—Dr. Sepliton (Medical Officer of Health), said that some time ago Dr. Sergeant examined the depot, and advised the Warrington Corporation to make certain alterations which would abate the nuis- ance., He believed the alterations had been made, but the nuisance still continued.—The CHAIRMAN said that from personal experience he could say that the nuisance was as distressing as ever.—Dr. SEPHTON considered the only way to clear the matter up was to apply for an in- junction against the Warrington Corporation.—Mr. A. JOLLEY : Its getting time we did.—The CHAIRMAN said he considered they had been humbugged long enough about the mattar. The nuisance had been going on for years, and the Corporation had been pretending to con- sider the matter all along, but refused to move. .Tbe nuisance was doing a great amount of damage to the property in the neiglibmrhood. He did not see that they should consider the Corporation because they were a Corporation if they had been private proprietors, an injunction would have been applied for long ago. (Hear, hear.)—Several members agreed that an injunction ought to be applied for, but ultimately ou the advice of the Clerk it was decided that a deputation should wait upon the Sanitary Works Committee of the Corporation, and it they could not come to an agreement, it was un- derstood, that an injunction was to be applied for in the usual way.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: – THE PENKETH WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: - THE PENKETH WATER SUPPLY.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL AND THE RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

At. a meeting of the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday night, Alderman Francomb in allud- ing to the Penketh water supply sid ho vopel to make a short statement;•hit tie should le pleased if the members or the Council would not discuss it as it was not on the minutes. If anyone objected the committee would withdraw it. The statement was to be made in the interests of the committee, and to put down some blunders that existed in Penketh. They had offered to supply the districts of Penketh and Orford, at a cost to the Rural Authority of 8/ per cent, on the capital outlay. That suns would include the charge for water, and would be gradually reduced as the income from the con- sumption of water increased. They were entitled to charge 10 per cent., but seeing that they could now bor- row at 3 1-Bth per cent, they had made proposals to the Rural Sanitary Authority which while very favour- able to them were on such a basis that they would be secured against loss. They did not wish to make any profit out of the Rural Sanitary Authority on the cost !of laying the mains. They asked the Authority to guarantee that they as a Corporation should not lose money on the undertaking. They wished to be as open ! as p,ssible with the people of Penketh and Orford. They vihd to do all they could for them, but at the same time they were compelled to guard the interests of the ratepayers of Warrimiton whom they represented. (near, hear.) Supposing the 8i per cent, came to £2OO atd income paid by the people of renketh for the water rate was £l5O, the Authority would have to pay the odd £5O to make up the 81 per cent, on the outlay. If next year the income paid*to the Corporation by the people who took the water was £2OO, the Authority would mot have to pay a single penny. That seemed to be misunders'ood by many people in Penketh. The minutes were agreed to. ! Councillor IlsATori : It is unfair to put the matter in the paper in the way you have, because you have not properly explained it. The CHAIRMAN ; I think every member of the Council owderstwndsit. _
Councillor lioneErrs: Councillor Heaton's objection is not so much to the 8,1; per cent as to the laying of the 12 innh main. whin!' the people seem to disagree with. The 'matter then dropped.

At the meeting of the Warrington floral Sanitary Authority yesterday, Mr. Owen, surveyor, reported that at the meeting with the Water Committee of the Warrington Corperation on the 10th of July, in answer to the question as to whether the Corporation would consent for water to be obtained from the Vyrnwry pipes belonging to the Liverpool Corporation, the Committee said at once that they would not recommend the Cor- poration to give any such consent. The Clerk and the Suveyor asked for a revision of the estimate for carrying water mains to Penketh and the Committee promised to go into the matter on receiving from the Surveyor the lengths of piping required to carry water direct to Penketh from Sankey Bridges, and to supply it on the different roads in the village of Penketh. On the 19th July the Town Clerk handed the Surveyor an estimate which had been prepared by the water engineer, for the use of the Water Committee, amounting to £3,510. At the same interview the Town, Clerk said that it was thonght the actual expenditure wovld not exceed £2,500. The Committee were prepared to hay down the mains to Penketh with a guarantee of a revenue of per cent, on the outlay 'which would be a sum of £212 per annum. At a meeting of the sub-committee it was decided that the amount of guarantee was too much.— The Surveyor then read the following letter from the ! overseers of Penketh : "We are obliged for the informa- tion contained in your favour of the 19th inst. We have taken means to ascertain the opinion of the inhabitants of the township in respect to the proposal of the War- rington Corporation to supply Penketh with Winwick water. We find that there is a strong and practically unanimous feeling against this water, not alone because of the expense but also because the Win wick supply is as hard as the Penketh well waters. This feeling has been strengthened since it has become known that the Tanning Company do not consider the Winwick water suitable ter their manufac- turers, and they decline to guarantee the use of any con- siderable quantity. The whole e.xprnse would therefore be thrown num the township. We trust that your authority will he able to devise some means whereby the Vyrirwry water can.be supplied to our township. Fail- ing this should' you be able •to safeguard the public health, without a supply of water Item outside we would consider it advisable for the present to let the matter rest. '',Ve are, dear Sir, yours truly Charles E. Parker, James Millington, William Ditch field, overseers of Penketh„" Mr. It. Garnett, who appeared as a depu- tation, disens=ed the matter with the Authority and finally gave it as his opinion that if they could not get their water supply Irani Vyrnwy pipes new, it would he better to allow the matter to rest until the Parish Councils Bill came into operation when lie thonght they would he much better off:--The Clerk said' hetid not think that if the supply was nhtained from the Vyrnwe pipes it wradd he ehea per for the ratepayers because 'would 'have to pay the atittfority for the collet:6bn of subject than droppedvrater rate, &C.—The
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

In comparison with some recent meetings the proceedings at the Town Council onjuesday even- ing were quite dull and decorous. Perhaps the councillors had come to a virtuous resolution to show the members of the big" pow-wow" in Lon- don a good example, But, as a matter of fact. there , was nothing of a contentiousnature in the business that the council ,had to transact. It is true that Councillor Dixon had another tilt, Don Quixote like, at that favourite windmill of his—the machi- nery at Longford But the Council listened patient- ly and the worthy Councillor's lament and then approved of everything the Sanitary Works Com- mittee proposed. Even the strange vagary of Councillor Muir in seconding Mr. Dixon's amend- ment and then renouncing it only provoked an indulgent smile. Councillor Muir will have his little joke you know.

From what Councillor R. T. Fairclough said in dealing with the Gas Committee's minutes,l gather that the committee has been quite smart in mak- ing its.coal contracts. The 25 per cent, that is to come off the miners' wages has been taken into ac- count in the price that the committee is to pay. This seems very like counting your chickens before they are hatched. Suppose the miners successfully resist the attempt to take the 25 per cent. off their wages, what then? The whole transaction seems to justify the contention of the miners' leaders that the only reason for demanding a reduction is that coalowners tender at needlessly low prices. If there had been no talk of a reduction the Gas Committee would still hare bought its stock of coal. If the reduction is effected will Warrington gas be any cheaper or any better?

Another little bit of information imparted to the public through the Council is that the abolition of the" Folly Fair" has not. been all gain. In fact from a co,cuniary point of view it has been all loss. According to Alderman Blackhurst there has been a falling'off in the revenue of the Markets Commit- tee and this is largely attributed to the abolition of the Fair; the other part of the loss being due to the continued decline in the receipts from the shops in the Market Hall.

The local hairdressers began their increased charges for haircutting on Thursday, and they ap- pear to be well satisfied with the results. They evidently mean to make their claims known in the town, and one of their aims is very praiseworthy ,indeed. I mean the total abolition of Sunday work in their trade. They, intend to call in the help of the law upon any hairdresser who will not take one day's rest out of seven. The association has begun very well, 25 out of 33 hairdressers having already joined it. The association have done well in joining the Trades Council, thus joining hands with the rest of the Trade Unionists. I hear that the barbers were very busy during the end of last week and on Monday, chiefly at haircutting. The public were evidently determined to put off paying 3d. for having their hair cut as long as possible.

The pastor of Wycliffe, the Rey. John Yong% is at present having a trip to Norway, in the City of Richmond. He left Warrington on Saturday last, and from a telegram received from him fr.)m Ber- gen, I learn that the City of Richmond, arrived a', Hardanger Fiord on Tuesday, and that the weather was all that could be desired. Hr. Yonge will be absent from the pulpit at Wycliffe for two Sundays

If there is one class of persons who are more gen- erally abused than another, I think it is that very useful class of social pioneers,the British pressmen. They are always" coming in" for it from some quarter or the other ;indeed if the public only knew the enormous task it is to suit its varied tastes in newspaper ware, it would be surprised at its own fastidiousness, and at the energy expended to gratify it. Who is it that interlards the obituary notice of" the deceased friend" with tender words of regret, and tearful notes of reminiscence ; who strikes the chords of happiness and brightness in the" wedding notice," or does the hundred and one things which make the barren occurrences of daily life entertaining, interesting, pleasing or exciting? It is the reporter. Yet, forsooth. he is treated like an unwelcome intruder from another world. This, for instance, is something like th e general type of encouragement that is Bung at him. The Rev. Albert G. Bale, of the Congrega- tional Church, at Melrose, Mass., has declared in a sermon that " reporters have no refinement and none of the spirit of God, and are a curse." That is, ~"o^, a ware and wopl tinge the of /Ina 14... e , , tat.. • .• • Christian ministers who wou.- . it, I should think.

The Warrington reporters are not an exception to the rule—l don't mean the rule enunciated by the Bev. Mr. Bale. They are subjected to the same disposi- tion on the part ot the general public to use them as public property—as human rags to wipe up social slops (if the figure isn't too strong); any- thing indeed from a social football to an intellec- tual elephant. And these reporters are very guile- less and honest, with the consequence that after doing a good service for their masters, the public, the latter often, turn mean and play dirty tricks on them, which isn't fair nor upright. There is a case in point this week. At the Clergy Daightera School sale of work a report got amongst the press- men that a fire had occurred in town. One repor- ter was told that the conflagration was at the police office. He repaired there and asked the officer in charge "Is this office on fire." Buz he looked about, and saw it wasn't, and did not wait for any answer. The rumour grew stronger and stronger and in- vaded the ranks of the constabulary and they too •iaent searching for the fire. By-and-by a certain official came and lead three of the reporters away to a certain church where he said the fire was. Upon ariiving there the pressmen asked Why, where is the fire—we don't see it." "So " said the official "Its in the cellar—its what they have• for heating the boiler." This style of taking a "rise" out of confiding pressmen is mean and despicable, and hasn't any sort of ingenuity or humour in it.

I am pleased to hear that Mr. Hollins Allen, who was formerly at the Warrington School of Art, has obtained the headmastership of the School of Art at Canterbury. Mr. Allen's parents reside in Mill-lane, and he received his elementary schooling at Peoples' College School. lie was subsequently a student at the School of Art, and won a scholarship and went to Kensington. His friends in Warrington will be delighted to hear of the success which he has gained in his work. Mr. Allen is not unknown in athletic circles, being a very expert rider on the bicycle, and he has gamed many prizes in this kind of sport.

div.head: LY MM.
div.p: LY MM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICRS.-ThR Baptist Chapel Sunday School Anniversary Services, Higher-lane, Ly min, were held on Sunday. The sermons, morning and evening, were preached by the Rev. J. %V. Varley, of Latchford. A children's service was held in the afternoon. Col- lections were made at all the services in aid of the schools. - - -

BROKE HIS LEO.—A married man, a boiler maker, from Openshaw, who was visiting Lymin with a num- ber of friends, met with a somewhat serious accident. The party were on the bowling green of the Fleece Hotel, jumping, when he fell over a form and broke his leg. Dr. Williamson attended to the injured limb, and the man was c,mveyed on a stretcher to the Railway Station, and sent to Manchester.—On Sunday a Bolton engineer, named Charles Lisley, slipped on the curb- stone in Bridgewater-street, and sprained his ankle badly. Dr. Williamson attended to him.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board-room, on Tuesday, when there were present— Messrs. J. Uregson (chairman), H. Harrison, J. Holt, W. Brazendale, J. Perrin, It. W ' hitelegge E.flolt, and S. Appleton Mr. Ridg way (law clerk), Mr. W. Mullard ; (clerk), Mr. J. Mort, (surveyor.) Mr. Pope, Booth'shill, appeared before the Board, and stated that he objected to pay the full year's district rate, as he was leaving in September. He objected on principle.—The Law Clerk explained that if he went out before the 18th September, he would only have to pay the six months rate. Mr. Pope said that he would make it his business to leave before that date, and the matter dropped. After some discussion, it was resolved by the Board to anpoint Mr. T. P. Kernon, of London, as clerk of the works of the Header sewerag,e scheme. at a salary of two guineas a week.—The Law Clerk road aletter from Mr. J. E. Cross, Mill-lane, fleatley i , n which it was stated that Colonel Legh would let the Local Board have certain land at Heatley if the Board would undertake to widen the road leading up to Heatley Railway Station and do the necessary fencing, kn., connected therewith. Mr. Perrin said that the Board could do the work at a third the cost if they undertook to do theinselves.—Mr. Holt explained that if would be a matter of some years before the work could be completed—rho Clerk was ordered to retain the proposal.

div.head: BEFORE TITF, MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE TITF, MAGISTRATES.
THE DRIVER AND THE CYCLIST.

Before the Warrington magistrate; on Monday, Henry Mellor, was charged with having his cart on the wrong side of the road in Bold-street, on the 20th inst., and not allowing a bicycle sufficient room to pass.—P.C. Bell stated that he saw defendant driving a spring cart up Bold-street, on the above date, and he was on the wrong side of the road. Mr. White a bicyclist, was going in the opposite direction, and had to jump off his bicycle and snatch it on to the footpath or he would have been run over.—Mr. Monks also gave evidence, and defendant was fined in the costs us. Sd.

A LIKING FOR PEARS. John Dutton, 13 years of age, residing in Lovely-lane, arose as early as five o'clock on .Satuday morning in order to see Mr. Braide's pear trees, which are about 100 yards off Lovely-lane, and surrounded by a wall five feet high. 5e was on the top of the wall and had just helped himself to two pears when he was espied by P.C. Evans who thought it better to lead him from further temptotion, and accordingly walked him down to the Police Station. At ten ten he was brought before Mr. John Burgess, who was in the chair, and Alderman Chandley, and charged with stealing a quantity of growing Dears value one penny. After evidence by P.O Evans, Mr. Braide said he was unable to grow either fruit or flowers, as they were stolen by lads before they came to maturity. Ills trees were stripped every year. The magistrates, in consequence of the lad being hurt by falling from the wall, dismissed him with a caution.

div.head: tIE lIID NO MORE " BOODLE."
div.p: tIE lIID NO MORE " BOODLE."

Samuel Grace, Liverpool, who said he was stepson to Councillor Petrie of that city, was charged before the Warrington magistrates on Monday, with riding from Liverpool to Warrington on the C.L.C. Railway, with- out having paid the fare, with intent to defraud the company. From the evidence it appeared that on the arrival at Warrington of the eleven p.m. train from Liverpool, the defendant was found asleep in a third class compartment. He was awakened and his ticket demanded or the fare. He was drunk, and he tendered a penny in payment for a ticket, as be said he had no more " boodle "then. He refused to give his name and address and was afterwards locked up. Defendant said he paid sd. at Liverpool for a ticket to Cressington but fell asleep and was overcarried. He lost the ticket. He admitted being drunk. The charge was altered to that of being drunk on the premises of the C.L.C. and the magistrates fined him 2s. 6d.

div.head: KINDNESS REWARDED.
div.p: KINDNESS REWARDED.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Tuesday, William Thomas O'Neill, was charged with stealing from the house of Thomas Taylor, Shepherd's-row, off Orford-st., a purse containing 4s. 6d., a gold ring, and a watch key, of the total valee of 12a RA The chi., Constable stated that the prisoner was a native of Staffordshire. The prisoner met with the complainant's son in town and they had a drink together, and afterwards the prisoner accompanied him home, when he asked to be allowed to lodge at the house. The prisoner was allowed to stop and asked them to call him at five o'clock the next morning as he had obtained work at Dallam Forge. When Mr. Ta- ylor went into the front room next morninJ, he found that his purse had been taken from his trousers' pockets and also the other articles named. Information was conveyed to the police and D.S. Monaghan arrested the prisoner who was drunk, the same evening. He was brought to the police staticn and searched, when the watch key was found upon him and identified as that of the c.mplain- ant's. The prisoner admitted giving the ring to a man named Ellis, and said he threw the purse in a garden off Froghall-lane, where it was found. After evidence by Mr. Taylor and D.S. Monaghan the prisoner was sent to prison for three months' hard labour.

div.head: VIOLENT CUSTOMER.
div.p: A VIOLENT CUSTOMER.

Thomas Concannon, who said he was employed on the Ship Canal, was placed in the dock on Wednesday morn- ing charged with assaulting P.C. Barlow in Dolman's- lane at a quarter to one the previous afternoon, and also charged with being drunk on licensed premises and refusing to quit the Shakespeare Inn. The landlady said the man came into her house, and he was served with a quart of beer by the servant. He afterwards got up and smashed the glass on the floor and wanted to fight. Witness went to him and he butted her with his head on the chest, and cut her fingers with a glass she had in her hand. She sent fora policeman, and prevented him from leaving the house before the policeman came. P.C. Barlow said from information received he went to the Shakespeare Inn. On the prisoner seeing him coming he ran into witness and kicked him several times. He (wit- ness) had to put the "snaps "on him, before he could bring him to the Police Station. Prisoner said he didn't remember anything about the matter, and the whisky he had taken had affected him. It was the first time he had been placed in that position, and asked to be treated leniently. The magistrates fined him ss. and costs for the assault and ss. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly or 14 days' hard labour.
"6 BROTHERS IN DISTRESS " AGAIN.

James Hopkins and George Hopkins, of Friar's Green, were each charged before the Warrington magistrates on Monday with being drunk and disorderly in the Market Place, and with refusing to quit the Blue Lion Inn, also with assaulting George Lambert, the landlord, Sarah Morris the barmaid, and P.C. Clark, on Saturday night. —Mr. A. Browne,who prosecuted, said that four men of whom prisoners were two, came into the public-house on Saturday night and ordered four glasses of beer,and one of them gave a 2s. piece. Sarah Morrii the barmaid, gave them is. 6d. change, when the prisoner James said that he had given her half-a-crown. He thereupon picked up a glass of beer and threw it at her striking her in the temple. George followed suit by throwing another glass at her which would have struck her temple also but she saved it with her hand. The two glasses were of course broken. Mr. Lambert, the landlord, then came to put prisoners out, but they knocked him down. They were removed from the house with great difficulty, and and when outside they commenced fighting between themselves. P.C. Clark arrested them and he was kicked on the way to the police station by them.—Sarah Harper, George Lambert, D.s. Monaghan, and P.C. Clark, corroborated Mr. Brpwne's statement, and the prisoners who are well-known characters, were sent to gaol for three months.

div.head: BREACHES OF THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.
div.p: BREACHES OF THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.

At the Borough Court, on Monday, James Barrow, 8, Silver square, was charged with unlawfully having in his possession a weighing machine which was unjust, on the 27th July. Mr. J. L. Whittle (Town Clark), pro- secuted. Mr. Whittle said the defendant was a coal- dealer, and Inspector Crabtree found his scales 9oz. against the purchaser. The first .time he examined them he found them one pound against the purchaser and the second time they were 9.,z. The scales were new three months ago, and with ordinary usage the scales should go lighter and not heavier as they were in this case. He was under the impression that the scales had been tampered with. Mr. Place, Market Inspector, corroborated, • The defendant was unable to say how the scales had become wrong. He was fined 50s. and costs.—Edward Smith, baker, Fennel-street, was charged with sending his cart out with bread with- out having balances to weigh it. Mr. Whittle said the ' impression had got abroad in the town amongst the bakers that it was not necesi,ary to carry scales and weights with them. Ile sent a circular to the bakers in the town informing them of the Act on the 29th June. On the 24th July Inspector Crabtree tint the defendan

delivering bread and asked him where his scales were. Defendant said he had forgotten to put them in the cart, but he would go back and fetch them, but it was found that he delivered bread afterwards without doing so. Inspector Crabtree corroborated Mr. Whittle's statement. Defendant was fined 5. and costs.

ASSAULT ON A FELLOW WORKMAN. At the OccasiGnal Court, on Thursday, before Messrs. Z. Armitage (chairman), and J. White, George Price was charged with assaulting James Lyon, in Burton- wood, an the Ist inst.—The two parties worked together at some new houses in course of erection in Burconwood, and on Tuesday, the prisoner who is deaf appeared to think that Lyon was saying something about him, and he knocked his head against the wall. Lyon further asserted that prisoner threw a trowel at him and cut him in the temple. Prisoner admitted knocking Lyon's head against the wall, but denied throwing the trowel. —He was bound over in one surety to keep the peace for six months, and pay the costs or in default 14 days. A QUEER WAY OF TREATING A NEW BROTHER-IN-LAW. Wm. Lowe, 17, Edgeworth-St., was charged at the Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, with assaulting and beating Thomas Spencer, on June 28.—Complainant said that he was in bed at 10 p.m on the above men- tioned date, when he was awakened by his wife telling him that the door had been burst open by someone. On going downstairs,witness found prisoner and two friends in the house. Witness asked him what he meant by that behaviour when he was knocked down by the prisoner, and received such injuries that lie was insensible for some time. He was carried into the house by Inspector Spinks and another policeman, and Dr. Peacocke was called in, who attended to him until became round.—ln- spector Spinks said that complainant had married the sister of the prisoner on the same day that the assault was committed.—Alderman Harrison : That is a queer way of treating anew brother-in-law.—lnspector Spinks (continuing), said he found a large amount of blood on the ground where the complainant had been lying.— Prisoner was given a fortnight to pay £1 and costs.

div.head: CLAIM AGAINST AN EMPLOYEE.
div.p: CLAIM AGAINST AN EMPLOYEE.

George Plumpton. file —too--I—Q-ce7, —Made a claim on Friday at the Warrington Borough Court, of £2, for compmsation for breach of contract by John &finer, Battersby-lane.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who prosecuted, said that the claim was brought against defendant in regard to damages Mr. Plumpton had sustained by de- fendant leaving his work without giving a week's notice. Defendant was a very experienced workman with a wage ot 365. per week, as a smith. The men who work the tools cannot proceed with their work until the smith had forged the tools. In Feb., 1892, a similar case to the present one was heard in the Warrington Court, and in cmsequence Mr. Plumpton put up the following not•ce in his works" Notice is hereby given that one week's notice would be required before leaving, from all hands working in these works, manufacturing the tools and the files from this date 15th February,and also one week's notice will be given before discharging any workmen" The defendant came to work for Mr. Plumpton in 1892 at 343. which was subsequently increased to 365. On Saturday week when he was paid, he said that he was coming back no more as he had got another place. The foreman pointed out the notice, but defendant took no notice of it and left. As there were only two or three smiths in Warrington, this placed Mr. Plumpton in a very awkward position, and he could not get one for a week. Mr. Plumpton had at the time an Indian Office contract, which made him liable to a penalty if it was inot completed by a certain time. Owing to the difficulty NJ( getting a new smith that time had now expired, and Mr. Plumpton had written to the Indian office explaining the circumstances and asking for a little more time to complete the contract, but had received no reply yet. A number of the workmen had to be mployed on inferior work during the week that there was no smith so that Mr. Plumpton had sustained con- siderable loss which he had placed at the nominal sum of 40s.—Mr. Plumpton and Mr. Mercer, the foreman, corroborated Mr. Browne's statement.—Mr. P. Davies for the defence contended that as no part of the wages was kept in hand, no notice was required, and also that the notice ought to be in a more prominent part of the works.—Defendant who was sworn said that he bad never seen the notice before the foreman showed it him when he left. He also declared that he told the foreman that had he known about the notice before he would have given a week's notice.—Two other witnesses were called for the defence.—The magistrates decided to allow the whole claim t. 4 be paid at las. per month and also ordered defendant to pay the costs.
THEFTS.

A boy named Daniel Farrington, of 85, Hoyle-st., was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Thurs- day for stealing a man's cap value 4U, the property of Lewis Jacobson, the previous day.—Prom the Chief Con- stable's statement it appeared that prisoner was seen with something bulky under his coat in the market on Wednesday, and on Dekctive Monaghan looking what it was, he found is was a man's cap. The boy on being questioned said that he had bought the cap and offered to take Monaghan to the stall where he had purchased it from. Monaghan went with hips and he took it to Jacobson's stall saying that he had bought it from him. Jacobson, however, said that he had not sold the cap. Monaghan then took the boy to the police station, and on the way he said Hi, t he had not bought the cap but had found it.—The maOstrates ordered the boy to receive six strokes of the birch rod, and to be kept in custody until the evening. Martin Hurst, 14, Friar's Green,was also charged with stealing from Wm. Brown, on the 29Lh ult., a man's coat, a pair of trousers, and other articles valued 16s.—William Bro TA had been ' away for his training with the Liverpool militia and re- turned to Warrington on Saturday evening, intending to ' lodge with prisoner. Prisoner met him to assist him to , carry his goods. They cdlled at a public house for a drink, and then went to Mrs. Leslie's second-hand shop , in Mersey-street, where complainant bought a pair of trousers. They then met a woman and went into the Roebuck Inn for a drink. While in there, prisoner said he would take the bundle of clothing to his . . .

mother's house, to which complainant consentea. Soon after, feeling uneasy,•complatnant went to prisoner's house and learned that he had not arrived. He called at several public houses and at length found prisoner in the Leigh •Armsselling the trousers. After a struggle complainant took them off him, but other articles of clothing were missing. It was afterwards found out that prisoner had tried to sell some things at Mrs. Leslie's shop, but Mrs. Leslie refused to buy them. The matter was reported to Detective Monaghan who arrested prisoner on Wednesday night.—Prisoner was sent to gaot for two months' hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Harrison Messrs. W. Pierpoint J. W. Hayward, and
S. Wrighi.

- - DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Fiir committing this offence the following were dealt with—John Taylor and John Skeldon, no address ; Michael Farraghan, 5, Dolman's- lane ; John Shields, Old-road; Thomas Ward, and Patrick Ward, Silver Square ; Bernard Mahon, 34, Gee- street ; James Wilson, Acton Grange. THEFT BY AN OLD Wousti.—Bridget Brown, aged 67 years, was summoned for stealing from the " Leigh Arms," Mersey-street, on Saturday evening, two pint glasses, one spirit glass, and a water jug, valued is. ed., the property of Joseph Edward James, the landlord.— Prisoner went into the Leigh Arms on Saturday even- ing, the worse for drink, and the landlord refused to serve her. She went into the tap-rOom,and sat there for some time, and then left the house. When she was in Bridge-street she fell to the ground and in doing so she broke the jug an one of the glasses. They were taken into the Leigh Arms, when the landlord identified them as his property. He gave information to P.C.Leathwood who arrested prisoner the same night.—The magistrates sent her to gaol for 14 days without bard labour.

DESERTEIZ—John Miller, 52, Thelwall-lane, was remanded on the charge of being a deserter from the Royal Marine Irfantry, Deal, in October, 1891. Prisoner was again brought before the magistrates on Wednesday and handed ever to the miiitary escort pre- sent in court. P.S. Taylor applied for and received the usual reward. OBSCENE LANOIIAGE.—Kate Dalton, was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment for using obscene language in Dial-street, on the 22nd inst. She assumed a very defiant attitude in the court and declined to pay the fine.
_ FIGHTINC.—John Barry, Sandy-lane, Orford, was charged with fighting in Dolman's 'lane on Sunday night. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months. _

STREET OBSTRUCTION.—CharIes Price, 1, Sankey-street, was fined 59. and costs for allowing a handcart to stand an unnecessary time in Sankey-street, on the 24th July, TUESDAY.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest, and Dr. Starkey

div.head: Smith.
div.p: Smith.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—The following were dealt with for this offence : Thomas Brown and Mary Monaghan in Bridge-street, ss. and costs each; John Walsh in Mersey-street, 53. including costs ; Thomas Martin at Friars-gate, ss. and costs; Margaret Brown, in Sankey-street, ss. .including costs. BEGOINO.—Davtd Godfrey, a well-known character to the police was chrged with begging in Buttermat ket- street, the previous evening. The man was drunk at the time and used very abusive language after soliciting alms. He Was sent to gaol for one month hard labour. SCXOOL ATTINDANCI4 CASES —Mr. G. Riley (school attendance officer) prosecuted in the following school cases for irregular attendance. Frederick Jones, residing with his parents in Gladstone-street was sent to the ship " Clio" as he was incorrigible. Moses Williams, forgeman, Winwick-road, was fined 103.; Richard , Stockton, labourer, Old Gardens, ss.* Daniel Poole, wire- drawer, Wakefield-street, 2s. ; John Pollard, ' labourer, Lythgoes-lane, 2s. 6d. ; James Melton, tanner, Winwick-street, 23. 6d. ; Martha Ann Medlicott, laundress, Brackley-street, 2s. 6d. ; Ellen flases, laundress, Egerton-s treet, ss. ; William Humphreys. bricksetter. Priestley-street, 2s. 65. ; James Backhouse, forgeman. Bostock-street, 5a..; and Henry Brown, wire- drawer, Brindley-street, 2s. Go.
Tucasim .—Alderman Sutton (chairman), Captain Ridgway, and Alderman Chandley Assalmr oarA WlFlL—William Baines Erwood-street, was charged with wanking his wife Eliiateth 'Baines on

the Ist inst.—Mrs. Baines said tkat her husband came home drunk on Tuesday night and complained that there was not sufficient supper. He then knocked her down and would have murdered her but she was rescued. Her husband had treated her badly for 17 years.—The husband gave a lamentable account of his wife's tad habits which was supported by Detective Monaghan.— Tho chief constable understood that the husband was to blame as well. The magistrates bound defendant over to keep the peace for six months in his own recogniz- ances. _ _

DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—Peter Hinds was sent to gaol for one month for this offence. ASSAULT ON THE POLlCH.—Joseph Clayton, Orford-t., was charged with being drunk and disorderly the pre- vious evening and with assaulting P.C. Cunliffe.—That officer stated that prisoner was very abusive to some soldiers in Butterinarket-street on the previous evening, and would not go home. Witness and P.C. Berry were obliged to take him to the police station, and on the way he kicked witness on the leg.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. FRIDAT.—Befor• Mr. John White (chairman) Alderman Harrison and Councillors H. Roberts, and Fleming. NOT AIMING STRAIGHT.—Mary COnWay, CnriMeS-yard- was charged with assaulting Catherine Robson, 31, Upper Bank-street, on the 21st inst. Mr. Browne defended. For the prosecution it was asserted that defen- dant passed Mrs. Babson who was with Mrs. Owen, and deliberately spat in their faces. Defendant said that she had not intended to spit in Mrs. Owen's face but it was for Mrs. ltobson. For the defence it was alleged that Mrs. Robson called defendant a foul name and tla,t defendant hissed her but never spat at her.—The magis- trates ordered each to pay their own costs. ASSAULT.—JuIia Forster, 80, Lythgoes-lane, and Mary Ellen Lawton, 2, Providence-street, were each ordered le pay their own costs on the charge of the former assault- ing the latter on the 31st ult. CROSS SUMMONSES FOR ASSAULT.—Mary Broderick, Dallam-lane, was charged with assaulting Patrick Carey and Mary Carey on the 29th ult. Mary Carey and Patrick Carey were also charged with assaulting Mary Broderick on the same date.—Mr. Davies appeared for Broderick. The case lasted a long time, and the magis• trates inflicted a fine of 53. and costs upon Mrs. Broderick, and dismissed the Carevs, and Mrs. Broderick ordered to pay the damage for a window that was broken.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY. —Before Major Pickmere (chairman) and Mr. John White.

'DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. For this offence, John Quinn, Buttonwood ; and Albert Kirk, Sankey Bridges, were dealt with. BICYCLIST IN TROUELE.—John Goulden was fined ss. for riding on his bicycle on the footpath in Penketb, on the 29th July. DRIVING ON THE FOO'TPATH.—William Chrimes was fined ss. for driving a horse and cart on the footpath at ' Poulton on. July 22. QUARRELSOME BaornEas.2-Peter Sutton was sum- , moned by his brother William Sutton, for assaulting him in Burtonwood,on July 16th.—William made a,long statement, from which it was gathered that he and hisi brother were in a public-house on the above-mentioned date, and had five pints of beer each. These pints ap- peared to have considerable effect upon Peter,who bean abusing William, and wanted to fight him, but William refused and left the house. Peter followed, and caught his brother in an oat field and knocked him to the ground, and kicked him, breaking his nose and one tooth, the result being that William was under the doc- tor for a fortnight. His side was black, and next day , Peter threatened "to finish" him. There had been ill-feeling between the two about some cottages in which each had a share, and which Peter had threatened to blow up.—P.C. Grundy spoke as to the injuries William had received,but did not see the assault.—Win. McMichael was called by Peter,and said that he had seen the row from beginning to end, and that it was all William's fault. The two had been wrestling together, and William had hurt himself by falling on the around. —The magistrates decided to bind over Peter to keep the peace for six months in •Jrie surety of £lO.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley.
_ DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence the following were fined: Samuel Sutton, Hartley-street ; John Gough and John Ford. _

BAD CHAILACTERS.—AIice Hampson, and Mary Murphy were charged with being guilty of indecent conduct. The former was committed for a month's imprisonment and the latter for 14 days' imprisonment. ASSAULT.—Ann Clucas, of Queen-street, was sum- moned for assaulting Esther Ann Taylor, of the same street.—Thomas James Taylor, husband of the last named, was summoned for using threats to Clucas.— Mr. Burton represented the Taylors and Mr. Lake appeared for Clucas.—Clucas was fined ss. and costs. The charge against Taylor was dismissed, v.

A MARINE STORE DEALER AND His SlGN.—George Howard, marine store dealer, Percival-lane, pleaded guilty to not having the words " Dealer in Marine Stores" distinctly painted upon his warehouse. The defendant said he had a sign on the warehouse, and was not aware the words named were necessary.—A fine of 53. was imposed. _ . _

ALLEGED INDECENT AssAutr.—rSamuel Walker Rogers, a young man, was charged with having on Saturday morning unlawfully and indecently assaulted Sarah Jane Nuttall, wife of John Nuttall, of Hamilton-street, Flulme, Manchester, a boatman. The woman's husband is mate of the Ship Canal gat " Laura," which left Runcorn for Liverpool at half-past eleven on Friday night. She did not go with it because she had had a quarrel with her husband and she was afraid he would illuse her. At midnight the prisoner met her at Top Locks and told her that if she had got left behind, he would take her to his father's house to skep with his sister. He took her past the Police Station on St. John's Brow, and after stopping at a house, he walked her further on, threw her to the ground and committed the assault -complained of. While she was screaming " murder" and struggling, another man came up and took 4s. Bd. from her pocket.—The prisoner was dis- charged.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MoNnaY:—Before the Mayor and Mr. U. W. Deacon. THEFT OF TIMBER—John Lister, Widnes, was charged with stealing a small quantity of timber from the Widnes Alkali Works, the property of the United Alkali Com- pany. Mr. Clerk,- a foreman at .the works, said the company did not wish to press the charze.Ficied ss.

COAL STEALERS.—Frances Malone, Nelson-st. ; Mary Ann Roath, Nelson-st. ; Mary Cooney, West Bank-st, •, and William fieyes, Wellington-street, were charged with stealing a quantity of coal from the Globe Chemi- cal Works. Cooney, who had been up before, was fined ss. and costs, and the others were bound over to come up for judgment if called upon.

div.head: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
SATIIRDAY.—Before Messrs T. J. Gillespie (in the chair), T. D. Grimko Drayton, T. H. Pearson, McCorquodale and Colonel Wood.

DIVINKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness.—James Looskin, William Carr,. and Michael Higgins. THE RECENT RACES.—EIonsz CRUELTY.—James Lawrenson was charged with cruelty to a horse by work- ing it in an unfit state on Juno the 30th. Inspector Thorns of Wigan deposed [6 seeing the defendant driv- ing the horse, which was attached to a wagonette, to the races on the day in question. The animal was in a di,- tressed cqndition owing to over work; the sweat was pouring from it. and its body was covered with marks made by the la all of the whip. The animal was tremb- ling violently. Inspector Lucking,R.S.P.C.A.Altrincham, gave corroborative evidence. Defendant was fined 20s. and costs. John Williams, of Leigh, was charged with a similar offence, on the s.inie date. Inspector Dowty spoke to seeing the defendant in charge of a wagonette with 13 passengers in it. The horse attached was over- worked and showed painful signs of being distressed.— The defendant denied that hc was in charge of a wagonette. He contended that the witness had made a mistake.—David Williams, defendant's son, Paid his father was not in charge of a wagonette on the day in question. He was with him (witness) in a trap.—ln- specter Dowty said that if the Bench doubted the authority of his statement lie had other officers to call who would porrob..rale what he had said.—The Bench finally c ncluded that there was a doubt in the case and dismissed the charge against d?fendatit.—James Mort, and James Lamford were each fined 10s. and costs for Overworking and fl)ggiov horses attached to wavnettes. Peter Crawford, Willianrnt'aper,John Bradford, Wiliam Talton, .Wigan, and William Ashcroft, w ere al
fined for similar offences committed during Newton Races.

A MINER FINED FOR NEOLECT.—James Liveley, fire- man, at Wood Pit, Ilaydock, where a shocking explosion occurred some years ago,was charged with neglecting to make an inspection of the workings prior to the men descending the mine.—Mr. Ellis jun., for Richard Evans and Co.' showed that the ventilation was defective through the defendant's neglect, and as a previous warn- ing had been given a heavy penalty was necessary.— The Bench severely censured the defendant, and fined him 40s. and costs. I A GENEROUS PaosEcuTon.—James Tunstall was chaeged with an offence under the Local Government Act of 1888, which has special interest to bicyclists anci their duties to the public. Mr. R. Stuart (solicitor), who prosecuted, said he was instructed by Major Seton, of Golborne, to press for the heaviest penalty that could be inflicted under the Act. The proceedings were taken under sub-section B of the Local Government Act of 1888, which laid it down to bicyclists that—" Upon !overtaking any cart or carriage, or any horse, mule, or other beast of burden, or any foot passenger, being or proceeding along the carriage way, every such person shall within a reasonable distance from and before pass- ing such cart, or carriage, horse, mule, or beast of bur- den, or such foot passenger, by sounding a bell or whistle, or otherwise give audible and sufficient warning of the approach of the carriage." In instituting these proceedings Major Seton had no animosity against the defendant, he simply wanted the law respecting the use of bicycles to be known throughout the length and breadth of the land. On the Bth of April his client was driving a pony attached to a trap in the direction of Earlestown. Defendant on a bicycle passed so close to the horse's head that the animal took fright, Major Seton being thrown out of the carriage, sustaining a fractured ankle, which had prevented him walking for two months. Ile was still lame, and might feel the effects of the acci- dent all his life. Defendant gave no warning of his ap- proach, and Major Seton desired it to go forth that bicyclists were directly violating the law when they passed conveyances or the public without giving audible warning of their approach.—Defendant having pleaded guilty, Major Seton, addressing the bench, asked for a heavy penalty, explaining that he intended to pay the ' fine himself, his object being that the case might be a public examnl3.—The Chairman said it was a serious offence, and the full penalty of 40s. and costs would be I imposed. • DESCRIBED HIM ERRONIOUSLY. —Matthew Winstanley, Earlestown. was charged with a breach of the Health Act, on the 28th June. Mr. J. E. Worsley proseCuted, and Mr. R. Stewart appeared for the defence. The evi- dence for the prosecution was to the effect that on the date named, the defendant refused to allow one of the Commissioner's Inspectors to examine his ashpit. Mr. Stewart pointed out that inasmuch as the summons described the defendant as the owner, whilst he was simply the occupier, ho war justified in asking that the case be dismissed.—The Bench dismissed the case on these grounds. _

NOT THE HAPPY FAMILY .—Robert Jackson ,a young man, i was charged with assaulting his stepmother, Ellen Jack- son, on the previous Sunday morning. The prosecutrix stated that her husband and the defendant were in the habit of keeping late hours, and when she spoke to them about it they quarrelled with her. On the previous Saturday night they did not come home until very late, and when she spoke to her husband he used abusive language to her. The next morning at breakfast time another " row "cropped up, and the defendant then dragged her into the back kitchen and struck her several times. The prosecutrix continued a long disconnected statement for some time, when the Chairman said, " Well, have you got any witnesses ? " The prosecutrix said "Yes, I have summoned my husband as a witness." The husband entered the witness box with great deliber- ation, and in a moment had entered upon a description of how the assault had been committed by his wife. He said she was always " nagging" at both him and his son, and on the Sunday morning in question she commenced a disturbance by shying a sugar basin and several other useful articles at his (the witness's) head. The defendant interposed as the prosecutrix's efforts grew bolder, and finally as she was going to transplant something else from the table to his head, the son said, "This won't do," and dragged the prosecutrix away. That was all the assault that was committed.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, peared on behalf of the defendant.—The Bench dismissed the case.

THE OTHER SEX, OR "WOMAN'S WAE."—Two married women named respectively Ann Dowd, and Winifred Bond, of Golborne, were charged with committing a breach of the peace at Haydock on the previous Satur- day night. A police constable stated that at 10 o'clock on the night in question his attention was attracted to the back of the houses occupied by the defendants and upon going round there he found the two women on the floor struggling. He learned afterwards that there had been a fight between Mrs. Dowd and a woman named Mrs. Wood. Mr. Stewart appeared for Mrs. Bond and stated that his client had gone to separate Mrs. Woods and Mrs. Dowd, when the latter pulled her to the floor. The Bench dismissed the case against Mrs. Bond and bound Mrs. Dowd over to keep the peace for three months. Mrs. Bond next charged Mrs. Dowd with an assault committed on the same day and at the same time. Her evidence was that when she.went to separate Mrs. Woods from Mrs. Dowd, the latter caught her by the hair and pulled her to the ground. Then she got on the top of her and beat her.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs.

100 E IT Our OF " Bony."—A forlorn looking woman named Julia O'Brien was charged in custody with break- ing the law by trying to break P.C. Slingsby's head, and also by further transgressing the law through not acting as a decorous citizen, she having imbibed so much that on the 22nd July she was observed in Penketh to alter- nately mistake the high road fora bed and a ballet stage. P.C. Slingsby stated how he was going along the road when he saw the defendant after some futile, though energetic efforts, to do a " polka mazurka," fall to the floor and decline to get up until she had bad a "nap." He was compelled to get the assistance of another police officer to take Julia to Warrington. She was tried at the Occasional Court there the next day and was com- mitted to the House of Correction for a 14 days' sojourn She accepted this as an apt of oppression and vowed that she would "take it out of the bebby." This was her simple, unpolished way of saying she meant to try and strike the police racer with her clog. She ultimately I changed her mind and kicked him with the clog and struck him in the face with her fist. She was taken I back bebre the Bench and remanded to those Sessions. She was now ordered to go to jail for 14 days. Commas AND THEIR " DRAWERS." - Roger Hunt, I Thomas Brown, and Thomas Whitfield, colliers were charged with obstructing the footpath in Penny-lane, on the 7th of the present month. A constabfe stated that he saw the defendants and about ten other colliers all 'standing on toe: footpath in the lane. He had had several complaints about the obstruction. Mr. R. Stewart. who appeared for the defence stated that Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. for whom the defendants worked had formerly paid all the men -together, but since they had introduced a better method of paying the men at their respective pits. This, however,involved the necessity of the map finding somewhere to pay their drawers, and as there was no proper accommodation they usually met in Penny-lane, but did not obstruct the footpath.—The case was dismissed.

div.head: GREAT STRIKE OF MINERS. QUARTER OF A MILLION OF COLLIERS
div.p: THE GREAT STRIKE OF MINERS. QUARTER OF A MILLION OF COLLIERS
ON SI RIKE.

On Friday last week the great coal dispute reached what may be called its first climax, when the men associated with the Miners' Federation came out on strike. The districts affected include all the great c.l- - of the country—North Wales, Lancashire, Stafford- shire, Yorkshire, Birrninghant, and the Midlands—the total number of men who have ceased work being estim- ated at something between 250,000 and 300,000. By those who have taken the trouble to frame a careful estimate, based upon figures from each district,' the number is placed at 280,000. The effect of so large a stoppage at is implied in this number cannot fail to • be wide-reaching and—at all events temporarily—disast• rous ; but sanguine views are held as to the duration of the strike. Stocks generally are large, this being due to the circumstance that owners have recently put the men on for increased hours, in order to prepare for the demands of thestrike period. On both sidesa determ- ination has been expressed to fight to the end, the men strenuously resisting the demanded reduction of wages, and the masters being equally urgent in their claims for that reduction.

The last report of the managing committee of the Lan- cashire and Cheshire Miners Permanent Relief Society states that in March last there were employed in the eateries of St. Helens and district about 5,500 men, including " coal-getters" or colliers, drawers, day-wage men, and pit-brow hands, and the whole of then stopped work on Friday. The St. Helens Colleries Company (Messrs. Pilkington Bros.) employed 655 and 663 men at their St. Helens and Ravenhead pits respectively; Messrs Bromilow, Foster and Co. Ashton's Green Colliery,found employment for 805 ; Collin's Green and Bold Colliery Co., 1281 ; White Cross Colliery Co., 839 ;Sutton Heath and Lea Green Colleries, 1091 ; Messrs. Glover, Urmson, and Glover, Plicenix Colliery, 189 ; and the Eccleston Hall Colliery Co. 69. A few men, however, will be retained at each pit, sufficient to keep the roadways, ' brows, and workings in good order during the strike, but under no circumstances will the getting or filling of coal be permitted that the officials of the miners' union can prevent. It is understood that the funds of the local lodges of the miners' union will Rot permit of the payment of the ordinary strike pay of 10s. per member with is. for every child, and it is found that there will I be a great deal of suffering in the poorer quarters of the town before work is resumed.

div.head: PROPOSED WITHDRAWAL OF NOTICES.
div.p: PROPOSED WITHDRAWAL OF NOTICES.

The Executive Committee ot the Miners Federation met on Wednesday in London. It was reported that the coalowners in several districts had proposed that the notices should be withdrawn on the understanding that no increase in wages should be asked for till prices reached the level of two years ago. The Executive re- commended that the proposal be considered at a ci4ngress to be held in London on the 22nd inst.
PARTIAL SUSPENSION OF RAILWAY TRAFFIC AT

ST. HELENS. Although only the early days of the coal strike, there are evidences on every hand of its paralysing effect. The London and North-Western Railway considered it necessary to take off the ordinary coal-train service from Monday morning, on the understanding that as coal proprietors got a train loaded the company would as soon as possible send an engine and take it to its destin- ation. This loading is a much slower process than the tipping from boxes into the railway waggons as they reach the pit-brow' and as a consequence a large number of coal-trains have been taken off. As a rule twenty-five engines are sent out of the Sutton sheds, St. Helens, each day to work the district traffic, but on Wednesday four- teen engines with fires out remain in the sheds. An : arrangement has been made for the drivers of mineral trains to take a share of the driving of passenger trains, and on Wednesday the whole of the passenger drivers had a holiday and mineral train drivers worked the passenger trains. By these means the time made by the two sets of drivers will be equalised. This week it is expected they will all make about four days, but nothing can be said as to what time will probably be made next week or subse- quent weeks. The laying up of the engines is economis- ing a large amount of fuel, of which the company have In this district about two months' supply in stock. A St. Helens firm of builders and contractors stated on Wednesday morniAg that the building trade was likely to be seriously affected on account of the failure of the brick supply. He said that already there was a difficulty and their carts had to wait a considerable time before they could get loaded. On inquiry at the well-known firm of Messrs. Doulton and Co., pottery and brick manufacturers, it was stated that the coal strike was affecting the works, and the supply of bricks to con- tractors was not what it ought to be. The machinery was stopped, but the men affected thereby were being found work in the yard. The Ravenhead Sanitary Pipe and Brick Company have four or five weeks' coal in stock, and the Houghdales Brick Company has fuel for three or four weeks. The ironfoundries seem to be in a fair position; judging from the replies received. The position at Haydock on Wednesday was unchanged. The colliers throughout St. Helens and Haydock are very quiet and orderly. It is satisfactory to learn that the St. Helens Corporation is not likely to be short of coal at their various pumping stations. The contracts are with the Whitecross Colliery Company, Sutton Heath, and Mr. Lyon, who contracted without having a strike clause.

MR. GRIMKE DRAYTON, J.P., ON THE SITUATION, A newspaper representative on Thursday had some conversation with Mr. Grimke Drayton, J.P., managing director for Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., at whose extensive collieries in Haydock, Ashton, Golborne, and St. Helens some five or six thousand hands are employed, in reference to the paragraph which had appeared in the newspapers stating that a Midland colliery firm had made a suggestion that notices should be withdrawn' on the understanding that no increase of wages should be asked for until prices came back to the 1891 level, and in reference to the resolution passed by the executive of the miners' federation thereon. Mr. Grimke Drayton said he did not believe any firm had made such. a Pro- posal. If so why was not the name of the firm pub- lished. The proposition was preposterous. It would be suicidal. He could only suggest that someone had sent the paragraph to the newspapers for fun. He could not give any idea as to the probable duration of the strike. The masters were prepared to listen to any reasonable proposal from the men, but the masters could not come forward first. They had offered arbitration, but the miners had refused and declined one halfpenny of a re- duction. The owners had been losing money wholesale, and it was batter for them that the miners had ceased work.

MINERS' MEETING AT ST. HELENS. A meeting, attended by about 2,000 miners, was ,held in the People's Palace, St. Helens, on Monday morning. Air. Peter Arliinley, who was voted to the chair, addressed the meeting as" gentlemen," interpreting the term that a gentleman did no work, and as they (the miners of the district) were not working, they must therefore be "gentlemen." (Laughter and applause.) They were engaged in a struggle for liberty—liberty to live. They were there as a protest against oppression by the employers, who wished to rob the working man of a fair day's wage for a lair day's work. He hoped and trusted he was saying nothing wrong when he said, from his experience of the neighhourhood, the men were not in a very robust condition, so far as wages were concerned, and that if they took 25 per cent, and the private reductions off the men, they would have very little to spare either for food, rent, or clothing. The present was a very serious crisis. Had the men brought it about ? No. They had not. It was the griping, grasping selfishness of the employers that bad brought it about. If the masters wanted to sell at a low price, they should go down and get the coals themselves, and then the public would see what they would sell them at.

Mr. George Dixon, a check-weighrnan, moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting of the St. Helens miners, after reading reports of the proceedinss of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation, and the Federation of Great Britain, held in Manchester and Birmingham, hereby agree with the resolutions passed at the same, and heretic pledge ourselves to resist with all our power the unjust demand of 25 per cent. reduc- tion, and we will be faithful to the Federation of Great Britain."

Mr. James Hart, a miner, seconded the resolution, and urged ihe men throughout the struggle to behave them- selves like men, and not like Hottentots. Mr. Thomas Glover. J.P., miners' agent, said they were there to try and justify their action in the step they had taken. Noon° knew better than himself, and many present would bear him out, that strikes and lockouts were no good for anyone, and they a body of men did not believe in them. But they were forced upon theme and therefore they had nothing else to do but try ana defend their own homes against the unjust, unfair, and unreasonable demands. It had been said in times past, and no doubt it would be said again and again, that the agents of the men by their agitation had caused this great struggle, but he wanted it to go forth that in that district the men had not been advised by him, but by a ballot of 98 per cent, they had declared in favour of re- sistance. Referring to the attitude of Northumberland and Durham, Mr. Glover said they had still the fossilised idea that wages should be ruled by the rise and fall of the markets, and that they were not justified in coming out. rhe Federation of Great Britain bad told thin plainly they must either join the mpvement or they would be put out of the Federathn altogether. He did not know how far they would go with them. Durham had had a meeting, and sent in for an advance, but alongside with asking for 17 per cent, they said( they would not strike. (`• Oh, oh"). It was a farce fur 1 , Durham to send in for an advance and at the same time say they would not strike, because the masters would say " The,y will not strike and we will not: give it to them." It was unfortunate to find they had in their ranks districts like these. Mr. Glover then referred to the manifesto of the employers, and emphatically a . serted that in his opinion South Wales had not been the means of bringing down their wages because they had brought down the prices in the market. What he wished to go to the public through the newspapers was that th'il attempt to realticit had been brought about by their em- p'eyers having seen that the, men in South Wales had

suffered a reduction of 47 per cent, through the action of the rotten sliding scale, and the idea was to bring the miners of the Federation to the level of the South Wales miners, rather than lift the South Wales men to the level of the members of the Federation. That they would not do. He did not admit that the South Wales coalowners had been under- selling in our markets, because South Wales coal did not come into our markets. Theirs were mostly export coals. The masters of the federated districts had reduced prices amongst themselves, and the reduction was not brought about by reason of competition with the out- side districts of the North of England, Scotland. and South Wales. This was the first, time in the history of the country that he had known employers to point to outside districts and say they had been the means of bringing prices down. He was sorry to have seen a statement that the 25 per cent, reduction meant only 2s. off 28s. It meant ss. off the one pound. Assuming the standard wage of 1888 to be 20s. add 40 per cent, or Bs. made 28s. The 25 per cent, would be taken off the 20s. as that it would reduce the'2Bs. to 235. He believed the public would never justify such a reduction at one stroke in men's wages. The colliers had come out nationally, and he hoped they would go in nationally. (Applause) . _

• The resolution was carried unanimously. The Chairman moved," That this meeting agrees that no lodge shall allow any strike pay until the men had played a fortnight." Ho said that if that were carried, he did not think there would be any strike pay, as he believed the strike would be over in a fortnight. This resolution was also carried, and the meeting, which had been of a very orderly charact.r throughout terminated with votes of thanks to the proprietors of the Peoples Palace, and to the chairman. .
In some of the largest collieries at St.Helens the ponies have been brought up and sent into the fields to graze. The general opinion is that the present crisis will be a long one.

It was rumoured on Monday night that a disturbance had occurred near one of the St. ilalens Collieries Com- pany's pits. Os inquiry it appeared that two men were quarrelling and got to blows. Mr. Glover was near at the time, and he separated tho combatants, but some- thing subsequently took place ia which it is stated a constable was assaulted. The affair did not arise out of the strike.

div.head: MURDER OF IN INFANT BROTHER.
div.p: THE MURDER OF IN INFANT BROTHER.
DEATH SENTENCE ON A LAD OF SIXTEEN.

_ At Leeds Assizes on 'Thursday, Fred Cook, aged'aix- teen, was placed on hid trial for the second time, on the charge of murdering his'haby brother, at Okley, on May 10th. On Wednesday the jury were unable to agree, after a protracted deliberation, a fresh jury being em- pannelled on Thursday, morning. The case for the prNsecution was that the prisoner fatally wounded deceased with a hatchet with malice aforethought, and afterwards signed a written confession at the police station. For the defence-it was suggested that the wound was caused accidentally whilat the prisontrand deceased were fooluthly.i?laying with the hatchet. After a deliberation of fifty minutes the jury returned a ver- nict of wilful murder, with a strong recommendation to mercy on account of the prisoner's youth and previous good character. PrisonTr, who throughout bad remained perfectly cool and undoncerned; was then sentenced to Leath.

div.head: POLICE AND THE SFRIKE.
div.p: THE POLICE AND THE SFRIKE.

Replying to a question put by Mr. Woods in the House of Commons on Thursday evening. the Home Secretary said the extra police in certain parts of Lancashire had been sent thither by order of the Chief Constable, and the Home Office had nothing to do with the matter. In- stances of disorderly conduct had occurred near Wigan, but the miners generally were behaving peacefully. It was the duty of all authorities in disputes of this kind to observe an attitude of strict impartiality, and any irri- tating display of force was greatly to be deprecated. The Chief Constable of Lancashire was fully alive to the im- portance of this, and had issued orders that all needless displays of strange constable.s should be avoided.
