WARRINGTON V . BROINIRTON.—PIayed on Saturday, and was a notable reversion of ti,arrington's inconsis- tent play. Messrs. S. M. Crosfield, J. J. Crosfield,Sugg, and others were away. Broughton took their first inn- ings, and after some good bowling by G. Clarke, Pod- more, and Bibby, Broughton were all out for 76. War- rington started with G. Clarke and W. H. Podmore, Payne and Roberts bowling. Runs were freely obtained, and although changes in the attack were made, all came alike to the batsmen, and there was a concensus of opinion that the runs would be obtained without loss. However, disappointment was in store for those who had thus surmised, f;A. at 39 Clarke fell a victim to Payne, whilst two runs later Voisey was also sent back. L. Smith joined Podmore, and the latter hit out merrily, beautiful strokes resulting in boundaries,but at 49 Smith was caught at point. Bibby, however, joinedihis collea- gues,and soon had matters righted,and batting in capital fashion,and in conjunction with Podmore,the Broughton total was gradually overhauled, being ultimately passed after an hour and twenty minutes' batting,and with but the loss of three wickets. The innings was continued, both batsmen showing clever hitting, but at 86 Podmore was bowled. His 43 was a fine effort, and will rank as his best for Warrington, made without a chance, and coming as it did after a good bowling performance, Podmore is to be congratulated on his all-round exhibi- tion. J. Smith joined Bibby, and early showed an aptitude to hit,driving one ball clean (-Alt of the ground. The century was passed,but only exceeded by six when Bibby was bowled by Windsor, his 27 being an invalu- able contribution, and his highest made in first-class cricket. Little interest was taken in the remaining play, but Bolton batted patiently for his runs whilst Smith was bowled on the call of time. Score and bowling analysis :

WAR MN GTO 3 PARISH CH.URCH.
SALE OF WORK AT THE RECTORY.

----- The sale of work at the Rectory garden, in aid of the Warrington Parish Church, was continued oil :Saturday, when it was opened by Mrs. T. H. Lyon, of Appleton Hall.—The Rector in introducing Mrs. Lyon, expressed his gratitude to Mr. Alfred Woods for the exertions he had made on behalf of the church. He would like to thank the friends who had visited them on Thursday for their great liberality. They had realized £2OO that day, which left £lOO yet to be raised. Referring to Mrs. Lyon, the Rector said he did not know whether it was right to expect ladies and gentlemen from the country to come to do so much for town parishes, but they had only to ask them and they would always find them ready to help.—Mrs. Lyon in opening the dayss sale said that there were times when they had to plead for a cause which, though deserving was not very popular, and then it was very bad indeed to be sufficiently eloquent to move anyone to give it Substantial support. But the appeal she was asked to make that day was very different, and needed no apology The noble old church so near them pleaded its swn cause better than she could, and the repairs and improve- ments lately finished were so obviously required, that she need only say that if anyone would only go and see for themselves what had been done, they would return very generously disposed. (Applause.) She was sure that they always felt great pleasure to be able to lighten the labours df the Rector of Warrington, and to help Mrs. Willis in her work amongst them. (Applause.) She would end by saying that as Warrington was never behind in giving assistance to the Church she was sure it would not fail them that day. She had now great pleasure in declaring the sale of work open.( Applause.) —Dr. White moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Lyon ' expressing his pleasure at her presence with them that day.—The vote which was passed with enthusiasm was acknowledged by Mrs. Lyon.—The buying then corn- tnenced, and in another part of the grounds the finals of the tennis tournament,and the tugs of war were brought off. During the afternoon the band of the First Volun- teer Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment played numerous selections of music on the grounds.

div.head: WONDERFUL CITY.
div.p: A WONDERFUL CITY.
ERECTED IN SIX YEARS.

Six years ago there was not a house on the whole of the Witwatersrandt. In November of 1886 a Govern- ment Surveyor, Mr. De Villiers, of Bosliof, Orange Free State, returning for the Christmas holidays from his annual exredition of surveying Boer farms in the Transvaal (previously:farms had never been surveyed,) being defined only by fotir beacons, so many hours horse-ride each from the other, and which gave about 5,009 rnorgen, or 10,000 English acres to each burgher was then intercepted by the then newly formed Trans- vaal Gevernment and 'requested to lay out a township of 800 stands. By February of the following year a second 800 stands had been laid out ; and to-day Johan- nesberg has 40,000 inhabitants, with business premises quite equal in point of architecture to the best English establishments. Stands of the first survey were sold at Is. and 2s. 6d. each—last month one was sold for £ll,OOO.

EVERLASTING GOLD. Approaching Johannesberg, the train passes through the towering head-gear of the various mines, glittering iron roofs, noisy batteries, irnmense heaps of mine tail- ings, into the city created by English brains and money. It is difficult to believe that half-a-dozen years ago this iicepe ef bustling industry was the bare, open veldt— now experts pronounce its mines to be inexhaustible— an opinion confirmed by an increasing output year by year. The city contains first-class hotels, clubs, banks, theatres, and business houses; but there are also 300 inns and drinking canteens—the Government being ap- parently guided by the principle. " Get money, honestly if you can, but get it." There is a free mingling of class with class, and the tone of social and religious life is not high.

div.head: SIGN OF PROGRESS.
div.p: A SIGN OF PROGRESS.

The editor of a local newspaper in two years has had two actions for assault, one libel case, one charge of fraud, perjury, and falsity ; and while I was there he re- ceived a visit from the chorus-girls of a theatre armed with sjamboks and was chastised for an unfavourable comment of their performances. There is an imitatlen of a school board system, but religious intolerance pre- vails.

SOME LOST TERRITORT. English capital has made not only Johannesberg but the Transvaal itself; and the opinions of persons best ablo to form one is that had the operations in gold been delayed only a year or two, the country would inevitably have come into the hands of the English, as its treasury was bankrupt and its Government officials unpaid. Slow though the character of he Boer is,he is not so dens 3as to allow the gold to be excavated from beneath his feet without mating the extractor pay for it, and it is a fazt within my personal knowledge that farms which eight years ago could have been purchased for a couple of hun- dred pounds have since been sold for £lO,OOO and £15,000. Of course, in too many instances shareholders' money has been literally thrown away ; managers, managing directors, and directors who did not manage, played their own little games, with the result that com- panies which counted their capital by hundreds of thou- sands of pounds never paid_otte penny of dividend.
DOW GOLD IS OCT.

The gold bearing Witwatersrandt and 50 miles around is really the watershed of the Transvaal. The gold is obtained by the reef being coarried and broken into pieces about the size of road metal. These are passed along a trough of water ta the stamps—large cylinders of steel lifted up by water power—and allowed to fall on blocks in the ground. The quartz, now pounded into powder, is carried by water to a sieve. The water, full of this fine powder, passes through the sieve and flows over a shallow bath of mercury. The gold,being heavier than quicksilver, sinks into it. The water then spreads, itself over plates of copper, upon which is a coating of cyanide ot potassium and mercury. This detains any gold that has escaped being caught by the first process. The stream subsequently passes over blankets, the hairy surface of which catches any gold that has escaped both processes. To gather the gold the mercury bath is emp- tied, and the sediment in the pit into which the water finally flowed is gathered and put into a retort and heated. The mercury evaporates, and there remains a lump composed of gold, iron, copper, silica, dm. •, the mass is melted, the gold sinks to the bottom, and the other material forms a slag which comes to the surface.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHOD.
div.p: THE PRIMITIVE METHOD.

In the alluvial fields, which are now almost deserted except at Zoutpansberg and a few isolated places, the gold is won in a much simpler way. The soil and gravel are shovelled into carts and conveyed to sluice boxes constructed on the edge of a stream of water obtained from a dam. The bottom of tne sluice-box is either paved with pieces of rough quartz, or ha a wooden grating ; the soil and stones are carefully fed into the stream, the stones regularly forked out, and at intervals the supply of water is turned off, the gratings are lifted, and the gold underneath, in pieces from a pennyweight to in cunce or more, collected. These alluvial fields have at one time formed the bed of a great inland sea or lake, which have been thrown up by a mighty convul- sion of Nature. The stones and the nuggets have all been rounded by the action of water,and have evidently been "shed from the main reef which has lately been Jollowed many miles from Witwatersrandt and, it is said, even into the Orange Free State.

div.head: BOOM:
div.p: A BOOM:

_ Indeed, thelatter may prove as rich in mineral as the Transvaal if the remarkable rise in the value of Tagers- fontein shares—from £5 to £2B (unless it was a gamble) would indicate. The history of the alluvial fields of Reitfontein is remarkable. Four years ago there were from four to five thousand men working on them,and so great was the rush that the Government contemplated a township, and purchased a farm for the purpose. Now there are not more than 200, and the township doss not exist even on paper. An enormous amount of money has been lost by the various companies which were floated in London ; one had a capital of £175,000, and never paid a dividend. The discovery of alluvial deposits was purely accidental. A prospector searching for a continuation of the Witwatersrandt reef, alter a long and patient exploration,came to the conclusion that the main reef did not reach thus far ; and decided on returning home, when one of his boys (all the natives are "boys," even if 60 years of age) brought into the tent a nugget of considerable size. Although since then nuggets ot 270 z.. 3.60 z., and Boz. have been found, the diggings are practically abandoned.

div.head: isttrto to tin etutor.
div.p: isttrto to tin etutor.
THE LA.W : RICH VERSUS POOR.

Sir,—Can it be denied that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor? The decisions of our courts frequently lead us to the conclusion that the maxim is incontrovertible. A man may take his wife on a pleasure trip, bruise her body and blacken her eyes and finally stab her to death ; he has money, he gets ten years—just the time he calculated upon in writing to his paramour, urging patience while he got rid of his wife and spared himself by ten years penal servitude. Cooke the policemen gets hanged for a similar crime, except that the former is the more heinous crime. Fcr contempt of court and the destruction of an important document a Duchess has six weeks confinement in all the luxury that wealth can supply—society, books, music, sump- tuous fare and furnishing. What a farce ! A riell man turns ruffian, he is mulcted in a fine which he pay and laughs at it. A poor scamp goes to prison, and serve him right, but why should not the ricla man be dealt with in a similar manner P Blind justice. Nonsense, she can see well enough and can detect a pocket lined with cash from an empty one. The latest freak of the blind godess—up to date at least—occurred at Scar- borough a few days since. " A lady with means," hail- ing from Cambridgeshire, visited Scarborough and carried on a successful trade in pocket-picking until she was detected in burying six purses in the sand. This led to her apprehension, when she tried to get rid of a postal order she had stolen. In extenuation of her con- duct her advocate pleaded for leniency because she was a lady with means £4BO a year in her own right, and had no need to steal," and therefore should be let down easy, and so she was. She was fined £2s—a flea- bite. She had no need to steal being wealthy,all the more need then that she should be more severely punished. What is a fine of £25 to" a lady with means" and £4BO a year Surely "there is one law for the rich and another for the poor." A poor woman would have got six months, or the sessions. Why should wealth buy this woman off her deserts from being treated like any other ocmmon thief, and have been taught oakum picking and other jail bird accomplishments, which may have a de- terring effect on ocher ladies " with means " who some- times forget the difference between meant and texa.—` am, sir, yours respectfully, July 225th, 1893.
CTMRO.

MINERS' WAGES AND MINING ROYALTIES. Sir,—l am sorry to find that no one has pointed out that there are some circumstances which have been over- looked in connection with the disastrous struggle which has now commenced between the miners and mine lessees. This is a dispute in which the whole nation with the exception of a privileged few, will suffer, and it be- hoves us all to use every endeavour to bring it to an end as soon as possible. Both employers and men make out a good case for themselves, and the public is naturally bewildered as to which side is right. But the fact is that this is simply one of the many cases in which the two adlies and agents in production, Capital and Labour, are falsely placed in antagonism while the enemy of both escapes. If the mine-lessees were the owners of the mines, then we could understand that the fight would be simply one between Capital on the one hand and Labour on the other. In such a case probably both could net be in the right. But such is not the case. Before the mine lessee ctn get at the mineral he has to pay in the first place what is generally called a " Dead rent." This, which varies in amount according to the situatiem of the mine, accessability to markets, quality of minerals, etc., has to be paid whether the mine is worked or not. Then npon each ton of mineral raised to the surface, Royalties of so much per ton have to be paid. If the mineral has to pass over any land not comprised in the lease, " way-leave " is charged ; there are also " water-leaves " for liberty of water course ; "air-leaves" for liberty of air-course for ventilation. From beginning to end the unfortunate lessee has to pay for the privilege of being allowed to dig the mineral out of the earth. . . .

Frequent accidents have Proved that mining is an oc- cupation in which the miners are exposed to terrible dan- gers. At the best, it is an unpleasant, hard task to win these mineral; from the bowels of the earth, and one would naturally expect that the workers in it would be well paid to compensate for the disagreeable and dan- gerous nature of the work. But owing to our Land System, it will be noticed that the more disagreeable or dangerous an occupation is, it does not follow that the better the pay to those engaged in it. In fact the con- trary holds good, the reason being that wages are fixed by the iron law (under present conditions) of supply and demand. _

All these li,yalties and other payments we have enumerated above have to be paid to the landowner by the capitalist before the question of wage to the miner or profit on capital invested are taken into account at a!1; and consenusntly we can perceive that it is quite possible for prices to be so low that the mine-lessee in order to have any profit at all must cut down the already too low, small wage of the miner. It is evident that the proposed reduction will bring that wage belsw the amount upon which men ought in common decency to be expected to live. The miner gives good value in his labour for all he gets. He only receives as wage a portion of the product of his labour. The lessee provides and risks his capital. Both parties have therefore a just claim for a fair return for the value they put in. But what has the owner done. Absolutely nothing. He never put the minerals in the earth, he is simply a drag upon industry. Why there- fore should his so-called 'claim' be given preference. if that pecause he has the good fortune to be the owner of the mineral therefore he ought to have a share in the product, it is evident, that labour and capital aught first to have each a proper recompense, and then, and not till then, the claims of the so-called • owner 'may be considered. The Commission which recently inquired into the mine-rents Ikc., state that about £5,000,000 a year is paid to the owners. I think this is an underestimate and the Committee themselves say that they had no reliable figures to go upon. During the previous coal strike an iron-master wilting to the "Daily News" pointed OUt that while he was paying £7,500 a year to his workmen in wages, he was paying £15,000 a year in Royalties to the land-owner. It is to this point the attention of both labour and capital ought to be directed.—Yours truly, EDMUND K. MUSPRATT
(President of Financial Reform AssnciatiAn). 18, lifaclrn's fley, Liverpool, Aug. 2nd, 1893.

div.head: PICNICS FROM WARRINGTON.
div.p: PICNICS FROM WARRINGTON.

On Monday 20 members of the Boy's Communi- cant's Guild, connected with the Parish Church, proceeded to Chester, accompanied by the Rev. A. A. Markham. A visit was paid to the cathedral, and a', dip" in the river was also indulged in. The party afterwards went by the ferry to Eccles- ton, where tea was partaken of. The return journey was commenced at 6-50 and Warrington was reached at 9-45, all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves. About 30 members connected with the Mothers' Sewing Class at Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission, had a pleasant picnic to Hale on Monday. They were conveyed there in a 'bus supplied by Mr. W. Russell, of Bridge-st. The party left the mission at 10.30, arriving at their destination at 12.30. After dinner the party went down to the shore and enjoyed a refreshing breeze and ramble. Tea having been partaken of, the party sallied forth to view and ad- mire the beautiful village. The village was all astir, it being " club-day." At 7.15 the return jour- ney was commenced. and Warrington was reached about 9.15, all being pleased with the day's outing. About 40 teachers and friends connected with Moly Trinity Sunday School, and Factory Yard Mission, had • a very pleasant and successful excursion to Llangollen on Monday. Amongst the party were the Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton (vicar), Rev. 11.R.Wild (curate), and Mr. Beacon (churchwarden). They departed from Bank Quay Station in a saloon carriage. at 7.30, and arrived at their destination about 10.30. The party at once proceeded to explore the very beautiful neighbour- ' meals—dinner and tea— itien Hotel, the catering ,on. There was a heavy .e earlier part of the after- canal to Berwyn was indulged aid to the Valle Crucis Abbey
_ the Horseshoe Falls, Crow Castle, and various placoi of interest in the neighbourhood. The return journey Was commenced soon afrer ,even o'clock, and all arrived safely home at about 9-43.

The members of the Wycliffe Church choir to the number of 26 journeyed to Cheater on Saturday afternoon, by the 1.40 p.m. train, arriving at Ches- ter at 2.30. The party proceeded to the banks of the Dee where a gondola was in waiting to convey them to Eccleston Ferry. They were afterwards conducted to the residence and grounds of the Duke of Westminster. Tea was partaken of at Ecclestou Ferry. After tea a portion of the party proceeded a little further up the river, calling tor the r.-.main- der of the party at 7.30 in showering rain. On the

. • return journey to Chester, the choir sang several well-known hymns and part songs. Chester was reached at 845, aria after a ramble about the city. the homeward journey was commenced, Warring-. ton being reached at 10.55 p.m.

div.head: AMLETICS.
div.p: AMLETICS.
CRICKET.

It would be quite permissable for any average person to take his lyre (if he hasn't got one he many have the Juvenile Man) and sit on a mossy bank beside a babbl- ing stream and sing to the empyrean fastnesses " Oh what a surprise." It would be wiser and better for him to sing it to the empyrean fastnesses. The notes of surprise weuld relate to the results of the match between Warrington and Broughton on Saturday. In addition to precedent being against our team, we had all the best players away, including the two Crosfields, Smith, Sugg, and others. The team which did go to 13roughton were assured and reassured by all well-wishing friends that they were going to be beaten again. To use the exact phraseology they were told, " o-o-O Awe! What a team ! Well, you will get a licking." Perhaps some of the players felt pretty sure of obtaining a defeat, hut one at least amongst them was sanguine of victory, and that was Mr. G. Clarke, the captain.

Avery extraordinary thing was doneiwhen the teams st.Qt on the ground. Warrington won the toss and Mr. Clarke said to the Captain of Broughton, who is "six feet of good looks," "You go in first." That gentleman locked nonplussed and queried: "Who go in first "Why you, of course." Someone expressed his surprise by recourse to an adjective with a capital d to it. Podniore, the Captain and the other Clark, had arranged this little move, which, though it bore on its face a generously, childishly, simple aspect, was a stroke of neat deplomacy, because the " wicket" would be all the better for Warrington when someone else had been playing on it! Even the 13rrroghton men began to suapect " some dark mystery " by and by, and vowed they couldn't understand such good nature from the team they had arranged to lick. Well, anyhow, they went in and came out for 76 runs. W. H.Podmore came out better than ever in his bowling, and he was given a chance, anyhow. He took five wickets for 44 runs, but four of those wickets were taken for 24 runs. G. Clarke and Bibby also displayed some neat bowling. The Captain wasn't pleased when this innings ended thus— Oh no, not much!

It was when Warrington began to bat that Broughton began to quake and the genial George commenced to bubble. Podmore, one of the first to go in, knocked 43, the largest score of the day, and which, added to his b..wling entitles W. H. P. to considerable congratulation. "Well played thou good and faithful servant," should Mr. S. M. C. say next week, although Mr. Clarke did not see sufficient in it to act as a call upon him to pay ex- penses! This latter is a dark secret only understood by a few. Bibby and G. Clarke both scored over 20 each, whilst Bolton scored 15 which was worth a lot consider- ing the good " cricket " he displayed in compiling the runs.

An interesting, if not a novel match, was played on Tucsday and Wednesday evenings on the Warrington cricket ground. The teams were for Warrington, Pod- more, Bibby, 1.. Smith, Voisey, Proud, Geffin, Dun, Connor, Brown, and Rushworth, and the other team was 16 of tha Warrington Football Club, captained by H. Ashton. "Surefoot " and Tommy Barnes were amongst the ranks of the latter. Warrington had their first in- nings and scored 145. Our Juvenile Man reports that he never saw a pantomime yet that made him laugh more than the way in which the footballers tried to stop or catch balls. Of course this does not say much for the pantos. Still he says it is calculated to induce a seraphic smile when you see a man like " Surefoot " holding his hands 12 inches apart to catch a cricket ball,for it shows that he is thinking of another kind of ball. The football men scored 58 for eight wickets.

The Sankey Wesleyans scored a capital victory on Saturday, when they had the Windsor Wesloyans as visi- tors. They took first innings and scored 101 for the loss *1 eight wickets towards which J. J. Booth scored 25 not out, F. Hardy, and T. Simpson 21 each, and E. Clare 10 The highest Windsor Wesleyan scorer was E. Ewcott who made 19, and then had the misfortune to be hit in the mouth owing to the ball bouncing off the bat, and was unable to finish his innings. Bailey performed a very remarkable feat with the ball taking five wickets in five successive balls, clean bowling three, caught and bowled one, and the fifth being caught by Li2ht, who was fielding in place of Booth who had retired hurt. Simpson claimed the remaining four wickets. Bailey's performance undoubtedly won the match as there were five wickets to fall less than ten minutes off time. San- key Bridges played better in every department than they had for some time previously.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Recently I have been watching with particular in terest the performances of" Bert," or H. J. Dainteth. About every other week he manages to take a prize of moderate value at local sports, and no longer ago than Saturday, at the League of the Cross Festival. Liverpool he took second prize in a two mile race. He is rather young, but of a large frame which, when he has de- veloped strongly, will stand him in good stead in physi- cal recreation. He is the son of Mr. T.Dainteth, Bridge- street, and promises soon to become a conspicuous cyclist in the neighbourhood.

The greatest thing of the season in Warrirgton will certainly be the bicycle championship which is ^oming off at the Football Sports on Monday. There are a great many entries. I have ~ot the hint that Fair and Bellian mean to make this a hard fight, and it is said that Bell an intends to retire if he comes off victorious. Ah well, one never knows Ssme people are content to re- tire when they do not come off victorious.

div.head: FOOTBALL SPORTS.
div.p: FOOTBALL SPORTS.

Providing there is fine weather on MOnday I think the football annual sports will be a success. If they are not it will not be the fault of those who have had to do with the arrangements, anyhow, for I know both from the entries and the prize list,thar. no pains have been spared, and that tho experience brought to bear by Mr. J. E. Warren and others must be productive of good results. I hope that the success will be a financial one because after the distressing rcsults of last winter a stimulus in the way of lucre is necessary. The affair will be a befit- ting prelude to the season which is so rapidly approach- ing. The prizes, to the amount of £lOO have been supplied by Mr. R. Bennett, of Legit-street, and are on exhibition in Messrs. Doinn's shop window in florse- market-street,

Ih6 promotion of sports by football teams is regarded with considerable favour by authorities on the game. The London" Star " for instance takes these sports at Warrington in a very happy manner, and at the conclu- sion of some comments says :—" These Northern foot- ball clubs devote no little of their energy to other popu- lar sports in their times and seasons. They are not merely content with goals and points in the chilly blasts of December and the Ides of March, but set to work promoting their handicaps on foot and wheel in the intervals with the same amount of enthusiasm and energy."

I learn that RoMak. the south of England champiou obstacle racer. has entered in the obstacle .race which forms one of the new features of the sports this year. This race will be one of the finest of the season, for amongst the entries are competitors from all ever the United Kingdom.

div.head: SWIMMING.-THE LADIES' BATH.
div.p: SWIMMING.-THE LADIES' BATH.

After the various dates of opening which were an- nounced and duly withdrawn, the ladies of the town be- gan to give up interest in the ladies' plunge bath. Con- sequently, when the bath was opened for the first time en Thursday there was not a very large number of the sex present—l say the sex, because I mean the sex. But probably, by-and-by,the interest which our civic fathers allowed to flag by their procastmation, will be re- kindled, and, I hope that by the opening of the next ,ason we shall have a ladies' swimming club formed in Warrington.

There 19 one commendable feature which I find in Con- nection with the bath, and that is its depth, which ranges from 2 feet 6 inches to 4 feet 6 inches. This will enable an average sized lady to walk all over the bath, if she cannot swim, and at the same time the shallowness of the water will be no hindrance to any female expert in aquatics. Another thing, when young girls wish to go there to learn to swim they cannot be told—not with much truth. anyhow—that " it is deep, my dear, you musn't go." There will be no occasion for any nervous- ness on the part of either a careful mother or a timid daughter. 'fhe conveniences and fittings of the bath ore of a first class character, and they include a vapour bath.

I made an inquiry this week about the attendances in the male plunge bath. Mere has been a very slight falling off since the first two weeks, but the average at- c-indance is now 2,000 per week. A great preportion of that number is made up of season ticket holders. Good old season ticket holdcrs ; What would the bath be with- out you ? "It would be a quieter spot than at present," suggests the Juvenile Man. He's a trifle too cynical.

div.head: WOMEN AND MICE.
div.p: WOMEN AND MICE.
A GRAPHIC DESCRIPTION.

A correspondent of" Woman " tries to explain why her sex are afraid of mice. She believes that a mouse in the chamber of Marat would have deterred Cnarlotte Corday from her dread purplse. Most women have ex- perienced the sensation. " You are sitting alone. read- ing, playing, writing, painting, or working. Suddenly . you instinctively feel a sensation of horror of some evil infl...ence that is present, bat, as yet unseen. You lilt your eyes. You behold, gliding over the carpet towards you, without noise, apparently without the trouble of walking a mouse. It Stops ; it fascinates you. You drop your book, your music, your brush, your needle, ' whatever it may be, but you make no other sound. You feel your blood freeze, and your limbs slowly paralyse ; your heart stops testing, your breath ceases, a cold .chill creeps over you."

Where my son works at, they have stopped for an indefinite period. My firm has been discharging numbers of men for several weeks, they have ncw stopped one shift, and lam working short time. BOWLING.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB v. WINNINGTON. A main of bowls was played between the above- = med clubs on the Warrington Liberal club green, on Saturday afternoon. The game was 30a side. 15 up in doubles and 11 single. The bowling green was in first-class condition and is considered to be one of the best greens in the district, due chiefly to the exertions of Mr. E. J. Mitchell, manager of the club. It will Ise remembered that when the teams met at Winnington, the home team came out victorious by 70 points. Last Saturday the Warringtonians repaid them with interest, by coming out victors by 138. After the match an excellent tea was provided, to which, needless to say, full justice was done. The visitors left Warrington at 9-30 well pleased with the reception they had met with, and they expressed a wish to come again before the season was over. HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.

The second of the re-opening services in connection with the above named chapel was held on Sunday, on the completion of the renovations. The alterations have cost about £6OO, and £450 have already been received towards that amount. It is proposed to hold a sale of work at a future date to wipe off the debt. The preacher on Sunday morning and evening was Mr. W. 11. llaslam, son of the Rev.l.l.Haalam, of Gittlersome, York- shire. There were good congregations at both services, and the amount collected was £ll 3s. 6d.

THE P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH. The good attendance at the P.S.A. meeting in Wy- cliffe Church is still maintained, and the membership increases week by week. On Sunday afternoon the chair was occupied by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, who deli- vered a short address, in which he expressed himself in hearty sympathy with the movement. The speaker for the afternoon was Mr. Milne, of Sale, who spoke on " Martyrs." Mr. R. Atkinson proposed. that letters of sympathy be sent to two of the members who had been bereaved during the week, which was agreed to. The Rev.J. Clarke, of Chester, also took part in the meeting. The soloist was Mr.. W. H. Wallington, who sang two solos, for which he received well merited applause.

div.head: INVENTION AND LABOR.
div.p: INVENTION AND LABOR.
By Mit. 11.
'WJIITuA.

The "Examiner "recently Rave in a short editorial just a passing glimpse as to what was going on in the world of science and invention. I may add ljust a little to this, more by way of drawing atten- tion to the subject than of saying anything really original. It must be clear tc the most indifferent of observers that we are fast reaching a time when the inventive faculty in man,coupled with scientific developments, will lorce entirely new conditions in the relationship hitherto held between labour and capital. We labourers are much in the habit of talking about grasping capital," and" selfish em- ployers." The fact is, we ignore, or, perhaps we knownothing about the law that twists both em- ployer and employe about pretty much as it likes. As, for instance, there seems to be a panic very much to the front just now in the money markets of the world. It has so disturbed the industrial world that one firm after another is shaking down. Those that are running are discharging half their workmen.

Now how many of those affected, be they em- ployer or employe, could give a clear account of this panic ? Very few, and the politician and law- maker is as dense as the rest of us on the subject. We are in the hands of specialists, and even tnese disagree. If it were not that each nation, like each irdividual seems to find its chief interest in selfish calca'ations we should never have these panics. We should see clearly that this " shrinking" 'globe exists for the benefit of all, and not for a few. But I want to take my fellow workmen along with me inithe search for some of the benefits resulting from 18th century research. We are told, and we only know it from being told, that we are better off now than ever our forefathers were. Of the thousand and one things that go towards making the path of life a primrose bed we should not have the least conception, were it not that the statistician and the politician kindly remind us of it. Sometimes a writer comes to the front and tells a bit of honest truth. Mr. Hobson in the Political Science Quarterly says : that the " net influence of machinery is towards the increased irregularity of employment except in industries where the demand fo . the commodities produced is regular, and the supplies rekihated by the organized action of those who control production.'' Further, "taking into consideration the two prime factors, namely, the number of those employed, and the regularity of those employed, machinery does not favour the in- creased steady demand for labour." I have nothing to say against the use of maohinery, nor against mother nature giving out her secrets at the call of the scientist. Nor yet would I bottle up the inventive faculty. Let all have full play but above all things, we workmen must play our part, so that, as then we shall be able to report pro- gress wticti called upon. I take the above quota- tiors as being a solid fact.; being so, we need seek no further for the supposed benefits supposed to be enjoyed by the labourer generally. Were I asked in what direction is science making its most remarkable developments, I should cer- tainly answer "in the invisible, and almost un- known world of electricity. Copper will, in this case, play a more important part in the wire mills of the world than it has hitherto done. I have no what the copper trade may be in England or on the continent. In the States it is a very large, and important one. For telegraphic purposes cop- per is likely to take the place of iron, as being more durable and suitable, and, as to cost, cheaper in the long run. As we may reasonably look forward to seeing the higl ways converted into electric roads, so we may know that drawn copper trolley wire will be used for haulings and general locomotive purposes. Copper is mined in immense quantities in the U.S. In the State of Montana is the famous Allice copper mine. It has produced millions of dollars' worth of gold and silver, and is now yield- ing large quantities of copper. The Anacunda is another. It was begun as a silver mine, but after running down a distance the lead developed into the biggest copper mines on record. Two thousand miners are employed day and night. Three thou- sand tons of ore are shipped out from the mines daily. Here is seen the finest of improved machinery and all is on a gigantic scale. Here are the biggest smelting works in the world, covering eighty acres of ground The ore producing rock, containing copper, gold and silver, is pounded into a mash with great stamps and then filtered and re,filtered, run through process after process, until it comes out at last in the shape of a metal sand, which is taken to the other a orks and reduced to metal. There are at these works acres upon acres covered with grinding machines, and settling vats. After all these processes the metal is taken into vast rooms where the fames of sulphur make one feel as if one were having bushels of matches burned under one's nose. _ _

Electricity is used to separate the gold and silver from the copper. The gold and silver in these is in such quantities as to leave the copper pure profit. There are about 2,000 smelters employed here at wages averaging 10s. per day. , The owner of this mine is an Irishman. I have gone into this rather lengthy description of a copper mine,because I wish to show the beginning of what I consider will be an industry that will materially affect the wire draw- ing firms of the world in the early future. Of course, there are lots of other copper centres, as on Lake Michigan, where the industry is equally im- portant. houses are now being built in which electri-

city heating does all the work of the usual coal Are. Mr. George Foster Peabody, of Brooklyn, N.V.,has dispensed with coal entirely,and all house- hold operations are now performed by electricity. The house is lighted by electricity, warmed by elec- tric heaters and cooled in summer by electric fans ; the cooking is done and all water heated by electri- city, and the work of ironing is 'rendered easy by the use of electric irsns, no longer "sad." Whenever power is needed,electric motors are employed,as for running a sewing machine or in laundry operations. Electric traction is proceeding here at a great rate. "Networks" of electric lines are being every- where projected. Of long distance line's, that bet- ween Chicago and St. Louis seems to be assured of final success. In Pennsylvania and Ohio there are several lines of over 100 miles in length, that are expected soon to be started, and each week the pro- jects appear to become bolder. As to street railways, it has been impossible for the large companies,even with their facilities increased to the utmost,to any- where nearly equal the enormous demand for the necessary electrical apparatus. Twelve months ago one machine.of which I had charge,turning out five miles of trolley wire a day, was found sufficient.. Now, there are two, with prospects of more,turning out 20 miles a day, improved machinery turning Out more work, but bringinzno more pay. Turning from copper there is bronze, and alumi- num. These are metals now drawn as ordinary iron wire. The aluminum business is a rapidly growing one. The metal is a singularly light one, so 'much so that it can be used for all kinds of art and decoration purposes. It can be put to good solid purpose also. Aluminum horseshoes have been tried with remarkably successful results, it is said, by the Russian government. As an experiment a few horses of the Finland Dragoons were shod with one aluminum shoe and three iron shoes each. The result showed that the aluminum shoes preserved the foot better than the iron ones. None of the aluminum shoes broke and they were used over again for reshoeing. Horses are now shod with this metal at a cost of £2—the set. All the aluminum now being made is made by electrical processes. At present its cost is about 2s. per pound. It is ex- pected in the near future to be down to Is. per lb. An aluminum and a copper rod of the same size would cost nearly the same. The production in the States is about 150 tons a year. The Metal Reduc- tion Co. of Patricroft, Lancashire, produces over 300 lbs. daily. It is also produced at Stoke-on- Trent. I merely make, as it were, passing reference to these matters in the hope of drawing workers' attention to what is going on around us. I don't agitate for eight hours day. I know that the time is near, when the less hours will be.forced upon us. Only workmen must devote their spare time more to study than they have done, or woe betide them. Turning to the June N. A. " Review," I read Mr. Carnegie's article " A Look Ahead." He says coal, iron, and steel, from Glasgow, Newcastle, or Liver- pool, reach the cities of N. Orleans, Richmond,- Boston or Philadelphia cheaper than the same articles can from Pennsylvania, Ohio, Tennessee or Alabama. Turn now, in the same number, to Mr. If allocles article on "Who are the wealth producers." He says :—ln the U.S.the same number of men who in the year 1810 produced wealth to the value of a thousand million dollars a year produce at the present day wealth, to the value of two thousand three hundred millions. This increase he rightly ascribes to scientific invention and discovery, and i-nproyed methods of dividing and improving labour.
r.E.in has for several years been ent!aged upon what he calls an ore-concentrator which will vastly simplify the prevailing method of extracting

div.head: SCIIOOL.
div.p: SCIIOOL.

Thursday was the occasion of the anniversary in connection with the Clergy Daughters' Charities at Warrington. The first part of the proceedings coil- sisted of the annual meeting of subscribers, which was held in Sr.. George's Mission, Hopwood-st. There was not a very large attendance at this gathering. Amongst those who were present were— Mr. H. B. Gilmour in the chair, the Dean of Man- chester (Dr. McClure), Gen. Sir Richard Wilbraham Canon Blackburn, Canon Penrhyn, Canon Postance, Canon Blundell (preacher), Rev. le. W. Willis, Rev. E. C. E. Carlton, Rev. J. A. N. Hibbert. Rev. Charles Lowe, Rev. W. Berridge, and Messrs. W. P. Fulla- gar, James Tinsley, Henry Greenall (treasurer).

div.head: ABSENTVBS.
div.p: ABSENTVBS.

Letters regretting unavoidable absence were read from the Bishops of Manchester, Liverpool, and Chester, and the Ven. Archdeacon Barber, Rev. Canon Gore, Bev. Canon Bridgman, Canon Heywood, and the Dean of Chester.

div.head: TRH CHAPLAIN'S REPORT.
div.p: TRH CHAPLAIN'S REPORT.

The Rector of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis) the hon. secretary and chaplain to the Clergy Daughters' School, in his annual report stated that he had held classes from Advent to Christmas and from Epiphany to Trinity for religious instruction in the collects for the Sundays. After Trinity he had arranged to read with the girls the Book of Genesis, but they had no sooner begun than scarlet fever broke out, and the school -was dispersed for six weeks, from June 9 to July 21, from which enforced vacation they had only just returned. The daily services had been continued without intermission while the school had been in residence. A confirmation was held by the assistant Bishop of Liverpool in the Parish Chureh on Monday in Holy Week, at which eight of the pupils were presented. Of 66 girls, 32, all the confirmed, are communicants. He was much pleased with the conduct and the whole tone ot the school, lie believed there was a most cordial and happy feeling between the girls and their teachers and the clergy. The report was adopted.

div.head: TILE WIDOWS' AND ORPIANS' FUNDS.
div.p: TILE WIDOWS' AND ORPIANS' FUNDS.

The ReVT-6an'On—P;7l4llYN, hon. secretary of the Clergy Widows and Orphans' Pension Fund, read the annual report of the Committee. The Committee expressed their deep sense of the loss they had sustained by the deaths of Canon Greenall, late hon. secretary to the pension fund, Canons MlNeile and Cross, and the Rev. George London. Two members of the Committee, Mr. Railton, of Manchester, and Sir Richard IA ilbraham, had tendered their resignations on the ground of inability to attend and increasing infirmities. It was recommended that the vacancies be filled by the Rev. Richard Green- all, rector of Grappenhall ; Mr. W. W. Woreley Taylor and Mr. John White, of Latchford. No other names had been sent in, and the retiring members of the Committee were re-elected. Since the last anniversary, Canon , Penrhyn further reported two special grants to the amount of £lO had been made. Of those to whom grants were made last year two (from Chester), being in bet- ter circumstances, had decided not to renew tlieir applications and three had died, but there were no fewer than eleven new applications. The meeting would be asked to sanction pensions, dona- tions, and payments for free scholars to the amount of £2,025, and if the Committee's recommendations were approved, there would be upon their list—from Chester, 18 widows and 9 orphans ; Liverpool, 9 widows, and 10 orphans ; Manchester, 30 widows and 18 orphans ; , and free education was provided for six orpisans, two from each diocese. The income of the charity for the year ended December 31, 1892, was £2,069 193. 10d., a decrease of £154 193. 9d.,upon that ot the previous year. It was pointed out that the decrease was mostly in the collections and subscriptions, and an urgent appeal was made for more liberal support from the clergy and general public.—On the motion of the Dean of Manches- ter, seconded by General Sir R. Wilbraham, the report was adopted, and the pensions as recommended agreed to.

div.head: DIVINE SERVICE.
div.p: DIVINE SERVICE.

After the business meeting terminated, a special ser- vice was held in the Parish Church, when the whole of the scholars attended, as well as a large number of clergy and others from different parts of the three dio- ceses. The preacher was the Bee. Canon Blundell, who delivered an effective discourse in which he made an earnest plea for funds to defray the deficit in the ac- counts of the Charity. Ile alluded to the great benefits of the institution, and also to the praiseworthy and noble character of its purpose. At the collection,which was subsequently made, the sum of £l5 2s. 7d. was realised.

div.head: DINNER.
div.p: THE DINNER.

Following divine service the customary dinner was held in the large dining hall at the Clergy Daughters' Schools. Mr. H. B. Gilmour presided, and he was sup- ported by the Dean of Manchester and Sir Richard Wil- braham. After the dessert the toasts of "The Queen," "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the Rest of the Royal Family,"were proposed and duly honoured. "The Bishops and Clergy of the Dioceses" was next sub- mitted by the Chairman. The Dean of Manchester, after alluding in particular to the great responsibilities of the bisheps, went on to consider the position of the institu- tion. First he spoke of the diminished attendance, and said that in the old days that anniversary was counted a great day in the county, and the gentry for miles around were in the habit of attending. They were put up at houses which are now existing no more, and altogether the affair was looked upon as a" jollification." But the now order of things which had come into vogue had infleenced that institulion, and, then agga, Warrington was a town which cild not have its special feature in the salubrity ( of its atniosphere, nor the beauty of its surroundings, and consequently anyone wishing to spend a day in the country might not wish to came here. (Laughter.) With respect to a complaint made that although the Manchester diocese did not subscribe the highestamount of funds it made the largest demand,he had an explana- tion. It was that as a great number of wealthy Manchester people had their businesses and the interests in Manchester, they subscribed to; the Chester funds considerably, througD Churches at Higher Broughton, Alderley Edge, and other places. He did not say one word against this, but he had a suggestion to make whereby the collection of funds would be more equally borne. He suggested that a treasurer and secretary be appointed in every diocese instead of in Liverpool alone as at present. (Applause.) Gen. Sir Richard %Vilbraham proposed "The President" which was duly honoured. Afterwards "The Charity" was proposed by Mr. Gil- mour.—Mr. H. Greenall (treasurer) then nude the fol- lowing statement: -" Since 1884 the income has been graduilly diminishing, while the expenditure has re- mained practically the same. The income in 1884 was £2,870, and had fallen in 1892 to £2,450. The average expenditure since 1884 has been £2,700, being at the present time about £250 per annum in excess of income. The adverse balance began in 1884, being at the end of that year about £3O, and it has gradually grown, until at the end of 1892 it has reached the sums of £745. The school nossesses a fixed income froun investments of about £3OO a year only, and, apart from pupils' pay- ments, is mainly dependedt upon subscriptions and col- lections. A serious falling Off has taken place in these two items, subscriptions have diminished since 1884 by about £9O per annum,and collections by about £l4O per annum. In order to illustrate the real benefit of the school to the clergy, I may state that the actual average cost of each pupil to the Institution is £4O per annum, whiliit the average amount paid for each pupil is about £IB, showing a benefaction of £22 per annum in respect of each pupil." The guests afterwards, for tile most part, attended the sale of work held in another part of the building.

div.head: RIVAL MINERS ORGANIZSTIONS.
div.p: RIVAL MINERS ORGANIZSTIONS.

An action which throws considerable light on the relations between the Miners' Federation and the Sliding Scale Committee in South Wales and Monmouthshire was tried at Glamorganshire Assizes on Thursday. The plaintiff was Mr. W. Abraham, M.P., (Mahon), agent of the Rhondda Miners' Association upon the Sliding Scale Committee. The defendant was Mr. W Brace,the South Wales agent of the Miners' Federation. the latter had uttered in the course of a speech words imputing to Mahon corrupt motives, and implying that he was under the influence of the masters white he was paid to protect the interests of the miners. The defendant had been asked to withdraw and apologise' and had refused to do so, on the ground that what he had said was " the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." The jury found for the plaintiff, and awarded him £5OO damages. , In consequence or a strike on the part of & large body of coal hauliers in South IS-ales, from fifteen to twenty thousand miners were n Thursday compelled unwil- lingly to suspend operations. The ostensible cause of the strike is the delay in publishing the results of the audit, by which wages are regulated under the sliding scale agreement ; but the colliers openly attribute it to the influence of the Miner's Federation.

In the action by the • Official 11..ceiver id the Anglo- Austrian Printing. 3 n4l Publishing Union against Mr. Agg-Garcine7, M P., Sir Henry Isaacs, and other direc- tors, to recover £lOO,OOO improi;erly paid to Mr. Bottom- ley, it was mutually arranged to-day that Mr. Agg,- Gardner should pay £5.000, and hp exonerated from further liability. the Judge thought he had acted iu an honourable manner. The actioa against Ulu other directors will proceed.

div.head: TEARS OF PENITENCE AT THE BOROUGTT COURT.
div.p: TEARS OF PENITENCE AT THE BOROUGTT COURT.
"ORDINARY DRUNKS."

No class of" business" clai'ms half so much time and attention of the magistrates of Warrington as the drunken cases. The following two cases came before the Bench on Wednesday last, and are simply typical " drunks.".

Ais'atiiVnamed Martin Coleman took the first " inn- ings." He seemed to do so with reluctance. He was a forlorn, lost looking man of about 40 ; slightly built with , ragged uneven hair, sunken ch;eks, and eyes which were wan and expressionless. He seemed to be in a state 'of stupification from the previoui night's carouse. He wore a blue serge shirt that did not fit him, and a jacket which, like that of a more virtuous person, was of many colours—blends from iron rust, gas-tar stains, and other colouring ingredients resorted to by tramps. When the clerk called to him " Martin Coleman," the person of travels reciprocated with. " Ye-yes. I'm him." "Then stand in the box." " Which is it."
" This is it" said att officer taking hirn by the part of his coat where there used to be a collar, and helping him Into the box.
" Now," resumed the Clerk, " you are charged with drunkenness in Sankey-st., yesterday. Are you guilty or not? "
Coleman paused and thought for some moments. Then his eyes closed slightly as though he remembered he wanted to go to sleep. . .

" Look lire ! Are you guilty or not 2" He wakened up with a start and murmured "Me ? . . . oh, well, or But a constable was put in the box without further ado, and he stated that the defendant was drunk the day before, and acting in a disorderly manner. A complaint had been received from a lady and gentleman in a trap, that they had been insulted by the defendant. " Now thenl" said the Clerk, "have you anything to say to that ? " " N-o. That is, not anythin' that's particular." " Do you want to ask the constable any questions." " Yes, certainly. Was I drunk ? " " You saw me." yes." " 811te of it P " Yes."

"Welt, that's rum. You saw-- but meybe yen ditidt. eh 2 Meybe-- "Then he stopped again, and looked stupid and dreamy and far away. The Chair- I man said, " We shall have to fine you ss. and costs or 14 clays.". " But I can't pas—don't send me to jail! don't! " His style had changed, and tramp though he was, he I evidently felt his position keenly, or he was a good actor, for his face looked pathetic now. Tears streamed from his eyes at the thought of prison, and ran along his nose' and stood there in their humbleness for a time, and then fell into space. Further supplications avniled nothing for he was taken into the cells. Next a married pair, named John White and Bridget White, of Dial-st., were charged with drunken and dis- orderly conduct. They were man and wife. The woman looked quite 60, and she was sparely built, with a thin face and disordered grey hair. Her husband stood in contrast as a man nearly six feet high,broad of shoulders, big-faced, with a long beard. The evidence given by a policeman was to the eff,:ct that the male prisoner was , creating a disturbance in Dial-st.,the previous night. He I had got hold of a man named Kelly and wanted to fight I him. The officer took him into his house, and was about ' to go away when White came out again and expressed the intention of " Spoiling Kelly's beauty." At the same time the female defendant appeared at the bed- room window and shouted at the. constable, and said her husband was a " wasterell." The officer commenced to take White into custody, but his wife followed and became so passionate, and so noisy, that they had to place her in a cell, ton. . . . .

Without waiting for an invitation to give her story, the woman rapidly and passionately accused the police of having " thrown her into the cold cells, and kept her time all night with nothing but a skirt and a chemise on, for she had left her bed to see 'after her husband." She said it was 'a shameful act ot injustice,and then worked down into more sentimental words, and finally burst into a flood of tears. At this sign a young woman rushed from amongst the spectators—she was crying too. Both women stood near each other sobbing; the father uttered never a word, but gazed steadily into the depths of his hat. The,Bench were a trifle perplexed, but finally they discharged the woman, and fined the man 54. and costs, or seven days imprisonment. fie pleaded for time to pay it, but it was refused ; and after gazing at his sob- bing wife and child for a moment, he moved silently off to the cells.

div.head: TALKING CANARY.
div.p: A TALKING CANARY.

A lady correspondent of "Nature Notes," while staying I recently in the little village of Churchill, Somerset,heard a talking canary. The bird belongs to a Mrs. Buckland, wife of a gardener, living in Churchill. " Joey " came into her possession when only six weeks old, and she, bring much alone in her house, got into the habit of constantly talking to him. When about a year old he one day quite suddenly began t. talk, and has talked in- cessantly until the present day,he being now eight years His repertory is not extensive, consisting of the remarks addressed to him by Mrs. Buckland—" Pretty Joey," "Kiss me," " Missus's pretty little Joey," and " I be missus's pretty little beauty, I be." He speaks in a beautifully clear, melodious trilling voice, all the words being perfectly distinct. "He talked incessantly,' writes the lady, " while I was in the room, interspersing his remarks with the usual canary's song. Mrs. Buck- • land has b,,eri offered considerable sums, both for the bird and for the loan of him for exhibition, but nothing would induce her to part with him."

div.head: CAIRO-ST. UNITARIAN CUAPEL.
div.p: CAIRO-ST. UNITARIAN CUAPEL.

On Sunday the Rev. B. Negarker, a minister of the Brahmo Somaj, of Bombay, preached two sermons at Cairo-st. Unitarian Chapel. His evening subject was on the " Progress of thought in India," being an exposition of the development of religious ideas in the Hindoo mind. The preacher traced the conception of God in nature as expressed in the Vedas in the very childhood of the race, then to the Upasishad conception, which sought out the attributes of God, marking the second stage of evolutionary thought ; then to the origin of the Bralimanical writings, which marked the ritualistic period, and on to the reform of Buddha, which sought , to restore their religion to a moral and spiritual basis. Tracing the development throught the period of their prophetical writings which had become theistic,he spoke of Christ's theism and teaching of the Fatherhood of God, and its corrollary,the brotherhood of man,as the highest expression of the spirituality of the Eastern mind. Re- ferring to the spread of Mahomedanism, it was mainly owing to its monotheism as opposed to the pantheistic teaching of the Western races. Just as the world ack- nowledged its indebtedness to Rome for its laws and
governm-ent. and N Greece for its arts an-d•Phi-lo‘s.o-p-h.y-a, so it would have to acknowledge its indebtedness to In- . .

dia and the East for its spirituTility and its conception-(:)f God, as the spiritual creator of the universe. In its pure theism was taught the unity of God, the universality of truth, and its adaptability to all the varying conditions of time, peace, and circumstance, and to the harmony of all Scriptures excluding the orthodox Christian's idea, that the whole truth had been confided to their care and keeping. To such a narrow limitation of Scripture the Eastern mind revolted altogether, and in a few graphic touches of Orientalism, he dismissed this Western ex- clusiveness of' God's love and truth as a continued cruci- _ . .
fixion of Christian thought, which blinded professing Christians to the real mission and work of Christ.
BOARD SCHOOL!

The annual school sermons were preached at Padgate on Sunday in Christ Church. The pulpit was occupied in the morning by the Rev. B. Percival, vicar of St. Peters, Warrington, who preached to a large congrega- tion. In the evening the Rev. H. I. Wadeson, 8.A., rector of Croft, occupied the pulpit, and preached to a crowded congregation from the words" Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth " In appealing for the support of those present towards the schools, he said that they stood at a crisis in their day schools. There was much to exercise the minds of Christian men. .1 here had come into use lately a system of free education by which any man Might claim for his child an education free of cost to himstlf. This was very good. But vol- untary schools had found a difficulty in carrying on during past years, and this increased their difficulty,and in many districts bid fair to .be the death blow to some schools. There was a danger unless Churchmen spoke out with a certain voice, of the School Board becoming universal. Would they like to see their children brought up without having instilled into their minds those prin- ciples of religion which they held so dearly ? They might say they had not all the truth, but he believed they had the body or it. The Roman Catholics had the right to bring up their children in their own faith. Were they then going to submit lightly ? The enemies of the Church were trying to tear that right from their hands. Let them speak in no uncertain way, and thus support the Church they loved. The anthem was " W hat are these that are arrayed in white robes and whence came they ?" the difficult treble solo being admirably ren- dered by Master T. Beevers. The Vicar was assizted in the conduct of the morning's service by the Rev A. A. Markham, 8.A., from the Warrington Parish Church. Mr. Blackwell presided at the organ during the day and deserves special mention for his training of the clicir who sang with great credit, The offertories were in aid of the day and Sunday schools. ST. JAMES CHURCH.

The annual dedication festival was celebrated in the above-named church on Sunday. At the morning-, ser- vice the pulpit was occupied by the Vicar (Rev. F. Slater). The curata (Rev. A. V. C. llorden) delivered an address at the children's flower service in the after- _
noon. The Rector of Warrington (Rev. F. W. Willis) preached to a large congregation in the evening. Col- lections were taken in aid of church expenses.

div.head: REMARKABLE PLAGUE OF WASPS.
div.p: A REMARKABLE PLAGUE OF WASPS.
A SALVATIONIST PICNIC ATTACKED.

Since Monday week thousands of Metropolitan juve- niles connected with the Salvation Army have been taken into the country for a day's outimr,and have been accompanied by many of the adult" officers". and "sol- diers." Petersham l'ark was chosen for one of the last of these outings, and a tea, provided by subscription among the members and friends of the Army,was placed upon the tables in the afternoon—jam, fruit, and cake being included among the edibles. The children had just seated themselves, and were making a vigorous onolaught upon the good things before them, when an , immense swarm of wasps appeared and settled upon the ' whole of the sweet stuff with which the tables were laden ; jam, fruit, and cake being literally covered with the insects. While thousands of wasps were thus busily engaged others made an attack upon time children them- selves, severely stinging some of them upon the hands sind face, and in a few cases actually flying into the Mouth, with the result that one little fellow was badly stung in the throat. The children fled in alarm from the tables,while the wasps remained for a time iw undis- puted possession of their contents. A "council of war" 1 having been held,some af the ;nen gallantly charged the tahlcs,covered the cake with cloths,and, seizing the pots ' of jam, ran with them to some of the trees, the branches I of which they bedaubed with the preserved fruit with a view to drawing the wasps away. This had the desired effect, and in a short space of time the jam-laden branches were thick with the insects, while the tables became almost deserted. But tie happiness of the juve- niles had been sadly marred, their tea being well-nigh spoilt, and their swollen hands and faces showing, in many cases, that they had been badly stung. Asa proof of the presence amongst us of a very dis- tinct wasp plague (writes a correspondent of the "Stan- dard" from Chelmsford). I may mention that my gardener has within a few weeks destroyed forty-one wasps' nests within a radius of 300 yards of my house. If a few people in the neighbourhood infested as we have been would combine, and pay an intelligent man to follow up the wasps, great relief would ensue.

Mr. J. P. Mearns,:the president of the St. Helens Fo ball Club, on Wednesday night, entertained at th• Well- ington Hotel, the members of the committee and others connected with the club to dinner. Mr. Me trns was heartily congratulated on his recovery from his recent accident. An excellent programme of music was gone through by the talented vocalists connected with the club.
